COMMENTARY OF THE BLESSED THEODORET ON THE VISIONS OF THE PROPHET DANIEL. PREFACE.

If it were easy for everyone to unfold the oracles of the divine prophets, to get past the surface of the letter, dive down into its depths and hunt out the pearl of meaning hidden there, it might perhaps reasonably have been thought superfluous to set down an interpretation of them in writing, since everyone would readily grasp the prophetic sense just by reading the text.

But we have all received one nature without all receiving equal knowledge. ("For to each," it says, "is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good: to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit," and all the rest is likewise distributed by apportionment.) So I think I am doing nothing unreasonable if I hand on written instruction to those unacquainted with these divine writings. I have been nourished on them from childhood, and I have gathered some small knowledge from many pious writers. Indeed, the divine law commands us to teach our descendants what we have learned from our fathers: "You shall teach them," it says, "to your sons and to your sons' sons." This is why the great teacher David too says, "Give heed, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter riddles from of old." Then, showing where he learned these things, he says, "What we have heard and known, and what our fathers have told us, has not been hidden from their children, for another generation." And teaching the source of this knowledge he says, "For he established a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, to make them known to their sons, so that another generation might know them, sons yet to be born, and they will arise and declare them to their sons." And showing the benefit of this teaching he adds, "That they may set their hope on God, and not forget the works of God, and may seek out his commandments." Since we have received this teaching from the fathers, then, we owe a just debt to those who have come after us and those who are yet to come, and it is fitting to repay it gratefully. Nor is it only the divine law that rouses us. Many of our distinguished friends have also urgently entreated us and compelled us to venture on this contest. Come then, let us make the prophecy of the most divine Daniel as clear as we possibly can to those who do not know it. Perhaps this labour will not be useless even to those who have been granted knowledge. Either they will find more than they had thought, or, finding their own ideas in ours, they will confirm through this agreement what they had hunted out for themselves, for the assent of a greater number somehow tends to strengthen what has been understood. We are attempting to interpret this prophet at present not because we despise the others (far from it! We know that all of them are instruments of the divine Spirit), but first

because our friends asked us for an interpretation of this one, and we think it fitting to grant those who asked the favour for which we were asked. Second, the folly and shamelessness of the Jews lead us to leave the others aside for now and to lay bare this prophet's predictions and make them plain. They have gone so far in shamelessness that they cut him off from the choir of the prophets and strip him of the very title of prophet. Their trick is shameless, but not without purpose. He foretold the coming of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ far more clearly than all the others. He not only foretold what Christ would do but also stated the time in advance, set down the number of years until his coming, and plainly listed all the miseries that would overtake the Jews themselves after their unbelief. So, being hateful to God and enemies of the truth, they naturally dare to say shamelessly that the one who uttered these and countless other oracles is not a prophet, thinking their own denial enough to confirm the lie. It is no wonder that men who raged against the Only-begotten slander the Master's loyal servants, for the second follows from the first. That is why the Lord says, "If they persecuted me, they will persecute you too." And again, "If they called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more those of his household?" To refute their shamelessness more than amply, let us put this question to them: What do you say is proper to a prophet? They might perhaps answer that it is to foreknow and foretell the future. Let us see, then, whether blessed Daniel did not learn these things beforehand and foretell them. Let us set aside for the moment what he says about Christ the Master and bring his other prophecies forward. We find that he foretold much about the kingdom of the Babylonians, much about those of the Persians and Macedonians, and much about that of the Romans. He foretold what the king of the Babylonians would suffer and how the Persians would take over his kingdom. Then he foretold that the Macedonian who would destroy the Persians would himself die very quickly, and that four would inherit the kingdom in place of one. He foretold that someone sprung from one of these would inflict countless terrible things on the Jews, and that with God's help they would be delivered from his savagery. Then, moving on from there, he foretells the might of the Romans, and that they will conquer all the kingdoms and collect tribute from all. What need is there to tell how much he foretold about the kings of the Egyptians and

of the Syrians? He foretold the terrible things they would do to one another, the peace treaties after that, the intermarriages and family ties, and then the implacable wars again after the reconciliation. How, then, is it not impious and unholy to banish from the choir of the prophets the man who foreknew and foretold all these things and left a written record of them? If these things are foreign to prophecy, what is proper to prophecy? But if they deny him membership in the company of the prophets because he does not put "Thus says the Lord" before his own words, let them tell us what Abraham the patriarch said of that sort, that the God of all should call him a prophet. For it was said of Abraham, "And now give the man back his wife, for he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you will be saved, you and all your house." And the blessed David says concerning him, his son and his grandson, "God rebuked kings on their account, saying: Do not touch my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm." And Samuel, the greatest prophet, who served in the temple from childhood, did not have the same form of prophecy as the other prophets. He too received foreknowledge, insights and predictions through dreams or through certain revelations by day. Fight openly against these men too, then, and plainly cast them out of the assembly of the prophets. But if you shrink from such drunken insolence against them, refrain also from slandering Daniel. For he is a prophet. He is a prophet who received knowledge of the future through yearning and longing for it, and who was taught what was to come through sweat and toil, fasting and hardship. He learned in advance, and taught in advance, not only what would happen to the Jews but how the common affairs of the whole world would be ordered. Consider, then, whether it is not utterly unjust to count among the prophets Obadiah, who foretold the evils that would befall the Idumeans alone, and Jonah and Nahum, who prophesied about a single city, Nineveh, while denying the title of prophet to blessed Daniel and calling him a stranger to spiritual grace. Yet he prophesied not about one city or a small nation, but about the greatest kingdoms, the Chaldean, Persian, Macedonian and Roman, and about what they would do in turn. And indeed, ungrateful as you are, you ought to have felt shame before Nebuchadnezzar,

that impious, savage barbarian, uninitiated in divine things, who cried out about Daniel and said, "The holy Spirit of God is in him." For it truly was the work of the divine Spirit both to tell a dream that someone else had seen and forgotten and to reveal its interpretation exactly and truly. Yet not even this persuades you to put an end to your madness against the prophet. Through the prophet you are waging war on the prophet's Master. But the prophet will suffer no harm from your schemes. The divine Scriptures show him to be a prophet, and the fulfilment of his prediction confirms his foreknowledge. Now that we see the events, we understand those ancient oracles, and guided by the events themselves we easily come to grasp them. You, though, display your own drunken insolence even through these things. For now we have refuted your shamelessness in summary form; the detailed interpretation will expose your folly more clearly. Come then: having sufficiently made both our own defence and our accusation against the Jews, let us first make clear the subject of the prophecy and then take up the interpretation word by word.

After Josiah (who was a pious king), his son Jehoahaz reigned over Judea for three full months and a few days. He had two names. In Kings and Chronicles he is called Jehoahaz, but the blessed prophet Jeremiah calls him Shallum. Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, took him prisoner and led him away captive to Egypt. In his place he appointed his brother Eliakim as king and renamed him Jehoiakim. Jehoiakim reigned eleven years and a few months. In the third year of his reign Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, marched against him and took captive no small number of those distinguished by noble birth. He also took some of the sacred vessels consecrated to the divine services, imposed tribute on Jehoiakim and departed for Babylon. Then, when Jehoiakim refused to pay the tribute laid on him, he marched against Jerusalem again, took the city and killed him. In his place he made his son king, whom the Jews called Jehoiachin, but who was renamed Eliakim.

The blessed prophet Jeremiah calls him Jeconiah: "As I live, says the Lord, even if Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, I would tear you off from there and hand you over to those who seek your life, whom you dread, into the hands of the Chaldeans." When he had ruled the kingdom for three months and a few days, Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, again sent an army and a general. He led Jeconiah away captive to Babylon and entrusted the kingdom to Zedekiah, his uncle on his father's side. Zedekiah reigned eleven years and then failed to pay the tribute imposed on him. So the king of the Babylonians marched against Jerusalem with a large force and besieged it, using famine as his ally against them. He brought siege engines against the walls and breached the wall. He killed most of the people, enslaved the rest and led them away captive, and gave both the city and the temple over to the fire. But the God of all, who allowed the Jews to suffer this because of their great lawlessness, did not strip them entirely of his care even while punishing them. To those in Judea he had given tutors, as it were: Uriah son of Shemaiah, and Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, a man illustrious in priesthood and prophecy. With those carried off captive to Babylon in the first captivity he sent blessed Daniel and his companions, Ezekiel, Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael. In this way, having exact teachers of the way of life under the law, they would not suffer great harm from mixing with the barbarians, but would have models to remind them of their ancestral virtue and wisdom. So great is the providence the God of all exercises for sinners! For their benefit he allowed those who served him loyally and were always eager to worship him to be led away captive, to endure harsh slavery, to fall into many dangers and to travel through life amid waves and surging seas. This is why he also says through the prophet Hosea, "I have slain the prophets for your sake by the word of my mouth." In the same way, while working out the salvation of the world, he allowed the holy apostles to suffer the sufferings that are on record. Exercising this providence for the Jews, he also arranged for blessed Daniel and his companions to go to Babylon with them. Daniel, who was young

and shone in the bloom of youth, was brought up in the palace with the God-loving youths. From childhood the divine grace blossomed in him, and he became full of every kind of wisdom and understanding. He gained great freedom of speech with the ruler, and by proclaiming the word of true religion he became the source of benefit to him. Nor did he benefit the king alone, but all his subjects as well. What the king learned through Daniel's teaching he passed on to his subjects, making a law that expressly commanded everyone under his rule to worship the God whom Daniel honoured. We have now stated briefly when this inspired prophet was carried off to Babylon, why, and how many good things he brought about, not only for his own people but also for the barbarians. We will set out the force of the prophecy more exactly in the detailed interpretation. So, calling on divine grace to help us toward clarity, let us begin.

here, that Nebuchadnezzar, having become king, made his expedition against the Jews as the third year of Jehoiakim's reign was drawing to a close. At the beginning of the fourth year the prophet Jeremiah, exhorting the people, said that this year was the first of King Nebuchadnezzar. And blessed Daniel, having said that the first captivity took place in the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, now adds, "In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar he dreamed a dream." He did not add these things idly, but so that we might learn the time exactly. This is also why the divine prophets record the number of years when they mention kings. "In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, then, he dreamed a dream, and his spirit was troubled, and his sleep left him. (2) And the king gave orders to summon the enchanters, the magicians, the sorcerers and the Chaldeans, to tell the king his dream." God's plan is clear to those with understanding. Wishing to make his own prophet known to the king through the dream, so that the king might receive good and saving counsel from it, he frightens him with the dream but takes away his memory of it. But just as the providence of the God of all is plain, so the king's derangement is obvious to all the pious. For how is it not the height of madness to ask others to recall your dream? Nevertheless, when summoned, it says, "they came and stood before the king." (3, 4) "And the king said to them, I dreamed a dream, and my spirit is troubled to know the dream. And the Chaldeans spoke to the king in Syriac and said, O king, live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will declare its interpretation." Their request was indeed reasonable, but their promise was boastful, for it is beyond the human mind to interpret divine revelations without help from above. The Chaldeans spoke in Syriac because they had been gathered from various nations, each of which had its own language while all shared Syriac in common, and they wanted to show that their answer was consistent. But even so they did not persuade the arrogant king to stop demanding of human beings what is beyond nature. (5, 6) "For the king answered at once and said to the Chaldeans, The matter has gone from me. If you do not make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you will be destroyed, and your houses

[Eze]kiel and each of the other prophets for the most part used this opening for their prophecy. This, then, is enough both to refute the lawlessness of the Jews and to show that he is truly a prophet

(2) "And the Lord gave Jehoiakim, king of Judah, into his hand, along with some of the vessels of the house of God." This too shows his spiritual grace. Not everyone is able to know the divine plans. But Daniel, who had been granted the divine Spirit, both knew clearly himself and teaches others that the city was captured, and some of the sacred vessels came into the enemy's power, because the God of all permitted it on account of the lawlessness and great impiety of the people and the king. And he had very good reason to write, "The Lord gave Jehoiakim, king of Judah, into his hand." He wanted no one to suppose that Nebuchadnezzar had overcome the city consecrated to God by his own power. Instead, everyone was to learn precisely that the city fell to the enemy because God had given it up and withdrawn the grace that had long guarded it. The God of all himself makes this clear through the prophet Isaiah when he says, "Shall the axe boast without the one who chops with it? Shall the saw exalt itself without the one who draws it?" By these words he teaches that he himself brings punishments upon human beings, but uses instruments suited to the purpose. "And he brought them," it says, "into the land of Shinar, to the house of his god, and he brought the vessels into the treasure house of his god." Someone might perhaps say, "Why, when it was human beings who had sinned, were the holy vessels consecrated to God handed over to impious men?" Those who say this do not know the purpose of God's plans. "For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him; but the spiritual man judges all things," as the divine Apostle says. The spiritual man is convinced that nothing is arranged by divine providence in vain, and, enlightened by the divine Spirit, he also learns the reasons. So too in the present question, anyone who chooses to understand spiritually can learn the answer. For great benefit came from this, not only to the Jews but to the barbarians themselves. First, the Jews were taught that the divine nature needs nothing. The God of all does not accept what human beings offer as though he needed it. Rather, he accepts it to teach them gratitude and to give them an opportunity to serve him and make some return. For how else could we have repaid God our benefactor, as far as we are able, for the benefits we have received, unless the

…would he accept these few and paltry things from those who offered them? Wishing, then, to persuade the Jews that he accepted the sacrifices they offered not to supply any need of his own but in condescension to their weakness, he rightly turned away from them and handed them over to captivity, and he gave the vessels they had offered, by which they thought they were serving him, into captivity along with them. For if he handed rational beings over to punishment, why would he spare lifeless things? Through the events themselves he also teaches them that they differ in no way from the Babylonians, the barbarians, the impious. They are as impious as the Babylonians, or rather more so. The Babylonians had neither received the law nor enjoyed the guidance of prophets, and so were held fast by ignorance. The Jews, though enlightened by countless prophets old and new and eyewitnesses of countless miracles, despised the God of the universe and went on serving lifeless idols. So he handed the vessels over to the barbarians, all but saying through the events themselves: "You differ in no way from the barbarians. You too defile these things for me by your lawlessness, just as they do, and it is all the same whether you have them or the Babylonians, for impiety rules both you and them." This was enough to convict the Jews, to discipline them, and to win them no small benefit. As for the Babylonians, so long as they honored the vessels, as they supposed, by putting them beyond human use and dedicating them to the gods they worshiped, they suffered nothing painful at all. But when King Belshazzar dared to use them at a feast, he was punished on the spot and paid the penalty he deserved. Through that punishment he taught everyone how great is the power of the God of those vessels, and that God had not been robbed of his own property against his will but had willingly given it up because of the people's great lawlessness. He had done the same long before with the ark. When Hophni and Phinehas, the lawless and abominable sons of Eli the priest, took it and went out to help their kinsmen, God exposed their impiety. He judged them unworthy of any providential care and handed them over to the slaughter they deserved, and the ark to the Philistines. In this way he again instructed Israel, teaching that he had no need of the ark but had made it for their sake, and that it was of no use to people who fearlessly transgress the divine law and choose to live in impiety. But he did not want the Philistines to grow proud, as though they had prevailed over God, for they thought the ark was itself the God of the Jews, taking the making of their own idols as proof. Nor did he want them to

bring great harm on themselves by this, as though they had taken the God of the Jews captive and dedicated him to their own gods as a kind of trophy. So he caused Dagon, the idol they worshiped, to fall and be shattered before the ark. The idol displayed the posture of worship, confessed its defeat by the event itself, and showed that the demon dwelling in it was a slave, and this happened not once but twice and many times. He also brought various plagues on them until they returned the ark and dedicated votive offerings that pointed to their punishment. So the benefit was twofold both then and in the case of Nebuchadnezzar: the brief permission granted by God benefited not only the Jews but the barbarians as well. 3, 4. "And the king told Ashpenaz, his chief eunuch, to bring in some of the sons of the captivity of the sons of Israel, both of the royal seed and of the phorthommim: young men in whom there was no blemish, handsome in appearance, understanding in all wisdom, knowing knowledge and wisdom, and discerning in prudence, who had strength in them to stand in the king's house, and to teach them the letters and language of the Chaldeans." The God of the universe chose the foolish things of the world, the weak and the despised, to put the wise and the powerful to shame through them. Human beings, however, look for beauty of body, stature and strength, and for wisdom, not the kind that knows divine things but the kind adorned with eloquence. From this, then, one can learn how wide the gap is between the divine and the human. The king's arrogance shows in his wanting to take as servants not only the other captives but even those of royal descent. Yet here the prediction Isaiah made to King Hezekiah is fulfilled. "Hear," he says, "the word of the Lord of hosts which he spoke to me: Behold, days are coming, and they will take everything in your house, and all that your fathers have gathered up to this day will come to Babylon, and they will leave nothing, said God. For they will also take some of the children you will beget, and make them eunuchs in the house of the king of the Babylonians." Blessed Daniel reminds us of this prophecy when he says that the king ordered him to bring in some of the captivity of the sons of Israel, both of the royal seed and of the phorthommim. In the Hebrew tongue he called [?] phorthommim, and Symmachus translated phorthommim as "chosen ones."

5, 6. "And the king assigned them a daily portion from the king's table and from the wine he drank, and ordered that they be brought up for three years, and that after this they should stand before the king. And among them, of the sons of Judah, were Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael." Here he teaches us the king's generosity: he did not provide cheap food fit for slaves, as one would for captives, but ordered them to enjoy the royal table. A little later he teaches their own self-control and ascetic wisdom. He does this not out of vanity but to set out instruction for the benefit of those who choose to be benefited. One can also see his modesty. He had said above that the king ordered young men to be chosen from the royal seed, radiant in beauty and outstanding in stature. Yet here, when he sets down their names, he mentions only the tribe of Judah and conceals their kinship with the royal house. 7. "And the chief eunuch gave them names: to Daniel, Belteshazzar; to Hananiah, Shadrach; to Mishael, Meshach; and to Azariah, Abednego." Some people regard this too as a right of masters. When they buy servants they change their names, so that the change of name will also mark their servitude. The chief eunuch did the same here: he took away their Hebrew names and gave them Chaldean ones, since the king had also ordered the young men to learn the language of the Chaldeans. 8. "And Daniel resolved in his heart not to be defiled by the king's table and by the wine he drank, and he asked the chief eunuch that he might not be defiled." Those who love God do not seek the God who is over all in one place only. Wherever they go they offer him the same service, and even in misfortune they worship their own Creator in the same way. Here one may find something truly extraordinary. These boys had been brought up among the Jews and taught the worship of God that was tied to one place. Then they were living in a foreign land, forced into slavery while still very young and compelled to live under other laws, and yet they were eager to keep their ancestral piety. They saw that the Babylonians defiled the food by invoking idols over it and polluted the wine with libations. So they disregarded the safety that lay in plain view, trampled on the pleasure of the royal banquet, and begged the chief eunuch to allow them to decline the royal food.

9. "And God brought Daniel into favor and compassion before the chief eunuch." Divine care follows our intentions: as soon as they chose divine things, they enjoyed divine help. One can find the same thing happening with Joseph: "For the Lord," it says, "was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man, and he poured out mercy on him and gave him favor before the jailer." From this, too, we learn that God has never left any who believe in him without his care. That is why another prophet cries out: "Ask the generations that came before you: who ever trusted in the Lord and was put to shame?" 10. "And the chief eunuch said to Daniel: I fear my lord the king, who appointed your food and your drink, in case he sees your faces looking gloomier than the youths of your own age, and you make my head forfeit to the king." The chief eunuch's fear was not unreasonable. He was a man who had not tasted spiritual grace. He looked at human affairs in a human way and thought that bodies could be nourished and flourish only on costly foods. So he feared that, with the others richly fed and these living ascetically, some difference would show in their faces, and he would suffer the ultimate punishment from the king who had ordered the opposite. When blessed Daniel saw that he was afraid, he turned his appeal to Amelsar, whom the chief eunuch had appointed guardian over him and over Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael. He says: 12, 13. "Test your servants for ten days, and let them give us seeds to eat and water to drink. Then let our appearance and the appearance of the youths who eat from the king's table be seen before you, and deal with your servants as you see fit." Nothing is stronger than faith in God. One can learn this from many places, and not least from the words of the divine Daniel. He believed and was confident that he would enjoy God's favor, and that by not eating the royal food he would look more comely, more handsome and sturdier than those who ate it, lived in luxury and enjoyed royal splendor. What greater piety could there be than that? He also skillfully blended persuasion into his entreaty. "Test your servants," he says, "for ten days,

and let them give us seeds to eat and water to drink." You yourself be the judge of our faces. If you find that such food does our bodies any harm, you may order whatever seems best to you, and we will not object. Such was the care this divine man had for the divine laws from childhood, and such was his faith in the Lawgiver. He said these things, and the other accepted his entreaty. 14, 15. "For he listened to them," it says, "in this matter, and tested them for ten days. And at the end of the ten days their appearance was seen to be good, and they were stronger in flesh than the youths who ate from the king's table." This divine prophet obtained what he wanted and proved his promises true to the man entrusted with their care. Because they enjoyed divine grace, they looked much better than those who enjoyed the royal table. 16. "And Amelsar took away their dinner and the wine they were to drink, and gave them seeds." He gained a twofold profit. First, he learned that even someone who fasts can gain bodily strength and good looks. Second, since he took for himself the food supplied for them, he was all the more ready to supply them with the seeds they wanted. Then, since Daniel had told only about himself, he now necessarily brings his partners in piety into view as well, and says: 17. "And to these four youths God gave understanding and prudence in all learning and wisdom." It was not the education of the Chaldeans, he means, that made them intelligent and filled them with all wisdom. They were granted understanding, wisdom and all knowledge by divine grace, and so they proved superior to everyone. "And Daniel," it says, "understood every vision and dreams." From childhood he saw divine revelations, not only in sleep but also awake, and he was able to interpret what was revealed to others. This is what "understood" indicates. We learn from this too that the God of the universe makes no distinction of age but seeks only piety and love of God. If he finds them in a young man, he ranks him above many elders. One can find him doing the same with Joseph and with the prophet Samuel. To Samuel, while he was still a very young child, he appeared and ordered him to announce the punishments coming upon the old man. This was an indictment of the old man and proof of the grace that was blossoming in the boy.

18–20. "And at the end of the days after which the king had said to bring them in, the chief eunuch brought them in before Nebuchadnezzar. And the king spoke with them, and among them all none were found like Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael. And they stood before the king. And in every matter of wisdom and knowledge on which the king questioned them, he found them ten times better than all the enchanters and magi in his kingdom." Amelsar knew [?] about the difference in their food and surely learned the power of divine grace, but the king perhaps knew nothing of it. How could he have learned it, since he went on supplying the food as before and it was Amelsar who consumed it? Yet he too received no small benefit, for he found them better than everyone chosen from the other nations: in beauty and stature of body, in wisdom and understanding of soul, in eloquence of speech and in every branch of learning. He did not make the comparison casually. He put certain questions to them and took experience as his teacher of the truth. He found them not merely superior but ten times better, and in the process he learned that the Jews are wiser than all other nations. Having said this, he added: 21. "And Daniel continued until the first year of King Cyrus." He did not add this idly but because he wanted to make plain the time span of the whole prophecy. For this reason he told us the beginning of the prophecy and added its end, so that by counting the years of the kings in between we might learn the entire span of the prophecy. He also teaches us that Daniel saw Cyrus, who granted release from captivity, and that in this present life he had the consolation of seeing his kinsmen set free. In the very first year of his reign Cyrus ordered that any Jews who wished could return to Judea, and he rebuilt the divine temple, having learned the prediction of the prophet Isaiah from blessed Daniel himself. For Isaiah had cried out plainly: "Who says to Jerusalem, You shall be rebuilt, and to the cities of Judea, You shall be inhabited; who tells Cyrus to be wise, and he will do all my will." "Thus says the Lord to my anointed, Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, so that nations will obey him, and cities will not be shut. For I will go before you and level mountains. I will shatter gates of bronze and

break iron bars, and I will open for you treasures hidden in darkness, secret and unseen." Having learned this, Cyrus allowed any of the Jews who wished to return to their homeland. The book of Chronicles also tells us the date. "In the first year," it says, "of Cyrus king of the Persians, when the word of the Lord through the mouth of Jeremiah had been fulfilled, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians, and Cyrus had a proclamation made throughout his kingdom, in writing, saying: Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judea. Who is there among you of all his people? The Lord his God will be with him, and let him go up." This is why blessed Daniel, too, when he was teaching the time span of the prophecy, put into his writing about the Jews [?] the words: "And Daniel continued until the first year of King Cyrus." Let us give the listener a rest here and sing the praises of our good Master, who strikes and heals, who scourges and cures, who uses both punishment and loving-kindness. To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

CHAPTER 2. 1. "In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar he dreamed a dream, and his spirit was troubled, and his sleep left him." From this we learn that as soon as he began his reign, he marched against Judea in the third year of Jehoiakim's reign. He ordered Jehoiakim to pay tribute, and he took others captive and carried them off to the land of the Assyrians. The prophet Jeremiah also bears witness to the dates, speaking as follows: "The word that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning all the people of Judah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah. This was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon." We find, then,

here that Nebuchadnezzar became king as the third year of Jehoiakim's reign was ending and launched his campaign against the Jews. At the beginning of the fourth year the prophet Jeremiah, exhorting the people, said that this was the first year of King Nebuchadnezzar. Blessed Daniel, having said that the first captivity took place in the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, now added: "In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar he dreamed a dream." He did not add this idly but so that we might learn the date exactly. For this reason the divine prophets, too, record the number of years whenever they mention kings. "In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, then, he dreamed a dream, and his spirit was troubled, and his sleep departed from him. 2. And the king ordered the enchanters, the magi, the sorcerers and the Chaldeans to be summoned to tell the king his dream." God's plan here is clear to anyone of sense. He wanted his own prophet to make the dream known to the king, so that the king might receive good and saving counsel from it. So he frightened the king with the dream but took away his memory of it. Just as the providence of the God of the universe is clear, so the king's madness is plain to all the pious. Was it not the height of insanity to ask others to remember one's own dream? Nevertheless, when they were summoned, it says, "they came and stood before the king." 3, 4. "And the king said to them: I dreamed a dream, and my spirit was troubled to know the dream. And the Chaldeans spoke to the king in Syriac and said: O king, live for ever! Tell the dream to your servants, and we will declare its interpretation." Their request was indeed reasonable, but their promise was boastful, for it is not within the power of the human mind to interpret divine revelations without help from above. The Chaldeans spoke in Syriac because they had been gathered from various nations. Each nation had its own language, but all used Syriac in common, and the Chaldeans wanted to make the reasonableness of their reply clear. Even so, they did not persuade the arrogant king to stop demanding from human beings what is beyond nature. 5, 6. For the king answered at once and said to the Chaldeans: "The matter has gone from me. So if you do not make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you will be destroyed, and your houses

…your houses will be plundered. But if you make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you will receive gifts and presents and great honour from me. Only tell me the dream and its interpretation.” These words show not only his rashness and savagery but also his great folly. It is the height of folly to think that the Chaldeans would gain more knowledge either from threats of harm or from promises of reward. (7) So they at once said to him: “Let the king tell the dream to his servants, and we will declare its interpretation.” What they mean is: “We admit that we are your servants, but we also know the limits of our nature. If we learn the dream we will be able to interpret it, but we cannot tell it to you, since it was known to you and then given over to forgetfulness.” Yet the foolish man kept on pressing them, demanding that they recall the dream for him. “The king answered,” it says, “and said: (8) I know for certain that you are buying time, because you see that the matter has gone from me. (9) If, then, you do not tell me the dream, there is one sentence for you. I know that you have agreed among yourselves to speak a false and corrupt word before me until the time passes. Tell me my dream, and I will know that you can declare its interpretation to me.” His demand in these words is arrogant and mad, but his accusation is entirely true. “You want to learn the dream,” he is saying, “so that you can jointly make up some false interpretation, [?] the length of time, and waiting for the moment when it turns out.” When the Chaldeans heard this (for it seems they had more freedom of speech with him than the others), they now spoke plainly and gave up on the dream altogether. (10) “For there is no man on the dry land,” they said, “who can make the matter known to the king, since no great king or ruler asks such a thing of an enchanter or a Chaldean. (11) For the thing the king asks is hard, and there is no one else who can declare it before the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with any flesh.” So, they say, it cannot happen as you think. Ask us for human things, not for things beyond nature. Above all, it befits kings to steer their kingdom justly and to ask from their subjects only what is possible. But what you now demand [?] you demand. Such knowledge does not belong to human beings clothed in flesh,

but to the bodiless nature, which knows all things exactly. This is what the Chaldeans said, and it prepared the way for what Daniel would declare. Since they had said that knowing these things belongs not to men but to gods, the inspired Daniel reminds the king of the dream and interprets it very exactly and clearly. He also teaches the king that such knowledge belongs neither to men who creep upon the earth nor to gods who do not exist, but to the God who made all things. Each of these points will be properly explained in its own place. (12, 13) “Then,” it says, “the king, in great anger and fury, ordered all the wise men of Babylon to be destroyed. And the decree went out, and the wise men were being put to death, and they sought out Daniel and his companions to kill them.” This was the act of a tyrant, not of a king. It was plainly unjust and empty of all justice, for arrogance and conceit, once they gain power, contrive destruction for their subjects [? the Jews]. But when the most divine Daniel saw this unjust slaughter, he questioned Arioch, who had been entrusted with this most savage killing, saying: “Officer of the king, why has this shameless decree gone out from the king’s presence?” It seems he did not know about it, because he had not been called to the assembly of the wise men of Babylon. The three years had not yet passed during which the king of the Babylonians had ordered them to be fed with food from the royal table and then, after that set time, to be brought in to him. And if the narrative has already related that they went in and were judged better than the others, let no one be surprised. Wanting to finish that story, the writer clearly told everything that happened at that time, and then he moves on to another story, about events that took place in the meantime. His ignorance of the unjust slaughter shows that he was not yet among those who had free access to the king when the king gathered the wise men of Babylon, since he asked Arioch about its cause because he did not know it. When he learned it, he boldly spoke with the king and asked him to grant him a little time to search out the dream and find its interpretation. Then he teaches us how he found it, not to gain glory for himself but to call us to the same zeal. (17, 18) “For Daniel went into his house,” it says, “and made the matter known to Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael, his companions. And they sought mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that Daniel and his companions would not perish with the rest

Relying only on human reasoning stripped of piety, they say and do everything to deceive people. But those nurtured by the truth will not bring themselves to say or do anything without help from above. They attach their requests to the providence that watches over all things, and so they stand unmoved, neither shaken nor tossed this way and that, but free from the storm of human reasonings. The inspired Daniel is a witness to this. He asked for a little time to discover the dream, but he did not spend that time simply in reasoning; he spent it in supplication and prayer. Nor did he trust in himself alone, but took those of like mind as partners in his supplication. And he was not disappointed in his hope. (19–22) “Then,” it says, “the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision of the night, and Daniel blessed the God of heaven. And he said: May the name of the Lord God be blessed from everlasting to everlasting, for wisdom and understanding are his. He changes times and seasons; he sets up kings and removes them; he gives wisdom to the wise and prudence to those who have understanding. He reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is in the darkness, and light is with him.” In all of this he shows his gratitude. Nor does he weave his hymn idly, but makes the discovery of the dream the material of his weaving. What he means is this: It is right to praise without ceasing the everlasting and eternal God. He is the source of wisdom and understanding, and he governs all things wisely and well. Through the changes in human affairs he exposes how unstable human prosperity is and shows his own power plainly to all. He appoints kings and easily deposes them again; he gives authority and takes it away whenever he wishes. He is also the giver of wisdom and prudence, but he does not give it indiscriminately; he gives it to those who wish to understand him. As he wills, he reveals things that do not appear at all but are hidden as if in a deep, because they have not yet happened. And since he is spiritual light and dwells in unapproachable light, he knows exactly everything done in the darkness. (23) “Therefore to you, O God of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, for you have given me wisdom and power, and now you have made known to me what we asked of you, for you have made known to me the king’s vision

to make it known to the king.” Such are the souls of the godly. In their needs they know that God is their provider and run to his harbours. And after they have been given good things, they do not allow the memory of his gifts to fall into forgetfulness, but repay God their benefactor with hymns. The modesty of this divine man also deserves notice. When he made his request, he took those of like mind as partners in prayer, and when he wove his hymn for what he had received, he mentioned them again. He did not say, “You have made known to me what I asked of you,” but “what we asked of you.” Having thus finished the divine hymn, (24) “Daniel at once went,” it says, “to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon, and said to him: Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon. Bring me in before the king, and I will declare the interpretation of the vision to the king.” This compassion too befits the prophet. He would not accept being rescued from the unjust slaughter with only his friends, but worked to save the Chaldeans as well. He hoped through this miracle both to free them from their impiety and to bring them to the God of all. (25) “When Arioch heard these words, he quickly brought Daniel in before the king and said to him: I have found a man among the exiles from Judah who will declare the interpretation to the king.” Here again it becomes clear to us that the king had not yet had any experience of Daniel’s virtue. If he had been known, Arioch would not have spoken so vaguely: “I have found a man among the exiles from Judah who will declare the interpretation to the king.” (26) “The king was overjoyed and said to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar: Can you tell me the dream I saw and its interpretation?” This too should be noted: he does not always call him Belteshazzar, but only when he is speaking with the king, who had given him this name. When he was asked whether he could tell the king both the dream and its interpretation, he answered: (27) “The mystery the king asks about is not something that wise men, magicians, enchanters or Gazarenes can declare to the king. (28) But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries.” He began his teaching admirably. He set aside that chorus of fools and exposed their weakness, and then said that God is the teacher who reveals mysteries. He added “in heaven” to set aside the gods that are made and worshipped here below.

By using the singular he sets aside the crowd of gods that do not exist, and by saying that God dwells in heaven he shows that the gods seen below are not gods at all but a deception that has its origin in human craft. “He has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what must happen in the last days.” After this opening, he again uses a blessing to win the king’s ear to goodwill. “O king,” he says, “live forever.” He was about to tell the dream, add its interpretation and foretell to the king the end of his kingdom, so he began this way, as if to say: “My prayer is that you live forever. So do not blame me for what the dream reveals.” Then he says: “Your dream and the visions of your head upon your bed, this is what they were, O king.” That is: what you saw at night is this. (29) “Your thoughts arose upon your bed about what must happen after these things.” He means: as you lay on your bed, you were wondering whether you would live forever, or whether by the law of human nature you would come under death; and you wanted to learn things that had not yet happened. “And he who reveals mysteries has made known to you what must happen.” Everywhere he proclaims the one God and drives out the error of polytheism. Then he also shows the modesty of his own mind. (30) “For as for me,” he says, “this mystery was revealed to me not because of any wisdom in me greater than that of all the living, but so that the interpretation might be made known to the king, and that you might know the thoughts of your heart.” He means: I received this revelation not because I am wiser than all men, but so that you might learn what you desired to learn. God used me as the minister of this knowledge, as his own servant. So he begins his explanation, and first tells the dream itself. (31–33) “You, O king, were watching, and behold, a single image, a great one. That image was great, and its appearance was extraordinary as it stood before you, and its sight was terrifying. It was an image whose head was of pure gold, its hands, chest and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, its legs of iron, and its feet partly of iron and partly of clay.” In these words he indicated four materials: gold, silver, bronze and iron. He did not mention the clay on its own, but only as mixed with the iron. By these he signifies the greatest and most universal kingdoms, which succeeded one another and ruled most of the inhabited world. It is clear that other kingdoms have also arisen, and some still exist now. But one cannot see them ruling over all nations or even most of them,

but only over one or two. He says, then, that the first of all was the empire of the Assyrians, which is the same as that of the Babylonians. Both peoples are Assyrians, but sometimes they had their royal seat at Ninus, which the Hebrews call Nineveh, and sometimes at Babylon. The prophet himself also testifies that these two are a single kingdom, for in interpreting the dream he says: “You, O king, are the head of gold.” And the blessed prophet Jeremiah says: “Babylon is a golden cup in the Lord’s hand, making all the earth drunk; the nations have drunk of her wine; therefore they were shaken; and suddenly Babylon fell and was shattered.” If there had been another Assyrian kingdom besides this one and older than it, what material could anyone call it? The most divine Moses also testifies that this is so. In his account of the world’s beginnings he says of Nimrod that he was a mighty hunter before the Lord, and then adds: “And the beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, Erech and Calneh.” Writers outside our faith also call the Babylonians Assyrians, and the Persians still call that land Assyria today. So the first material, the gold, signifies the kingdom of the Assyrians and Babylonians, and he calls it the head because it came first. The second, the silver, is the kingdom of the Persians and Medes. Cyrus came from both peoples, from the Medes on his mother’s side and from the Persians on his father’s. He destroyed the kingdom of the Assyrians, that is, of the Babylonians, and transferred the kingship to the Persians. The prophet called this kingdom chest and arms to show its kinship with two nations. By the right arm he signifies Cyrus’s father’s descent and by the left his mother’s. Their union is assigned to the chest, because the chest holds the heart, the storehouse of thoughts, and marriage contracts are concluded by deliberate thought. The bronze he called the Macedonian kingdom, which appeared after the Persian one and likewise ruled over all. He assigned to it the belly and also the thighs, indicating by the belly the sole rule of Alexander, and by the thighs the division of the kingdom that took place after his death. The iron he called the Roman kingdom, which succeeded the Macedonian. He assigned to it the legs, since they are near the end of the whole body and can bear the whole body. The soles of the feet are also of iron, but mixed with clay. By this he hints not at another kingdom but at the same one, which would become weaker than it had been and be mixed with the weakness

of clay. He set out the difference between the materials to show a difference not in value but in strength. Silver is more [?] than gold, bronze is harder than silver, and iron is far more solid than bronze itself. So the difference lies not in value but in strength and power. We must also ask why he saw these materials combined in an image, for nothing is revealed by the God of all idly or in vain. An image has outward forms, not realities. The present life is like this: it has nothing lasting or permanent. That is why the blessed Paul cried out, “The form of this world is passing away.” And elsewhere he urges, “Do not be conformed to this age.” And the blessed David, exposing the emptiness of human prosperity, says: “Surely all things are vanity, every living man. Indeed, man walks about as an image; he stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it.” The present life is subject to sudden changes, for everything that is seen is mortal, temporary and perishable. An image has none of the working of real things, but shows only the outward forms of kings, rulers and subjects, and even its form is easily broken. So the God of all fittingly chose an image. He wanted to teach that arrogant king how empty human pride is, and to show him that human affairs change very easily. So he set an image before him in a dream and divided its parts among different materials. In this way he taught the frequent, successive changes of kings, and persuaded everyone that he alone has lasting power, without beginning or end, and a kingdom that is simply eternal. After this the blessed Daniel goes on to tell the rest of the dream. (34–35) “You were watching until a stone was cut from a mountain without hands, and it struck the image on its feet of iron and clay and ground them to nothing. Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver and the gold were ground together, and they became like chaff from a threshing floor in summer. The force of the wind carried them away, and no place was found for them. And the stone that struck the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.” This is how the dream ends. But it is fitting to begin the interpretation from the bottom. So let us first ask what this stone is, which at first appeared small but was later shown to be very great and covered the world. Let us listen to God himself, speaking through the prophet Isaiah: “Behold, I lay in Zion a precious stone, a cornerstone, valuable, chosen, for its foundations, and everyone who

"…whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." Let us also hear the blessed David prophesying and crying out: "The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner." Christ the Master himself put this testimony to the Jews in the holy Gospels, saying: "Have you not read: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes"? And the blessed Peter too, addressing the Jews and bringing forward the Lord's prophecy, says: "This is the stone that was despised by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner." And the blessed Paul says: "Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the cornerstone." And elsewhere he says: "No one can lay a foundation other than the one that is laid, which is Jesus Christ." And again: "They drank," he says, "from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ." So we are taught by both the Old and the New Testament that our Lord Jesus Christ is called a stone. For he was cut from a mountain without hands, born of a Virgin without marital union. Divine Scripture often calls a birth contrary to nature a quarrying. For Isaiah, reminding the Jews of the begetting of a child granted to Abraham contrary to nature, said: "Look to the solid rock from which you were hewn." So the mountain is the tribe of David, and the stone is Christ according to his humanity, cut not according to the law of nature. He who once seemed small, because of the nature he had put on, was suddenly shown to be a very great mountain, filling the whole world. "For the whole earth was filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas." He will strike the image on its feet of clay and iron; that is, he will bring the last kingdom too to an end and make it vanish and disappear. For no other kingdom will succeed it; rather, he will unveil his own kingdom and display it to all. And he will wipe out even the memory of all those kingdoms, like dust that rises from a threshing floor and is scattered by the wind. Having thus told the king the whole dream, he went on: (36, 37) "This is the dream, and we shall tell its interpretation before the king. O king, king of kings." He did not say this to flatter, [Ps. [?]; [?] 42; Acts 4:11]

but using the customary title. For he held power over all who ruled nations and were called kings. "You, O king, king of kings," he says, "to whom the God of heaven has given a kingdom mighty, strong and honored in every place." For it is not by human strength, he says, that you have prevailed over all, but because God, who holds the heavenly kingdom, has given you this authority, so that you lead and rule over the people in every place, "wherever the sons of men dwell. The beasts of the field and the birds of the sky he has given into your hand, and he has made you lord of them all." By beasts he means the barbarians who live more like wild animals; by birds, those adorned with understanding, who surpass other men and are winged in their thought. Of all these, he says, he has made you king. "You, then, are the head of gold"—that is, your kingdom. For he is not speaking of the person but of the kingdom itself. Indeed, after his death Evil-Merodach reigned over the Babylonians, and after him Belshazzar. If he had been speaking of the person himself when he said, "You are the head of gold," how are we to understand "After you shall arise another kingdom inferior to you"? For he is not indicating the kingdom of his sons but the Persian kingdom. So the head of gold is not Nebuchadnezzar himself but the whole kingdom of the Assyrians, or Babylonians. (39) "And after you shall arise another kingdom inferior to you": the Persian. He calls it inferior not as weaker but as second. "And a third kingdom, which is the bronze, which shall rule over all the earth." He means the Macedonian. Alexander son of Philip ruled over the whole earth, having subjected all men within twelve years of his reign…

(40) "And there shall be a fourth kingdom, strong as iron; just as iron crushes and subdues all things, so it shall crush and subdue all things." He means the Roman kingdom, which became very strong and prevailed over practically all nations, and received tribute and taxes from all. He used "crush" for this, and "subdue" for obedience, good order and a law-governed polity. (41) "And whereas you saw the feet and the toes, part of iron and part of clay, it shall be another, divided kingdom, and some of the root of iron shall be in it, just as you saw the iron mixed with the earthenware clay." He said "another" not in respect of kind but in respect of [Notes: B: … placed this [?]. A: ὅπου … ἀνθρώπων, supplied from B. Lacking in B. … of clay [?] … and part of iron.]

the quality of its power. For if he had meant "another" in kind, he would have called it a fifth, just as he had called the others third and fourth. But since he knows that the final stages of the iron kingdom are weaker, he called it "another" because of its weakness, and with good reason. For above he showed it to be very strong indeed, since such were its beginnings. Yet he says that not even its last stages will be entirely weak. "For some of the root of iron," he says, "shall be in it, just as you saw the iron mixed with the earthenware clay. (42) And the toes of the feet were part of iron and part of clay." This needs no interpretation from us, for the Prophet himself interprets it, saying: "Part of the kingdom will be strong, and part of it will be broken." To this he adds: (43) "And whereas you saw the iron mixed with the earthenware clay, they shall be mingled by the seed of men." This shows above all that this kingdom is not another one besides the iron, but the same one in a weaker condition, part of it strong and part weak; yet the bond of kinship will join the weak portion to the strong. That is what "they shall be mingled by the seed of men" shows. There will be, he says, a mingling and intermarriage between these and those, but discord will nonetheless destroy the claims of kinship. "For they will not cleave to one another," he says, "just as iron does not mix with clay." This, then, is how we have understood the interpretation of the inspired Daniel. But it is fitting also to bring forward the opinions of some who interpreted it before us, for in this way the truth will be shown more clearly. Some writers said that the fourth kingdom, that is, the iron, was Alexander the Macedonian, and that the feet and toes made of iron and clay were the Macedonians who reigned after him—Ptolemies, Seleucids, Antiochuses and Demetriuses—some of whom ruled weakly and others very vigorously, and who intermarried and embraced kinship with one another. But they ought to have observed, first, that he said Nebuchadnezzar himself was the head of gold, that is, the kingdom of the Babylonians, or Assyrians. It was succeeded by the kingdom of the Persians and Medes together, for Cyrus sprang from both nations and ruled both, and having overthrown the kingdom of the Babylonians he ruled over the Persians. The Persian kingdom, which was the second, Alexander the Macedonian overthrew, and the blessed Daniel said that he ruled over all the earth. This kingdom he named the third; and no other succeeded it but that of the Romans. They ought,

therefore, first to have understood from the numbering and from the events indicated, and to have learned, that the third is the kingdom of the Macedonians, that is, the bronze, and the fourth that of the Romans, that is, the iron. And even if those points seemed altogether rather obscure to some, they ought at least to have discerned the whole prophecy from its end. For immediately after showing the weak, clay end of the iron kingdom, he added: (44) "And in the days of those kings"—that is, the kings of clay and iron who have intermingled and embraced kinship with one another, yet have not gained concord even from kinship—"the God of heaven will raise up a kingdom which will never be destroyed, and its kingdom will not be left to another people. It will crush and winnow all the kingdoms, and it will stand forever. (45) Just as you saw that a stone was cut from a mountain without hands, and it crushed the clay, the iron, the bronze, the silver and the gold." This plainly shows the end of present things and the endlessness of the kingdom of heaven. For when the iron kingdom has become weak and has taken on the admixture of clay, "the stone cut without hands" will appear and "will crush the clay, the iron and the bronze, the silver and the gold," and will make them vanish entirely, and will grant to the worthy a kingdom that has no successor, eternal and without limit. "For it will never be destroyed," he says, "and it will not be left to another people; and it will crush and subdue all the kingdoms, and it will stand forever." If anyone disputes this and will not have it so, let him show what human thing is eternal, or what kingdom of men will not come to an end. For it is simple-minded and utterly foolish to await the consummation of the present age and yet to say that some kingdom in this present life will be endless. And if they too agree that these words signify the kingdom that God will give to the worthy, then he did not call the Macedonian kingdom iron; for the present life did not come to an end while that kingdom held power. Rather, the Roman kingdom overthrew the Macedonian and holds the helm of the world. And if they say that these words signify the Lord's first coming, let them show that the supremacy of the Romans was overthrown immediately after the appearing of our Saviour. For one finds quite the opposite: it was strengthened, not overthrown, at the time of the Saviour's birth. For the Master's birth took place in the reign of Augustus, who was the second to reign

but who made practically all men his subjects, enrolled the whole world, as the Gospels say, and decreed that tribute be paid. Strengthened by him, the kingdom of the Romans has lasted until now. So if the Lord's first birth did not overthrow the supremacy of the Romans, it remains to understand his second appearing. For the stone that was already cut without hands earlier, and became a great mountain and covered the world, will at his second coming strike the image on its feet of clay; that is, it will appear at the very end of the iron kingdom, when that kingdom has already grown weak. It will overthrow all dominions and consign them to oblivion, and will grant his eternal kingdom to the worthy. Having interpreted these things, Daniel necessarily added: "The great God has made known to the king what must happen after this. The dream is true, and its interpretation trustworthy." It is worth marveling at the care that the God of the universe takes for all men. For he does not deprive even those who live in impiety of his providence, but deems them too worthy of every care. Thus he did not leave this barbarous, savage and impious man uncared for. First, through the revelations, he shows him how perishable is the good fortune of the present life, how precarious kingship itself is, and that nothing in human prosperity endures, but like flowers or lilies it withers or is extinguished. These things were enough to bring down his boastful and conceited brow, to persuade him to think as a man, and to expect the end both of his life and of his kingdom. First, then, he cares for him through these things. Next, through his forgetting of the dream, he exposes the lying of the magi and Chaldeans, and shows the truthfulness of his own servants; and through his servants' wisdom he reveals his divine power. He draws to his worship [?] those who did not know him; or rather, he compels those who demanded worship from everyone to worship his holy servants. The history teaches us this too. At first he marveled at the prophet's wisdom and confessed that the prophet's God was the God of the universe; but after a little time had passed he returned to himself, "like a dog to its own vomit," as the divine Scripture says, and made a golden image, sixty cubits high and six cubits wide. He set it up on level ground, so that it might tower over everything and be seen equally by all, and he ordered all his subjects to worship it. This was no ordinary kind of arrogance, but one directly opposed to God and hateful to God. For God had shown him in a dream a very great image made of four materials, and through them had revealed to him the succession of the four kingdoms. So, setting his own pride against God, he made an image himself, giving it as great a size as human skill could provide. But he did not make it of gold, silver, bronze and iron; he made it of a single material, gold, thinking, wretch that he was, that he would prove God's predictions false. Blessed Daniel, interpreting the dream, had said that he was the head of gold, that is, the kingdom of the Babylonians, or Assyrians, and that the other parts of the image, made of the other materials, were those that succeeded the head; so he made the whole image of gold. (17) "For our God in heaven, whom we serve, is able to deliver us from the furnace of burning fire, and he will rescue us out of your hands, O king." Who would not rightly be amazed at the courage of these blessed youths, at their wisdom, their piety, their justice regarding the laws, their self-control in everything? For not to be terrified of that mighty tyrant, ranged against them with practically the whole human race, nor of that enormous blaze, not merely threatened in words but there before their eyes, bears witness to a courage in them firmer than adamant. And to put the divine laws before the present life: what greater justice could there be? Their self-control is proclaimed by their neither using bold words against the king nor, on the other hand, disgracing their race by cowardice; and their prudence and wisdom are proclaimed by the piety they set against his impious and blasphemous words. For he said, "Who is the God who will deliver you out of my hands?" But they cried out: "Our God in heaven, whom we serve, is able to deliver us from the furnace of burning fire, and he will rescue us out of your hands, O king." "Do not think," they mean, "that our God is like your gods. You rightly despise them, since they owe their existence to material and craftsmanship. But our God is the Creator of heaven and earth and of all things, and has a power that the visible world displays; for the power beyond these things is not easy for those uninitiated in divine matters to perceive. It is him we honor, and we await his help; for he is able to set us free both from your hands and from the furnace of fire that you have built." What they said next leaves no room for greater courage or love of God. For having said, "Our God in heaven, whom we serve, is able to deliver us from the furnace of burning fire, and he will rescue us out of your hands, O king," they immediately added: (18) "But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods, and we do not worship the golden image that you have set up." "For we do not serve our Master for wages," they mean, "but, spurred by love and longing, we choose the service of our God above all things. That is why we do not even ask unconditionally to be freed from our troubles, but we accept the Master's dispensation and providence; and not knowing what will be to our advantage, we leave it to the Helmsman to steer as he wills. That he has power to free us from the evils you threaten, we know clearly; whether he also wishes to do so, we do not know. But we leave the government to him, since he is wise, and we accept his verdict, trusting that it is for our good. So whether he rescues us or not, your image and your gods we refuse

to worship. Such are the souls you have drawn up your battle line against. Fight us any way you like: you will neither win us over with honors nor overawe us with threats, for to us God is the most beloved and the most fearful of all." What could be loftier than these words? To them one may fitly apply that apostolic saying: "For we do not know what to pray for as we ought." But the savage and utterly mad tyrant was so filled with fury that his face showed the turmoil of his soul. He ordered the furnace to be heated as hot as possible and commanded the holy men to be bound; and so that the punishment would not be delayed by taking off their clothing and shoes, he ordered them to be handed over to the fire along with these, that is, with their saraballa, tiaras and periknemides. Saraballa are a kind of Persian cloak; tiaras are head coverings; and by periknemides he means the so-called trousers, or the leather leggings worn over them, or leather shoes. Thus bound, the holy men were delivered to the fire. He ordered them burned in this way for the sake of speed and dispatch, but divine grace arranged from it another mystery [?]. For the nature of the fire dissolved the iron bonds laid on them, yet kept their highly flammable garments unharmed. The flame consumed the accusers of the holy men and the ministers of the impious order, who were standing outside; but it could not come near the saints themselves. Turning its back on those inside, it went for its own worshipers, as though exacting punishment from them on behalf of the Master's servants. Inside, the heralds of piety enjoyed such safety and care that they trod on the coals as if on roses. (23) "They walked," it says, "in the midst of the flame, singing hymns to God and blessing the Lord." This too displays their consummate wisdom: they did not ask, it says, to be freed from their dangers, but praised the one who was governing their affairs in this way and had counted them worthy of this noble confession. One can see the new resembling the old. For the blessed apostles Peter and John, after being flogged by the band of Pharisees, went out rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus; and the most divine Paul with Silas, after the beatings the magistrates inflicted on them at Philippi, while confined in prison and fastened in the stocks [?], "about midnight," it says, "were praying and singing hymns to God." So too these blessed

youths, dancing in the furnace, kept on weaving the divine hymn. First Azariah, becoming the mouth of them all, and surrounded by waves of flame, "opened his mouth," it says, "in the midst of the fire and said: (26) Blessed are you, O Lord, God of our fathers, and praiseworthy and glorified is your name forever." Who could admire as it deserves the wisdom of this opening? For it was not in prosperity and good fortune, nor while his life flowed along smoothly, but in so great a furnace that he praised the God of the universe and called him the God of the fathers, at once showing the humility of his mind and proclaiming the virtue of the fathers. "We praise you, Master," he means, "we who have as our fathers those whose God you were pleased to be called. For you said to your servant Moses, 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' This name of yours is praiseworthy and glorified, not at some particular season or fixed time, but for all

(27) "For you are just in all that you have done to us." "We praise you," he means, "because we know the justice of your judgment; for by a right and just verdict you ordered us to be enslaved and taken far from our own land." "And all your works," it says, "are true, and your ways are straight. "All these things," he says, "you have brought upon us because of our sins. (29) For we have sinned and acted lawlessly in departing from you." "It was not without reason," he means, "that you handed over to our enemies even the city you had consecrated and let us become captives; it was because we have sinned and acted lawlessly in departing from you." The words "from you" carry great emphasis. They mean: from the Maker and Creator, the good Master, the one who nourished and guarded us, who freed us from slavery to the Egyptians, who divided the sea, who led us on foot through the deep, who [made] the dry rock

(30) "And we have not listened to the commandments of your law, nor kept them, nor done as you commanded us, so that it might go well with us." Here again he showed how surpassing his piety and wisdom were. "For keeping the laws and commandments," he means, "brought nothing to you, the Lawgiver, but secured an abundance of good things for us. That is why you had laid down those laws, providing us with the means of salvation. Since, then, we have transgressed, (31) 'all that you have brought upon us, and all that you have done to us, you have done in true judgment.'" For the punishment is worthy of the sin. Then, describing that punishment, he says:

"Since we did not serve you, our King," he means, "but despised your goodness, you rightly forced us to serve a most cruel and harsh king, who knows nothing whatever of justice, and whose subjects go along with their king's wickedness. 35, 36. “For the sake of Abraham,” he says, “who is loved by you, and for the sake of Isaac your servant, and Israel your holy one, to whom you spoke, saying: ‘I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the shore of the sea.’” These things, he says, you promised them, O Master, whom you loved and made renowned, so that their race would rival the sand in number and be like the stars in brilliance, loftiness and splendour. Then he sets the actual state of affairs beside the promises. 37. “For, O Master,” he says, “we have been made fewer than all the nations, and we are brought low in all the earth today.” And so as not to accuse the promises falsely, he immediately added the cause, saying: “because of our sins.” For it was not you, O Master, he says, who broke your promises; rather, we transgressed the covenant. Although we had become many according to the promise, too many to count, we were made few because of our sins. This is what he hinted at when he said, “We have been made fewer.” For he did not say, “We are small and few compared with all the nations,” but “We have been made fewer,” that is: we did become too many to count, in accordance with your promise, but by transgressing your commandments we became few instead of many. Then he shows God the calamity that grips them, not as though teaching one who does not know, but by recounting their sorrows to call him forth to loving-kindness. 38. “And at this time,” he says, “there is no ruler, or prophet, or leader.” For we have been deprived, he says, of kingship, of prophecy, of priesthood, those great and divine gifts of yours by which we were continually guided. “Nor burnt offering, nor sacrifice, nor oblation, nor incense.” And to show why it is impossible to sacrifice, he went on to add: “Nor a place to make an offering before you and to find mercy.” For your law confined the service of sacrifices to one place, and to offer you sacrifice in any other place is a plain transgression of the law. The Jews do not want to hear this; instead, shutting their eyes and stopping their ears, they dare to perform everything unlawfully. But these holy youths, understanding the purpose of the law, said that there was no place to make an offering before him and to find mercy. And since it is impossible, he says, to obtain this while we are far from that holy city, we have found another way of worship, O Master. 39, 40. “For with a contrite soul and a spirit of humility” we offer you our supplication and beg that it be accepted. “As with burnt offerings of rams and bulls, and as with tens of thousands

This holy man did not say these things casually; he had been taught them by the prophet David, who says in the fiftieth psalm: “If you had wanted sacrifice, I would have given it; you will not be pleased with burnt offerings. The sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise.” And again, speaking in the person of God: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Here he called God’s “face” his goodwill, the restoration of freedom and the recovery of his care; while they enjoyed these, they were able to see the divine temple and the worship performed there, through which they imagined they saw God, although he is incorporeal and invisible. Since, then, you have brought about such a change in us through punishment, 42. “Do not put us to shame, but deal with us according to your forbearance and according to the abundance of your mercy. 43. And deliver us according to your wonders, and give glory to your name.” For these reasons, he says, grant us pity and loving-kindness; for you are merciful by nature and show long-suffering toward all, and your power keeps pace with your will, as the wonders you continually perform bear witness. For what is done for us will also cause your name to be hymned, not only by us who are saved, but also by those who see our salvation. “Give glory, then, to your name, O Lord.” (44, 45.) “And let all who do evil to

your servants be put to shame, and let them be disgraced and stripped of all power, and let their strength be crushed.
