The holy youths were right to cry out, "For his mercy endures for all ages, and for ever and ever." For look: this man had acted with such cruelty and arrogance. He had tried to seize the worship that belongs to God, and to punish God's servants cruelly and savagely. Yet God leads even him toward piety. He shows him his own wonder-working and makes visible to him the angel sent to help the saints. He astonishes him first by the number, showing four instead of three. Then he astonishes him by the loosing of the bonds, for he saw them unbound instead of bound. Then he astonishes him by their safety: "For they are not harmed," he says. Astonished at this, he lays aside his arrogance and addresses them: "And he says, 'Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out and come here.' And Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out from the middle of the fire." The foolish man who had said, "Who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?" has learned that there is a God of inexpressible power, who commands the fire to show the saints a nature contrary to its own. The one he did not believe to be God, he came to know as God, and God Most High. When the saints had come out, all the satraps, governors, and generals marvelled. They saw that the saints' bodies had been kept unharmed, and that not even their hair had felt anything from that flame. And not only their hair: their clothing and their sandals also remained intact, so that they were free even of the smell of fire. Then Nebuchadnezzar, having seen these things, sings a hymn and says: (95) "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who sent his angel and delivered his servants, because they trusted in him, and defied the king's command, and gave up their bodies so that they might not serve or worship any other god except their own God." The foolish man keeps learning God's power by experience and then consigns the miracles to oblivion. He did the same in the case of the most divine Daniel. He rose and worshipped him, and ordered that an offering and incense be presented to him. So now too, having seen the deliverance of these saints, he praises God and admires the men because they defied the king's command and, he says, preferred a pious death to a lawless [?]

(96) "And now," he says, "behold, I issue a decree that every people, tribe, and tongue that speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be destroyed, and their houses shall be plundered, for there is no other God who can deliver in this way." He had truly learned this by experience. He had torn down the sanctuaries of many so-called gods, robbed their treasuries, pulled up their altars, and slaughtered their priests, and he never met with any act of divine power on their behalf. But when he turned his fury against those dedicated to God, he saw both God's boundless power and his inexpressible long-suffering. God kept his own servants unharmed, and for the time being he did not make the king pay the penalty for his madness. When the king persisted in impiety, God punished him moderately a little later, and then, when he repented, counted him worthy of his kindness. (97) "Then," he says, "the king prospered Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon, and promoted them, and made them rulers over all the Jews in his kingdom." This is the kind of care the Master takes of those who are eager to serve him. The holy youths were right to cry out [?], "There is no shame for those who trust in you." Let us too, then, make this hope our own, and value the Maker and Governor above the whole of creation. Let these blessed youths be for us a model to profit by, a pattern of piety, and guides leading us to God and to the gifts that God bestows on those who are worthy. May we all attain these gifts, by the grace and lovingkindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. For those who had been forced to serve against their will took the king's change as their opportunity and stopped obeying. 12. "But leave the growth of its roots in the earth; and in a band," he says, "of iron and bronze, in the grass outside and in the dew of heaven he shall lodge." He had fallen into derangement, madness and frenzy. He was raving, carried away like one of the Corybants, and raging against everyone, so he had to be put in bonds. Yet even these were not enough to keep him indoors. He escaped and lived in the wilderness, suffering in the open air and eating grass like cattle. This is what he means by saying: "And his portion shall be with the beasts in the grass of the earth; his heart shall be changed from that of men. (13.) And the heart of a beast shall be given to him, and seven times shall pass over him." This too shows God's long-suffering. He limits the punishment to a short time, waiting for the repentance that the discipline will bring about. Then he shows that the [?] will come to pass beyond dispute:

14. "The word is by the decree of the watcher," he says, "and the request is the word of the holy ones." The word, he means, cannot be false, for the one who spoke it is a holy angel, a watcher, incorporeal. And these things have been said, he says, and are coming to pass, not in vain but "so that the living may know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men, gives it to whomever he pleases, and will set the most despised of men over it." The angel said this, he says: the things concerning the tree will happen for this reason, so that through them everyone may learn that there is one

God, Lord and King, who sets up the kings on earth and hands the kingdom to whomever he wishes. To show his own authority, he sometimes makes even the lowliest man a king, one thought to be nothing at all, and makes those of the highest rank obey him. Having thus finished telling the dream, the king says to Daniel: 15. "This is the dream that I, King Nebuchadnezzar, saw. And you, Belteshazzar, tell the interpretation in my presence" (that is, truly and exactly), "because all the wise men of my kingdom cannot make its interpretation known to me, but you can." And he shows the reason: "Because," he says, "the holy Spirit of God is in you." The others rely on human reasoning, but you learn hidden things from God. 16. "Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, stood dumbfounded for about an hour, and his thoughts troubled him." Human weakness had to be shown first, and then the grace that inspired him had to come to light. "So the king answered and said: Belteshazzar, do not let the dream and its interpretation hurry you." He saw that Daniel was disturbed, and since he was eager to learn what he did not know, he had to encourage him. So he says to him: Do not be in too great a hurry, but take your time to find out what the dream signifies, and then make it plain to me. "So Belteshazzar answered and said: My lord king, may the dream be for those who hate you, and its interpretation for your enemies." Very wisely and prudently, he begins with this preface, praying that the painful things may be kept away from him, and yet he still declares the truth. 17, 18. "The tree," he says, "which grew great and strong, whose height reached to heaven and whose breadth reached to all the earth, whose leaves were flourishing and whose fruit was abundant, in which there was food for all, under which the wild beasts dwelt and in whose branches the birds of heaven lodged—it is you, O king." Daniel's wisdom deserves admiration here. He did not simply say "the great tree" but "the tree which grew great and strong"; that is: You were not great from the beginning but became so little by little, and you did not have your strength from birth but acquired it gradually. So he goes on to add: 19. "For you have grown great and strong, and your greatness has grown and reached to heaven, and your dominion to the ends of the earth." He applied these words to heaven and earth very aptly and fittingly too. He said that the dominion reached

to the ends of the earth, meaning the authority. But to heaven, he says, it was no longer the dominion that reached, but the greatness, meaning the fantasy of his mind. 20, 21. "And whereas the king saw," he says, "a watcher and a holy one coming down from heaven, who said: 'Strip the tree and destroy it, but leave the growth of its roots in the earth; and in a band of iron and bronze, in the grass outside and in the dew of heaven he shall lodge, and his portion shall be with the wild beasts until seven times have passed over him'—this is its interpretation, O king." And to make his word credible, he had to add: "And it is a decree of the Most High, which has come upon my lord the king." From this one can learn precisely how useful the apostolic teaching is: "Let every soul," he says, "be subject to the governing authorities." For the blessed Daniel too calls the impious king himself "lord." Obeying the law of authority, he uses the proper titles, while still revealing the truth of the dream, painful though it is. 22. "For they will drive you," he says, "away from among men, and your dwelling will be with the wild beasts. They will feed you grass like an ox, your body will be drenched with the dew of heaven, and seven times will pass over you." Some have said that the seven times are seven years, others three and a half. For the divine Scripture does not divide the year into four seasons, but into the two most general ones, winter and summer, so seven such periods make three and a half years. You will spend that long, he says, in your calamity, "until you know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he pleases." Since you dream of being a god, or rather of being even greater than God, God takes away even your human reason and will make you like the beasts. Then you may learn by experience what man is and what God is, what human good fortune is and what divine kingship is, and that the latter cannot be obtained unless God wills it. 23. "And whereas it said," he says, "'Leave the growth of the tree's roots,' your kingdom will remain yours from the time you know the heavenly kingdom." Once you have been deprived of the kingdom and have endured all those things, you will recognize the giver of the kingdom. Then, having recognized him, you will receive your former authority back. In this way, by both the taking away and the giving back, you may learn exactly who is the pilot of the universe, who wisely directs and governs all things. Having described what will happen, he offers an exhortation and the best of advice, and he applies a remedy suited to the wound.

24. "Therefore, O king," he says, "let my counsel please you. Redeem your sins by almsgiving and your iniquities by compassion for the poor." With these words he points to the insatiable cruelty the king had shown toward his subjects. Do you want to receive kindness, he says? Then show it to those who share the same nature as you. That is how you will persuade the Judge to quench the threat and leave it unfulfilled. "For perhaps," he says, "there will be long-suffering toward your transgressions." The prophet, then, put forward this counsel. But the king remained hard and unbending, so he received the wages of his lawlessness, and the painful things he had heard he saw with his own eyes. Then Scripture also indicates how long the divine long-suffering lasted: when twelve months had passed, the threat contained in the prediction was carried out in fact. He had received that much time for repentance, and he wasted the term set for his repentance. The blessed Paul might fittingly say to him: "Or do you despise the riches of his kindness, forbearance and long-suffering, not knowing that God's kindness is leading you to repentance? But by your hardness and your impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath, when God's righteous judgment is revealed. He will repay each one according to his works: eternal life to those who by patience in good work seek glory, honor and incorruption; but wrath and fury to those who are contentious, who disobey the truth and obey unrighteousness. There will be tribulation and distress for every human soul that does evil." This is exactly what happened to Nebuchadnezzar, who did not make proper use of God's long-suffering. He himself is the witness to this, as follows:

26, 27. "And after twelve months he was walking in the temple of his kingdom in Babylon, and going about on the walls of the city with all his glory, and on its towers. And the king answered and said: Is this not great Babylon, which I built as a royal house by the might of my strength, for the honor of my glory?" See how swollen his pride is; see how excessive his arrogance! I, he says, [made] it a royal city [?], establishing palaces in it for the honor of my glory, and I did these things because I had the greatest strength and had mastered everyone. But while he was snorting and swaggering and using such words, the Lord God at once [?] the punishment.

28. "For while the word was still in the king's mouth," he says, "a voice came from heaven." Since he had dreamed of ascending to heaven, he receives his sentence from there. Since the kingdoms below were not enough for him and he madly desired those above as well, he is stripped even of those below. Having wished to seize heaven, he is driven from the earth too. "So a voice came from heaven: To you, to you it is said, King Nebuchadnezzar." The pronoun is not doubled for nothing, but to rebuke more clearly the one to whom these things are said. It still calls him king, pointing both to the glory he still had and to the disgrace that would come before long. "Your kingdom," it says, "has passed from you. (29.) They will drive you away from among men, and your dwelling will be with the wild beasts. They will feed you grass like an ox, and seven times will pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he pleases." Then, to show how swift the punishment was, he says that the deed followed the word at once:

30. "In that very hour," he says, "the word was fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar, and he was driven away from among men." He was driven out, first, because of the affliction itself. He had been given over to madness and raving, and he would have done countless evils if he had been left free. Second, he was driven out because of the hatred everyone had for him. While he was in good health they tried to hide it, but when he fell into calamity they turned on him, loathing his cruelty. "And he ate grass like an ox," he says. It is typical of the deranged not only to say and do irrational and disorderly things, but also to eat whatever comes their way. Even now one can see people troubled by demons doing and suffering this. He not only ate grass like an ox, but also "his body was drenched with the dew of heaven." Since he was suffering in the open air, wrestling with frost and scorching heat with a naked body, his skin inevitably took on another color. "Until his hair grew long like lions' hair, and his nails like birds' claws." Since he was not shorn as usual, nor had his overgrown nails trimmed, over so long a time he inevitably grew [such] hair and nails. [?] showed that he was neglected and uncared for.) For having lost divine providence, he did not receive care even from his own household, though he had a wife, children and relatives. Instead he kept roaming the uninhabited places like a wild beast, [eating] the food of irrational animals [?].

"and though he was in the greatest honor, he did not understand, but was compared to the senseless cattle and became like them," and since he had treated his subjects with a bestial mind, it was fitting and entirely just that he [?] the beastly [?], having used that [?]. He who had said, "Who is the God who will deliver you out of my hands?" [now says:] I, who dreamed of ascending to heaven and setting my throne above the stars, have been taught by experience what is right. I have learned self-control through punishment, and I have recognized that I am a servant. "Therefore I lifted up my eyes to heaven," and as soon as I did this, "my understanding returned." That is: I was freed from my derangement and regained the strength of my reason, and at once I recovered a sound mind. "And I blessed the Most High, and praised him who lives forever, for his authority is an everlasting authority, and his kingdom is from generation to generation." Having learned by experience what man is and what God is, he calls him Most High and Living and names him eternal King, and he recognizes his own lowliness. That is why he says: 32. "And all who dwell on the earth were counted as nothing." Until now I thought I was the greatest and most exalted, but now I know clearly that the whole of human nature, compared with God, is nothing. Looking for a word for lowliness and finding none adequate, he put down "nothing," which expresses well enough how frail and easily dissolved our nature is. God he called Most High [?], Lord, Living and eternal King, but all human beings he called nothing. In the same way, the blessed Isaiah, when comparing the divine nature with the idols, brought the human race into view. "For if all the nations," he says, "were reckoned as a drop from a bucket and as the tilt of a scale, and will be reckoned as spittle; and Lebanon is not enough for burning, and all the four-footed beasts are not enough for a whole burnt offering; and all the nations are as nothing and were counted as nothing before him—to whom will you liken the Lord? And with what likeness will you compare him?" Such was the benefit Nebuchadnezzar gained from his calamities that he thinks and speaks about God like a prophet. And, as if in a kind of harmony,

he weaves his whole hymn out of creation. "All who dwell on the earth," he says, "were counted as nothing, and he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth." This too is the teaching of another prophet. For the blessed David says: "Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth." This is what Nebuchadnezzar proclaims as well. "Whatever he wills," he says, "both among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth": he governs and rules not only the earth but the heavens themselves. Then he also shows that his power is irresistible: "And there is no one," he says, "who will withstand his hand and say to him: What is this that you have done?" We must accept what he does, whether it is pleasant or painful, for it is reckless to resist and to find fault with what he governs so wisely. Having come to know and confess these things, he says, and having glorified the Most High, I came back to myself and, with piety, recovered my former kingdom. 33. "At that very time my understanding returned to me, and I came to the honor of my kingdom, and my form returned to me." He had been squalid and filthy, as we may suppose. But he had his hair cut, his overgrown nails trimmed and the filth washed off, and he received divine grace. Then it was recognized that this was a man, the one who had formerly ruled the greatest of kingdoms. "And my lords and my nobles sought me out," he says. For they too laid aside their hatred and came to feel goodwill and affection toward me. "And I was established in my kingdom, and greater majesty was added to me." This phrase too is full of piety. He did not say, "I acquired greater majesty," but "it was added to me," pointing to the giver and proclaiming the [?] of good things.

34. "Now therefore," he says, "I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise, exalt and glorify the King of heaven, for all his works are true and his ways are justice, and he is able to humble all who walk in pride." Having experienced painful things and then been freed from them, I praise and hymn the one who, to my profit and with great wisdom, brought both upon me. I know him to be King of heaven and Lord of all, who acts in truth, governs all things justly, and is able to humble those who behave proudly. Since we have learned, then, how pride and conceit ruin those who give way to them, and how anyone who delights in them reaps no good fruit, let us acquire humility, the mother of all good things.

For the Lord too calls this possession blessed, since its yield is the kingdom of heaven. "Blessed," he says, "are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." He also sets himself up as a model for those who wish to benefit, saying: "Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart." And to show how great its fruit is, he immediately added: "And you will find rest for your souls." If the Maker and Lord of all calls himself lowly and shows it by his deeds as well, what other advice does man need—man, who is dust, clay, a clod, ashes, vanity, the flower [?], grass? For the divine Scripture calls him all of these. Let us, then, be put to shame by the modesty of the Master, who, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that we might become rich through his poverty. Let us learn how mortal our nature is. Seeing how quickly present prosperity tips the other way, let us not think arrogantly about present things. Let us rather laugh at how changeable and unstable they are, and long to obtain those good things whose nature is lasting and permanent. May we all enjoy them, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

CHAPTER 5. Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-Merodach, Belshazzar. 1. "King Belshazzar made a great feast for his nobles." He was the son of Nebuchadnezzar, but he did not succeed him directly. Evil-Merodach, his elder brother, reigned first. The history of the Kingdoms teaches us this, and so does the blessed prophet Jeremiah, who says: "And it came to pass in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-fourth day of the month, that Evil-Merodach [?] king of Babylon, in the year in which he became king, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought [him] out" VARIANT READINGS. 33 μέγα: absent in A. 34 B: "tenth." 35 B: "in the year in which." 36 Ἰωακ.: absent in B.

…him out of the house where he was kept, and spoke kindly to him, and gave him a seat above the thrones of the kings who were with him in Babylon, and changed his prison garments, and he ate bread continually in his presence all the days of his life.” Now this Joakim is the same as Jechoniah. For Joakim his father, also called Eliakim, in whose reign blessed Daniel was taken captive, Nebuchadnezzar killed in Jerusalem and threw outside the wall, as divine Scripture teaches. After Nebuchadnezzar, then, Evil-Merodach reigns, and after him Belshazzar. The most divine Daniel left out any mention of Evil-Merodach, because he is writing prophecy, not simply history. For this reason he did not record everything Nebuchadnezzar did either, but only the things that had to be remembered because they were useful. Under Belshazzar, too, God displayed a very great wonder, one that could instill reverence and fear and guide people toward piety, not only those living then but those who would come later. So Daniel did not think it right to bury so great a benefaction in silence. He considered it a holy duty to put it in writing and leave it to everyone as a reminder and a lesson. Therefore he says: “King Belshazzar made a great feast for his thousand nobles, and before the thousand was the wine.” That is, there was enough for the thousand; it had been prepared for that large a number. 2. “And while he was drinking,” he says, “Belshazzar, at the tasting of the wine, said to bring the gold and silver vessels that Nebuchadnezzar his father had brought out of the temple in Jerusalem. And the king and his nobles and his consorts and his concubines drank from them.” Through this the prophet teaches us not only how extreme his impiety was, but also the harm that comes from drinking wine without measure. “For while he was drinking,” he says, “the king, at the tasting of the wine, said to bring the gold and silver vessels.” Drunkenness buried his reason, and intemperance gave birth to madness against God. Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken the vessels dedicated to the service of God, because God had handed them over. But he honored them as he thought fit and set them free from human use. This man dared to use them as if they were common. For he did not only say it; he also [?] the deed to his words.

3. “For the gold and silver vessels were brought,” he says, “which Nebuchadnezzar had brought out of the temple of God in Jerusalem.” He did well to show how extreme the outrage was, for besides the temple

he mentioned God as well, and to show the distinction of the [?] he added the name of Jerusalem. For these vessels, he means, were not dedicated to any of the so-called gods, who have only a name, but to the God over all himself, who chose Jerusalem and filled the temple there with his own glory. These things were not to be touched. They were dedicated to the God of the universe, not because he needs anything, but because he accepts the gratitude of those who make offerings. Yet the impious king brought them out into the open and drank from them. And not only he, but also his nobles and his consorts and his concubines drank wine. That is, he made the instruments of divine worship into instruments of drunkenness, and the women who fed his licentiousness [?] he ordered to enjoy the wine from them. Then the prophet shows the very height of the impiety, adding: 4. “And they praised the gods of gold and silver and bronze and iron and wood and stone.” For this utterly vile man, sodden with drink and reveling in the divine vessels, forgot the Lord of all and honored with hymns gods that do not exist. They are made of lifeless matter, and not even the craftsman's art has lent them any power to act; they have received only a shape, with no activity in it. But the Ruler of the universe did not allow his long-suffering to bring harm on the people of that time and on those who came after them, and he showed his own power at once. 5. “For in that very hour,” he says, “there came forth the fingers of a man's hand, and they wrote opposite the lampstand on the plaster of the wall of the king's house, and the king watched the fingers of the hand that was writing.” He had praised idols that are deprived of all activity and had despised the God of all. So the Creator of the universe teaches him that his divine nature is invisible and incorporeal. He shows him only fingers writing, teaching him that he would not have seen even these if God himself had not supplied the occasion for it. The king's fellow diners also gained great benefit from this. They were taught that God is powerful as well as incorporeal and invisible, while the gods they had praised are not only material and lifeless but also utterly ineffective and weak. That this wonder struck great fear into everyone the prophet has testified, saying: 6. “Then the king's countenance changed, and his thoughts troubled him, and the joints of his loins were loosened, and his knees knocked against each other.” But if the sight of fingers writing so terrified the one [Apparatus notes: B has “was dedicated”; for “made,” B has “having become”; for “fingers” (astragaloi), A has “fingers” (daktyloi); B has “to him”; A and B have “were troubling”; for “knocked against each other,” A has “clattered”; before “writing,” B adds [?].]

who governed the greatest of kingdoms, so that the joints of his limbs were loosened by fear and his limbs trembled and shook, what would this God-hated man not have suffered if he had seen fiery whirlwinds or thunderbolts, or grim-faced angels terrifying him with their strange forms? Not even the great Daniel could bear the sight of these without fear. Truly, “Why is earth and ashes proud?” Filled, then, with such great fear, 7. “He cried out mightily to bring in the magi, Chaldeans, and Gazarenes.” Fear produced the outcry, and the turmoil in his soul pressed him to learn the answer. Then he offers a prize to whoever reads the writing and gives its interpretation: royal clothing, a gold necklace, and the third rank after the king. But the godlessness of the magi and Chaldeans was exposed. They could not manage to read the divine letters, even though so great a prize was set before them and strongly urged them on. 9. “And King Belshazzar was troubled, and his countenance changed upon him, and his nobles were troubled with him.” From this it is clear that the Lord was taking thought for the benefit of the others. He did not take away the king's life at once. First he showed him the fingers of the one writing. Having struck him with this and filled him with fear, he arranged for the wise men of the Chaldeans to be summoned. He exposed their falsehood and weakness and made Daniel's wisdom necessary, so that through Daniel's tongue he might both convict this man and benefit the others. Only when these things had happened would he bring punishment on the impious king. While the king and the banqueters were in this turmoil, 10. “The queen, in response to the words of the king and his nobles, came into the banquet hall.” That is, while they were deliberating about what to do, each suggesting something different as fear drove them, the queen came in. It seems to me that she was his mother. His consorts, together with his concubines, were taking part in the banquet, for he himself drank from the gold and silver vessels, and so did his nobles and his consorts, that is, his wives, and his concubines, the women who lived with him not lawfully but out of licentiousness. But she came in after the uproar, and it is likely that, being old, she was not then taking part in that drunkenness and that cordax-dancing, that is, dancing. “And the queen answered,” he says, “and said: O king, live forever.” This, it seems, was a form of address offered to the kings of that time

by their subjects. The custom has prevailed even to the present day, for some foolish people are in the habit of calling the present emperors “eternal” too, and some even add this when drawing up contracts, serving ignorance rather than impiety. So the queen says: “Let your thoughts not trouble you, and let your countenance not be changed.” Then she gives the reason why she drives out his fear: 11. “There is,” she says, “a man in your kingdom in whom is the holy Spirit of God, and in the days of your father wakefulness and understanding were found in him.” From this, too, one can see that she was more likely his mother. That is why she teaches him what happened long ago as though he did not know it. She makes blessed Daniel known to him, acknowledges that he is full of the divine Spirit, and uses the very words of Nebuchadnezzar. For Nebuchadnezzar too said the same things about Daniel, and she added that “in the days of your father wakefulness and understanding were found in him.” By “wakefulness” she meant the sobriety of the soul, and by “understanding” the perception of hidden things and the insight into things that escape most people. “And King Nebuchadnezzar your father,” she says, “appointed him chief of the enchanters, magi, Chaldeans, and Gazarenes.” Then she adds the reason: 12. “Because an excellent spirit is in him.” That is, he possesses a surpassing grace of the Spirit. Then she lists the forms the Spirit's working takes: “And prudence and understanding, interpreting dreams, and declaring hidden things, and loosing knots—Daniel.” Having become a vessel of the divine Spirit, he gives wise counsel on everything and speaks with understanding on everything. He makes plain the riddles of dreams and frees from their obscurity things hidden in a kind of [?] concealment. Things that are, as it were, under bonds and seals, guarded as if in storerooms, he releases from their bonds; he loosens and opens them and brings inside those who wish to enter. This is what is meant by “declaring hidden things and loosing knots—Daniel.” For this reason, she says, “the king gave him the name Belteshazzar.” Since he saw him illuminated by divine power, he honored him with the name of his own god. “Now then, let Daniel be called, and he will declare its interpretation to you.” She does not say, “Let Belteshazzar be called.” Having learned the prophet's power by experience, they prefer the Hebrew name to the Chaldean one, which is why from here on [?] they call him Daniel. 13. “Then,” he says, “Daniel came in before

the king, and the king said to Daniel: Are you Daniel, one of the sons of the captivity of Judah?” It seems that, out of great impiety, this man had avoided Daniel's company after his father's death. That is why, struck with sudden fear, he calls the magi and the Chaldeans, having driven even the memory of the prophet from his mind. But when his mother reminded him of the wonders done in his father's time, and Daniel was called and came in, he recognized him at once. Had he not known him, he would not have mentioned his race and brought up the captivity of Judah. All the same, he asks: “Are you Daniel, one of the sons of the captivity of Judah?” And before Daniel had even answered: 14. “I have heard of you,” he says, “that the holy Spirit is in you, and that wakefulness and understanding and excellent wisdom have been found in you.” What the Prophet said about Israel can fittingly be said of this man too: “When he slew them, then they sought him.” For see, fear of the divine power forced this man too to call the One who is God, instead of those who are not, and to praise the grace of the Holy Spirit. It forced him to accuse the wise men of Babylon of being unable to understand the divine writing, and to beg the prophet of God to make plain what no one knew. He promises to give him the purple, the necklace, and the third rank in the kingdom. But blessed Daniel laughed at the impious man's royal promises and said to him: 17. “Let your gifts be your own, and give the rewards of your house to someone else. But I will read the writing to the king and make the interpretation known to you, O king.” Truly apostolic is the prophet's voice. For when the Lord sent the apostles out as heralds to all people, he commanded them, saying: “Freely you have received, freely give.” And this blessed prophet said to the king: “Let your gifts be your own, and give the rewards of your house to someone else. But I will read the writing to the king and make the interpretation known to you, O king.” In other words: I have not learned to sell divine things, nor to take human wages for divine mysteries; so receive the knowledge of what is unknown free of charge. 18. “God Most High,” he says, “gave the kingdom and the greatness and the honor and the glory to Nebuchadnezzar your father. 19. And because of the greatness that he gave him, all peoples, tribes, and languages trembled and were afraid before him.” Do not think, he says, that your father conquered the whole world by his own strength, and brought the

countless races of nations, speaking different languages, under one kingdom. The Lord of the universe, the Maker of all things, who governs all things wisely, gave him the kingdom, and it was by divine decree that fear of your father lay upon his subjects. “And whom he wished he exalted, and whom he wished he humbled.” He received such authority from God, he says, that he could bring low those who stood high, and make the very obscure and lowly illustrious

20. “And when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened to act proudly, he was brought down from the throne of his kingdom.” Just as, he says, “he exalted whom he wished and humbled whom he wished,” though by no means always by a just verdict, so the King and Lord of all gave the kingdom to your father as he willed. But he saw him indulging in pride beyond measure, ruling the kingdom with boastful arrogance, and caught by the disease of pride. So he deprived him of the royal throne and took away the honor that everyone paid him. He not only stripped him of the kingdom but also drove him out of human society. He handed him over to derangement and madness and made him live with wild asses and beasts. He took on the life of the creatures whose savagery he had imitated. Daniel reminds him that his father ate grass like oxen, and that, wandering naked and suffering in the open air, he lost the former color of his body and took on another, produced by frost and scorching heat. And he endured all these things, he says, “until he knew that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he pleases.” But he learned what he needed to learn by experience. Events themselves taught him that nothing human is secure, and that the God of all, whose power is eternal, steers human affairs as he wills and holds out the gift of kingship to whomever he wishes. 22. “But you,” he says, “his son Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart before God. Did you not know all these things?” You were not brought to your senses by your father's misfortunes, and you were not willing to learn God's power from what he suffered. 23. “But you have lifted yourself up against the Lord of heaven.” He does well to teach those present not to worship the things that are seen, but their Creator and Lord. At the same time he refutes the king's arrogance and teaches that the vast heaven has the invisible God as its creator. “But you,” he says, “have made your heart loftier

Had you not been sick with such arrogance, you would not have ordered the vessels of his house to be brought. “And you and your nobles and your consorts and your concubines drank wine from them.” That is, you used the vessels dedicated to God for heavy drinking and drunkenness. Then, dramatizing the extremity of the impiety, he says: “And you praised the gods of gold and silver and bronze and iron and wood and stone.” And continuing the mockery: “which do not see, and do not hear, and do not know.” And yet you could have perceived their impotence from their matter, from the craftsmanship applied to it, and above all from the insensibility of their parts. They lack knowledge, sight, and hearing; they do not have the working of even one of the senses; they are nothing but bare images. Yet not even this persuaded you to see what you ought, and you go on praising gods that cannot help. “But the God in whose hand is your breath, and all your ways, him you have not glorified.” He did well, and very wisely, to set the idols and the God of all side by side, for the benefit of his hearers. Having shown that the idols neither see nor hear, he did not go on to say of the God of the universe that he sees and hears and knows. Instead he stated what is greater than all these: “your life and your ways are in his hand.” For it is a greater thing than living to give life to others and to take it away again whenever one wishes. So he showed that the idols lack life and all sensation, while God, the Lord of the universe, is the giver of all life; he gives it and takes it away, governing as he wills. Yet even so, he says, this God, so great and so mighty, who has authority over life and death, who appoints and deposes kings—him you not only did not praise, but you even go on insulting him in your drunkenness, reveling in the vessels set apart for him. 24. “Therefore the fingers of a hand were sent from his presence, and it inscribed this writing.” He did not say, “He himself wrote,” but, “the fingers of a hand were sent from his presence.” God commanded them to appear, and did not even show you the whole of the one writing. Wishing to expose your arrogance, he struck you with fingers alone and filled you with such great fear. Now learn, he says, both the writing itself and the interpretation of the writing. 25–26. “This, then, is the writing that was [?]: Mane, Thekel, Phares. And this is the interpretation of the word.”

He calls the interpretation a "synkrima". "Mene: God has measured your kingdom and brought it to an end"; that is, he saw that you were unworthy of the kingdom, and decided to declare you stripped of it. 27. "Tekel: it has been weighed in the balance and found wanting." Through these words the prophet taught not only that king but us as well that nothing is unweighed with God: even his mercy and long-suffering are granted to human beings by a certain measure and weight. "Since, then," he says, "you have overstepped the bounds of his loving-kindness, receive the divine sentence." 28. "Peres: your kingdom has been divided and given to the Medes and Persians." Here we must ask why the God of all, after disciplining Nebuchadnezzar, restored him to his kingdom, but at once deprived this man of both his kingdom and his life. On examination we find, first, that Nebuchadnezzar had not seen anyone else paying the penalty for impiety, and so the just verdict of God judged him worthy of pardon; but this man saw his father's very great punishment and drew no profit from it. Fittingly, then, the just Judge limited the punishment to a fixed time in the one case, but in this case granted no pardon at all. Besides, God foresees all that will happen and knows it as clearly as if it had already happened. Foreknowing the one man's repentance, he ordered his affairs accordingly; foreknowing this man's impiety to the very end, he cut short its growth by death. As soon as Belshazzar heard Daniel's interpretation, he ordered him to receive the promised prize, the purple robe and the gold necklace. Then, having adorned him in this way, he had a herald proclaim to his subjects that he had appointed him third ruler of the kingdom. But none of this [?] the divine sentence.

30. "For in that very night," it says, "Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans was slain." Here he called him a Chaldean to show that this was the end of the Chaldean kingdom. Truly, "it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God," as the divine Apostle says. It is fearful "to despise the riches of his goodness and forbearance and long-suffering," and not to worship and serve him as best one can. "For who," as the prophet says, "has hardened himself against the Lord and stood firm?" For this reason blessed David also urges: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the provocation." And blessed Paul, interpreting this, gives the advice: "Take care,

brothers, that there is not in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, leading you to fall away from the living God. But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called 'today', so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin." For sin often charms us with pleasures, as it charmed that foolish king through drunkenness, and so knows how to harden our heart and make it resistant, so that it readily takes in the disease of impiety. Let us therefore flee the devil's deception, I beg you, and prefer lasting virtue to sin, which offers only brief pleasure. Then we shall prove strangers to the company of Belshazzar and enjoy the fellowship of Daniel, in Christ Jesus our Lord, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

The Greeks call him Cyaxares. 31. "And Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being sixty-two years old." The kingdom of the Chaldeans came to its end as God had foretold, and rule over the world passed to the Medes. So Daniel had foretold when he interpreted "Peres": "For your kingdom," he says, "has been divided and given to the Medes and Persians." But after Darius the Mede had reigned for a short time, Cyrus took over the rule and transferred it to the Persians. The historian Josephus says that Darius was the son

of Astyages and Cyrus's uncle on his mother's side, but that the Greek writers gave his name differently, calling him Cyaxares. He says that Darius and Cyrus, his nephew, campaigned against Babylon together, took the city by siege and killed Belshazzar [?]

[?] to believe what blessed Daniel wrote. At the end of the narrative about Darius, Daniel tells us that he prospered in the reign of Darius and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian, and so shows that Darius's reign was one and Cyrus's another. If they had made a single campaign against Babylon, there would also have been a single reign. As it is, he says that the one reign was distinct from the other. And at the end of the prophecy Daniel says: "And King Astyages was gathered to his fathers, and Cyrus the Persian received the kingdom." So Darius and Cyrus did not reign together and kill Belshazzar. Rather, Darius the son of Ahasuerus reigned first, and Cyrus afterward. Nor does Josephus's account agree with the Greek histories. Nowhere in them can one find that Cyaxares the son of Astyages was the same Darius who, Josephus says, campaigned against Babylon with Cyrus. Josephus's account is therefore entirely implausible. Following the divine Scripture, I find that this man was Nebuchadnezzar's daughter's son. God commanded Jeremiah to put bonds on himself and [send] them to the neighbouring kings of the Edomites, Moabites, Ammonites, Tyrians and Sidonians, and charged him to say this to them: "Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Thus you shall say to your masters: I made the earth by my great strength and my uplifted arm, and I will give it to whomever I see fit. I have given the whole earth to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, to serve him; and all the nations shall serve him, and his son, and his son's son, until the time of their own land comes." Since Daniel speaks of Belshazzar as the son, we must look for the grandson. If anyone objects that Darius is called a Mede, let him learn that this does no harm to the argument. Cyrus, too, was the daughter's son of Astyages, who was a Mede and reigned over the Medes, and yet he is called a Persian, for people usually take their national names from their father's side. So it is likely that Darius had a Median father and a Chaldean mother, and was called by his father's nationality. If this is not so, let those who wish to point out the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar who inherited his ancestral kingdom, and we will not quarrel at all about the matter. For every right-thinking person would agree that the prediction of the great Jeremiah is entirely true. But suppose someone holds that Darius was not Nebuchadnezzar's daughter's son but his son's son, because the prophet said, "They shall serve [?]

and his son, and his son's son." Let him learn the idiom of divine Scripture: it usually traces genealogies through males, so when it wanted to say "grandson" it said "son of the son". But blessed Daniel testifies that he was not the son of the son when he says, "Darius the Mede received the kingdom." And the divine Jeremiah foretold that Nebuchadnezzar would hand the kingdom down to his grandchildren. So the truth can be found from the two prophecies together. From Jeremiah's we learn that Nebuchadnezzar's grandson too would hold the kingdom. From blessed Daniel's we learn that when Belshazzar, Nebuchadnezzar's son, died by divine decree, Darius the Mede received the kingdom. Considering this, and knowing that the prophets do not lie, we find that he was a Mede on his father's side, a Chaldean on his mother's, and a grandson of Nebuchadnezzar. This is what we have found in seeking the truth of the two prophecies. But let each person think about it as he pleases, for no harm will come from uncertainty about his lineage. Come, then, let us take up the detailed interpretation.

CHAPTER 6. When Darius had become king, it says, (1, 2) "he appointed one hundred and twenty satraps over his kingdom, to be throughout his whole kingdom, and over them three officers, of whom Daniel was one, so that the satraps should give account to them and the king should not be troubled." Truly, nothing can dim piety. It sends out its rays everywhere, whether it is found in a slave or in a captive. Nothing can overshadow its radiance; it flashes out its own light. This can be seen in many other cases, but above all in the story of blessed Daniel. Though he had become a slave and a prisoner of war, living in a foreign land and moving among barbarians, he shone out. Under Nebuchadnezzar he received homage from that most fearsome king. He was distinguished under Belshazzar too, and was admired in the same way under Darius. The succession of kings brought no change in his honour: they were snuffed out by death, but he kept the same brilliance under them all. Yet those who take over a kingdom or any other office are usually very slow to trust those who were closest to their predecessors. He, however, had the same freedom of speech with all of them, received the same privileges, and was entrusted with the same authority. So, under Darius, he became one of the three officers. By "officers" I think are meant those now called prefects, and by "satraps" the governors of the nations. Blessed Daniel, being one of the officers,

3. "surpassed," it says, "both the officers and the satraps" (that is, the governors of the nations) "when set against them"; that is, when placed side by side, compared and examined together. Then it gives the reason for his superiority: "Because an excellent spirit," it says, "was in him"; that is, he received far greater and more abundant grace from God. We learn from this that even those entrusted with secular offices receive from God some grace of wisdom for the good government of their subjects, even if they have no share in piety. Blessed Daniel hinted at this when he said, "Because an excellent spirit was in him"; that is, he had received grace in proportion to his piety. Seeing this, it says, "the king set him over his whole kingdom." For he understood that the man was dear to God and enjoyed help from above, and so he entrusted him with the administration of the whole kingdom. But the greatness of the honour stirred up envy. 4. "The officers and the satraps sought," it says, "to find a pretext against Daniel from the kingdom," or, as some copies have it, "in matters touching the kingdom." That is, they went to every length, eager to catch him offending against the laws of the kingdom; in other words, they wanted to frame against him what is now called a charge of treason. But they missed their aim. "For they found no pretext," it says, "nor any fault or error in him, because he was faithful." So blessed Daniel received this testimony not only from those who loved him but also from those who plotted against him. While he kept his piety toward God, he also showed great loyalty to the kings. When they had contrived countless schemes and still could not find him offending against the laws of the kingdom, 5. "the officers said," it says, "'We shall find no pretext against Daniel except in the ordinances of his God.'" For they knew how exacting his piety was, and there they set the snares of their wickedness. 6–9. "And the officers and the satraps came to the king and said to him: 'King Darius, live forever. All the generals in your kingdom, the governors, consuls and satraps, have taken counsel together to establish a royal statute and to enforce a decree, that whoever asks a petition of any god or man for thirty days, except of you, shall be thrown into the lions' den. Now therefore, O king, establish the decree and publish the document, so that the ordinance of the Medes and Persians may not be altered, so that it

may not be changed in any respect.' Then King Darius ordered the document and the decree to be issued." Nothing is more abominable than envy. It drove these men to impiety and made them propose an impious decree that barred those who wished to pray to God. For they forbid this not only to themselves but to all others under the king's rule. And so that their crime might not be obvious, they added that no one should ask anything of any man and receive it within the thirty days, but should make his needs known to the king alone throughout that time. Having surrendered the eye of their mind to envy, they did not see that the king cannot provide everything people ask for: not health, not life, not the gift of becoming fathers of children, not plentiful rain, nor any of the other things we receive by asking God. Having lost their wits, they ascribed to the king what belongs to God, and persuaded the foolish king to agree with them and ratify their impious request. But blessed Daniel paid not the slightest attention to these impious laws. "At once," it says, "he went into his house, and with the windows of his upper room open toward Jerusalem, three times a day he knelt on his knees and prayed and gave thanks before God, as he had done before." See how many things the passage indicates at once, revealing both blessed Daniel's piety and his courage. First, it says that when Daniel learned the decree had been issued, "he went into his house"; that is, when he learned of the law that had been laid down, he utterly despised it and went on doing exactly the opposite. Then it adds another detail that clearly shows his courage: "For the windows," it says, "were open." He did not pray in secret, it means, but openly, in full view of everyone, not out of a desire for show but in contempt for the impious law. Another detail is added that points to the same courage: "in his upper room." He did not offer his prayers to God at ground level but as if from a lookout, so that he was plain for all to see, both because he stood up high and because his windows were thrown open. "And he prayed," it says, "toward Jerusalem." He did this not only to provoke his accusers, but also in fulfilment of an ancient law. For when Solomon had built that temple and was celebrating the festival of its dedication, he prayed, calling on the grace of God and begging that the temple be filled with it. Among very many other things he added this: "And if you deliver your people to their enemies, and their captors carry them away captive to a distant land, or

and they turn their hearts in the land to which they have been carried away, and plead with you in the land of their exile, saying, 'We have sinned, we have done wrong, we have acted wickedly'; and they turn back to you with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies to which you have carried them, and pray to you toward their land, which you gave to their fathers, and toward the city that you chose and the house that I have built for your name; then hear from heaven, from your prepared dwelling place, and be merciful to the sins they have committed against you and to all the transgressions by which they have transgressed against you, and grant them compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive." Taught by these words, blessed Daniel offered his prayer facing Jerusalem, and not once a day but three times, and he kept this up continually. His posture, too, showed the contrition of his mind, for he went on kneeling as he made his confession to God. While this was going on, those who had become vessels of envy indicted Daniel for breaking the law. They read out the law that had been laid down, denounced Daniel and proved his transgression. The king was grieved when he heard the charge, and, becoming an advocate instead of a judge, he tried to show that Daniel was innocent. The text indicates this when it says: 14. "Then the king, when he heard the word, was greatly distressed over it, and strove for Daniel's sake to deliver him." But those malicious men, whose whole life was villainy, saw what the king intended. That is the meaning of "The men kept watch on the king"; in other words, they realized that he was taking Daniel's side. Then they say to the king: "Know, O king, that it is a law of the Medes and Persians that no decree or statute the king establishes may be changed." "You are not free," they say, "to overturn what you have enacted, for the laws of the Medes and Persians require that laws once laid down be kept first of all by the king." Forced by the apparent reasonableness of their argument and by the number of the accusers, the king handed blessed Daniel over to the lions, but he prayed for his safety, saying: "Your God, whom you serve continually, will himself deliver you." The words are pious, but they do not agree with what he had done before. For if you bear witness to such power in God, how could you enact a law that no one should pray to him for thirty days? It seems that Darius was kind, gentle in character and rather inclined to piety, but timid and very easily deceived. Otherwise, as ruler of a kingdom, he would not have been led by his subjects instead of leading them. He also appears to have greatly admired Daniel. "For the God," he says,

"whom you serve continually"—that is, for whose sake you even despised my laws and to whom you offer unceasing worship—"will reward you for your piety and free you from the dangers that surround you." Then, trusting in the power of God but also suspicious of the accusers' plots, he blocks the mouth of the den with a stone and seals it with the impression of his ring, so that they could do no harm to Daniel. For he was confident that God would not let the lions injure Daniel's sacred and holy body. Having done this, 18. "the king went away to his house and lay down without supper; no food was brought to him, and sleep fled from him." These things bear witness [?]. It was a mark of his kindness that he would neither take food nor let sleep touch his eyelids at all, but stayed awake, grieving over Daniel's unjust punishment. It was a mark of cowardice that, feeling as he did, he did not stand up to the accusers and use his royal authority and power to save the man who was being wronged. Having spent the night in this way, 19. "King Darius rose early, at first light." That is, while it was still dark, around twilight, so that he even needed torches; that is what "at first light" indicates. "And he went in haste to the lions' den. 20. And as he drew near to the den"—that is, before he had reached it—"he cried out to Daniel with a loud voice; the king spoke and said to Daniel." Before he had even reached the den itself, his warm affection compelled him to shout, to call Daniel and to ask whether, enjoying God's help, he had proved stronger than the savagery of the lions. "Daniel," he says, "servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the mouth of the lions?" Every one of these words shows that the king was devout and that he rejoiced in Daniel because of his piety. First, he calls him the servant not of himself but of God. Then he calls Daniel's God living. He praises him too: "whom you," he says, "serve continually"—that is, you who were not kept from this worship even by the force of the law. The words "Has he been able to deliver you from the mouth of the lions?" mean "Has he willed to make you stronger than the lions?" For he would not have called God powerless when he had called him living. Hearing this, Daniel answered: 21. "O king, live forever." The customary

…he puts a greeting before his own words, meaning, "May you live as long as possible." For even now, as we have already said, some people are accustomed to address the emperors as "eternal" in the documents of contracts. 22. "My God," he says, "sent his angel and shut the mouths of the lions, and they did not harm me, because uprightness and righteousness were found in me before him; and before you too, O king, no transgression was found in me." For God, he says, being just and governing all things justly, saw that I preferred his service to the impious laws and that I have never committed any offense against your kingdom, and so he made me stronger than the harm of the lions, and showed them to be images of lions rather than lions. 23. "Then the king," he says, "was exceedingly glad over him, and ordered Daniel to be brought up out of the pit." For he was overjoyed and filled with delight, since he had come to know the power of God and had learned that the man he loved was safe, and he at once ordered him to be brought up out of the pit. Then, seeing him safe and sound and having suffered no injury from the lions' attack, he ordered Daniel's accusers to be thrown to the lions together with their sons and wives. "And they had not reached the floor of the pit," he says, "before the lions overpowered them and crushed all their bones." This too was the work of divine justice and wisdom. For so that they could not say that the lions had kept away from Daniel because they were full and sated, and so belittle the miracle out of envy, those who were thrown in bore witness to the lions' savagery: the lions snatched them as they fell, and before they had been let down to the ground, catching them out of the very air, they made a meal of them. By paying a fitting penalty, then, they proclaim the justice of God; and by being so very easily devoured by the beasts they display the wisdom of God, and teach everyone that it was not the lions' satiety but Daniel's longing for God that made him [?] stronger than the harm of the lions. Seeing this, 25. "King Darius wrote to all the peoples, tribes and languages dwelling in all the earth." He considered it impious to hide so great a miracle and not to let all people share in the [knowledge of true] piety. So he writes as follows: "May peace be multiplied to you"; that is, may you enjoy peace continually. This resembles the greeting we use; for we too, when we write letters, are accustomed to put first: "In the Lord

26. "From my presence a decree has been laid down in every dominion of my kingdom, that all are to tremble and fear before the God of Daniel." I wish, he says, that all people under my authority should worship the God of Daniel, and not casually or at random, but should offer him their worship with awe and trembling. And he adds the reason, saying: "For he is the living God, and he abides forever." For he is enduring and admits no change; he is always the same and remains forever. To this he adds: "And his kingdom shall not be destroyed, and his dominion is to the end. (27.) He helps and delivers." He abides forever, he says, possessing an indestructible kingdom and a lordship that admits no end, one that delivers and redeems those who have believed in him. "And he works signs in heaven and on earth." One can see his wonders, both those done in heaven and those on earth, by which he displays his power. He has shown us this on the present occasion too: "For he has rescued Daniel from the mouth of the lions," and made him stronger than beasts whetted by hunger and rage. This, then, is what the letter taught the world. The end of the narrative records that "Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian"; that is, he continued to shine in both reigns and was distinguished in everything. As for us, now that we have learned the power of piety, we ought to choose it, to put it before everything, and to give way to it in no circumstance; and even if all people together should make war on us because of it, we ought to meet their assault eagerly, trusting in its power. For in this way the choir of the blessed apostles too, besieged by practically the whole world, remained invincible and made their enemies their subjects. In this way the blessed Daniel, plotted against by so many satraps and officials, was shown superior to those who warred against him; and just when his enemies thought they had won, they suffered utter destruction. Since we have such examples, then, let us keep our devotion to God sincere, so that we may continually enjoy his aid. May we all obtain it by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages.
