1. "In the first year of Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, Daniel saw a dream, and the vision of his head upon his bed, and he wrote down the dream." Up to these words the blessed Daniel wrote his prophecy more in the manner of a history. First, right from the beginning, he related [?] what happened to them after they had been taken captive, and he added how great a care they enjoyed from the God of all. Then he narrated what penalties Nebuchadnezzar paid for his cruelty and arrogance, and after that what punishment Belshazzar suffered for despising the sacred vessels. When Belshazzar had been destroyed by a divine stroke and the kingdom had passed to the Medes, he recorded what concerned himself and Darius, telling how Darius was disposed toward him, and what plots he endured from the generals and satraps, and how he received divine help. Having narrated these things as a historian would, he now begins to teach the predictions he was taught through the [revelations] [?]. And first he sets out the revelation of the four beasts, which closely resembles the dream of Nebuchadnezzar. For the king saw four materials in one image, and the prophet four beasts coming up out of one sea. But so that we are not forced to say the same things twice, let us begin the detailed interpretation, for from that this will be shown more clearly. "In the first year of Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, Daniel saw a dream, and the visions of his head upon his bed." That is, he saw this revelation while asleep; for since he is going to record also what he saw by day, he rightly teaches us which things he saw in a dream and which while awake. "And he wrote down the dream," he says. For he did not choose to hide what God had shown him, but wrote it down for the benefit of all. "The beginning of his words. And he answered and said." That is, he began the narrative

2, 3. "I, Daniel, was watching in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven burst upon the great sea. And four great beasts came up out of the sea, differing from one another." Now Nebuchadnez- [Notes:] …in B. "Beginning": see the scholion [?]. "And he answered" [?].

-zar sees an image, [learning] the vanity of affairs, and that they are "outward forms" rather than realities, as the divine Apostle says; for none of them is lasting or secure, but all things flow away, perish and wither. But the blessed Daniel sees a sea, and is taught about the waves of the present life. For since, having been taken captive, he was compelled to see a foreign land, it was fitting that he should be taught about the surge and storm of life. The king, as one who prided himself on gold and silver and bronze and iron, receives through these the riddles of the kingdoms, learns the successions of kings, and is taught not to be proud of a kingship that is subject to swift change. But the prophet, as one who despised those materials, sees "four beasts," and is taught that these fearsome kingdoms, which terrify all people, will themselves come to an end, and that only one kingdom remains without end, the one which the God of the saints has prepared for the saints. So he calls life a sea, since it has countless towering waves, and he calls the changes of affairs the winds that strike it. For just as, when the south wind blows, the waves run toward the north, and when the north wind stirs up the sea, the surge is driven back toward the south, so when the Assyrians held the helm of the world, they drew all their subjects toward themselves; but when the kingdom passed to the Persians, the course of the subjects at once shifted toward them as well. Again, when the Macedonians took the scepter, everyone abandoned those whom they had previously obeyed and brought the customary tribute to these. And when the Romans assumed power over all, everyone flocks to the West, taking no account of the Macedonians, for they too were counted among the subjects. Fittingly, then, he likened the changes of affairs to winds, which drive the waves of the sea now here, now there. For this reason he also mentioned four winds, since there have also been four successions of kingdoms. He also teaches us how the beasts differed from one another. 4. "The first," he says, "was like a lioness, and it had wings like an eagle's. I watched until its wings were plucked off, and it was lifted up from the earth and made to stand on the feet of a man, and the heart of a man was given to it." By the lioness he signified the kingdom of the Assyrians, or rather of the Chaldeans, for it was the first to rule most of the world; and the animal is royal. And he says its wings were like an eagle's, for this creature too rules over all birds. So just as in that image

Nebuchadnezzar said he had seen a head of gold, and the most divine Daniel, interpreting it, said, "You, O king, are the head of gold," so here too he assigned the mightiest of beasts to the first kingdom, not to credit it with greater strength, but to show that, as the first, it was more honored. Nevertheless, he saw that "its wings were plucked off"; that is, it was stripped of all its subjects and deprived of its former power. "And it was lifted up from the earth," he says, meaning that it ceased to reign. "And it was made to stand on the feet of a man," he says; that is, it became equal to its subjects. "And the heart of a man was given to it." It learned by experience, he says, to think as a human being and not to overstep the limits of nature in the imaginings of its mind. For when they held the rudder of the kingdom, they were sick with conceit and boundless arrogance; that is why the blessed Isaiah says, "God will bring [punishment] upon the great mind, the ruler of the Assyrians." Fittingly, then, having learned by experience how affairs change and how precarious prosperity is, they think as human beings, they know themselves, and they have acquired a human heart. This, then, is how he described the first beast. He continues:

5. "And behold, another beast, like a bear, and it stood on one side, and there were three wings in its mouth between its teeth, and they said this to it: Arise, devour much flesh." Here he signifies the Persian kingdom. He says it is like a bear because of the cruelty and harshness of its punishments. For of all barbarians the Persians are the cruelest in their punishments: they flay people alive, devise long-drawn-out torments by cutting off the limbs one by one, and make death bitter for those they punish. That is why, he says, they said to it, "Arise, devour much flesh," not permitting it to do this, but foretelling what would happen and bearing witness to its cruelty and savagery. "And three wings," he says, "in its mouth." For it ruled three parts of the world: the east, the north and the south. Cyrus, the first king of the Persians, brought the whole East under his rule as far as the Hellespont; his son Cambyses subdued Egypt as well and made the Ethiopians his subjects; Darius son of Hystaspes conquered the Nomad Scythians, whose lot is to inhabit the northern part of the world. Xerxes son of Darius tried to add Europe to his subject lands too, but he was defeated by the Athenians in a sea battle, returned in disgrace, and learned the harm that greed brings forth. For this reason he says, "Three wings in its mouth."

Some of the copies read "ribs," but it makes no difference. For whichever reading is adopted, it teaches that it enjoyed the fruits of the three parts of the world and received tribute from every quarter. And he rightly added "in its mouth," to show the contributions supplied by everyone. And since this kingdom was not entirely destroyed, but continued to hold some portion of its former dominion, he did not say that it suffered what the one before it suffered, when it was deprived of its wings, "made to stand on the feet of a man, and given the heart of a man"; instead he said it stood on one side. "It stood," he says, "on one side"; that is, having ruled the three parts of the world, it was deprived of the greater part but kept dominion over one part. For although it once ruled all Asia and Libya, it was deprived of Egypt and Ethiopia; it no longer rules the Palestinians, the Phoenicians and the Syrians; it has been stripped of dominion over Asia too, and the Euxine Sea has passed beyond its scepter; it rules only Persis, Media, Assyria and a few neighboring nations. That is why he says, "It stood on one side." Having said this about the second beast as well,

6. "After this," he says, "I watched, and behold, another beast, like a leopard, and it had four wings of a bird on its back, and the beast had four heads, and authority was given to it." By these he signifies the Macedonian kingdom; and very aptly he likened Alexander to a leopard, because of his speed, sharpness and versatility. He said the beast had "four wings of a bird," because Alexander, like a bird, swept through the four parts of the world and brought all of them under his rule; and by "the four heads" he signified the division of the empire after Alexander. For four kings were established in place of one: Ptolemy son of Lagus was entrusted with the helm of Egypt; Seleucus was entrusted with governing the East; Antigonus ruled Asia; and Macedonia was ruled, as some say, by Antipater, or, as others say, by Philip, also called Arrhidaeus, Alexander's own brother. So the four heads signify the four dominions after Alexander, and the four wings signify the power of Alexander himself, which prevailed over the four parts of the world. He said authority was given to the beast because Alexander was seen to rule even peoples whom his predecessors had not ruled. Yet even the kingdom that prevailed over all [came to] an end.

7. "For after this," he says, "I watched in the vision of the night, and behold, a fourth beast, fear- [Notes:] For "and he says," another reading has "for." B reads "Syria." B reads "as some have said." B reads "Arideus." Patrologia Graeca 81.

-ful and exceedingly terrible, and its teeth were of iron and great, and its claws of bronze; it devoured and crushed, and trampled what was left with its feet, and it differed exceedingly from all the beasts before it." By the fourth beast he means the Roman kingdom. He gives it no name, since the city of the Romans, assembled from many nations, ruled the world: at first it was ruled by kings, then at times it was a democracy and at times an aristocracy, and later it returned to its former monarchy. He calls the beast fearsome and exceedingly terrible because this kingdom has become more powerful than all the others; and in the image too he made iron the fourth material, and added, "Just as iron crushes and subdues all things, so it will crush and subdue all things." Here too he says, "The beast's teeth were of iron," so that it is clear that here also he signifies the same kingdom. "It devoured," he says, "and crushed." And indeed the Romans imposed heavier tributes on their subjects. "And it trampled what was left with its feet," he says. By the feet of the kingdom he signifies the army, by which no small losses are inflicted [?] on those who live in the cities and in the countryside. "And it differed exceedingly from all the beasts before it." For the kingdom of the Romans proved more powerful and more illustrious than the kingdoms before it. "And it had," he says, "ten horns." He indicates here that toward the end of this kingdom ten kings will arise at the same time, some of whom will be powerful and others very weak. He taught this also in the dream of the image, for there too the toes of the feet were ten, and they were partly of iron and partly of clay; and the blessed Daniel, interpreting it, said that "part of the kingdom will be strong and part weak." So it is clear that both dreams signify the same things. "And it had ten horns," he says. (8.) "I was considering its horns," he says, "and behold, another horn, a small one, conspicuous, came up among them, and three of the horns before it were uprooted before it; and behold, there were eyes like the eyes of a man in this horn, and a mouth speaking great things, and it made war against the saints." Here he signifies the Antichrist, who springs up among the ten horns and uproots [?] those before him; he indicates that he will destroy three of the ten kings who will be living at the same time. He calls him a small horn because he springs from a small tribe of the Jews. "Conspicuous" [?]

…by the eyes he hinted at the shrewdness and cunning with which he will deceive many. And also “a mouth,” he says, “speaking great things,” that is, boastful and overweening things. The blessed Paul teaches us this clearly when he says: “Let no one deceive you in any way; for that day will not come unless the apostasy comes first and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship, so that he enters the temple of God and takes his seat there, proclaiming himself to be God.” Hinting at this, the blessed Daniel too said: “And a mouth speaking great things, and it made war with the saints.” For he will try everything, he says, in his eagerness to make all people sharers in his wickedness and in his punishment. But in doing these things, he says, he will not … [?]

9, 10. “For I watched,” he says, “until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took his seat. His garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was a flame of fire, its wheels burning fire. A river of fire issued forth and flowed before him; a thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The court sat, and books were opened.” The horn, he says, dared all those things, speaking great, boastful and overweening words and making war on the saints, until the court sat. We must recognize that God is incorporeal, simple and without shape. He admits no bounds and has an unbounded nature, yet he often gives shape to the visions as he wills, for our benefit. So we can see him appearing one way to Abraham, another to Moses, another again to Isaiah, and likewise he showed yet another sight to Ezekiel. So when you see how the revelations differ, do not suppose the Godhead to have many forms, but hear him saying through Hosea the prophet: “I multiplied visions, and by the hands of the prophets I was represented in likenesses.” He said “I was represented in likenesses,” not “I was seen,” for he shapes the visions as he wishes. In the same way the blessed Ezekiel saw the one who appeared as made of electrum and fire, and after describing the revelation he added: “This was the likeness of the glory of the Lord.” He did not say that he had seen the Lord himself, or even the glory of the Lord itself, but the likeness of the glory of the Lord. Here too, then, the blessed Daniel is taught God's eternity by the figure of the Ancient of Days. For so some of the translators understood it,

and in place of “Ancient of Days” they have put “he who makes the days grow old.” He sees also the purity of the hair and the brightness of the garments, and so he is taught the perfect spotlessness and holiness, not only of the divine nature, but also of what we understand as belonging to it, namely justice, providence, care and judgment. For since he had seen the horn using boastful words and stitching together countless plots against the servants of God, he is taught by that purity flashing on every side that these things are dared, not because God overlooks them, but because he permits them for the sake of his ineffable plan. And lest anyone in turn suppose that, being good, he wishes to help the saints but cannot, Daniel also sees the throne made of flame, and the wheels likewise of the nature of fire, and a river of fire carrying the throne along, and a thousand thousands ministering and ten thousand times ten thousand standing by. Through these he is taught God's power, through the former his undefiled and spotless purity, and through his great age his eternity, wisdom and gentleness. To these he adds: “The court sat, and books were opened.” That is, he judged that the time for judgment had now come, and he unrolled the record of what each person had done; for he calls the records of memory “books.” And if anyone thinks that these words also hint at the promise the Lord gave the apostles, when he said, “Twelve thrones will be set, and you will sit and judge the twelve tribes of Israel,” there is nothing unlikely in that, for the promise of the Truth cannot lie. 11. “Then I watched,” he says, “because of the sound of the great words that the horn was speaking; I kept watching until the beast was slain and perished, and its body was given over to be burned with fire.” Because of the madness of that horn, he says, when the court sat, the fourth kingdom too was destroyed, “and the body of the beast was given over to be burned with fire.” We should note that he did not say simply that the beast was given over to be burned with fire, but “its body.” By the beast he is hinting at the whole kingdom, and in that kingdom some are nurslings of piety and others are workers of wickedness, and, following divine Scripture, we are accustomed to call the former spiritual and the latter carnal. So he rightly did not say that the beast was given over to be burned with fire, but the body of the beast, that is, the coarser and carnal people, who have had no spiritual thought at all. 12. “And as for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was taken away, and a prolonging of life was given to them until

a time and a time.” For the dominion of the other beasts, he says, had already come to an end, even though they had spent a span of many years in power, for a definite time had been set for each to reign. With these things happening in this way, he says, the other kingdoms having already ceased earlier, and those of the fourth kingdom who deserved punishment having been handed over to the fire — 13, 14. “I watched,” he says, “in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a Son of Man, and he reached the Ancient of Days and was brought before him. And to him were given the honor, the dominion and the kingdom, and all peoples, tribes and tongues will serve him. His authority is an everlasting authority, which will not pass away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed.” Truly one might fittingly say to the Jews what the prophet said to them long ago: “You had a harlot's face; you became shameless toward everyone.” For what could be clearer than these words? Indeed the prophet proclaimed these things more in the manner of the Gospel and the apostles than in the riddling manner of prophecy. The Lord says in the Gospels, “You will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with his angels,” and the blessed Paul says, “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout of command, with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God, and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord.” The blessed Daniel clearly taught us this same thing when he foretold the second appearing of the Savior. He plainly calls him Son of Man because of the nature he assumed. He shows him coming on the clouds, as he himself promised, to display his authority, and receiving the honor, the dominion and the kingdom from the Ancient of Days as man. The blessed David also says this in the second psalm, speaking in the person of the Lord himself: “The Lord said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” And the blessed Daniel says this too: “For all peoples, tribes and tongues will serve him.” And to show that the kingdom has no end, he says: “His authority is an everlasting authority, which will not pass away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed.” Having written down the revelation in this way, he added: 15. “My spirit shuddered within me, I, Daniel,

and the visions of my head troubled me.” For the sight, he says, was dreadful, and my ignorance of the riddles stirred up my mind and filled it with turmoil. 16. “So I approached one of those standing there and asked him for the exact truth about all these things.” By “those standing there” he means the thousand thousands and the ten thousand times ten thousand. With these numbers he was not stating a definite figure, but indicating a multitude, beyond counting, of those ministering and those standing by. The more honored did not only stand but were also commanded to minister, while the rest showed their servitude by standing in awe. In human courts some of the attendants stand, making the court appear more fearsome, while others go out and come in, bringing replies to the judge. In the same way, in that most fearsome court Daniel saw the myriads standing by and the thousand thousands entrusted with ministering. So he approached, he says, and asked what the interpretation of the revelation was, and he learned the truth from one of those standing there. 17, 18. “For he said to me: These four great beasts are four kingdoms that will arise on the earth and will be taken away. And the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and will possess it forever, forever and ever.” We must pay careful attention to the fact that here too he spoke of four kingdoms, just as with the image there were four, and we must not think that the clay is a kingdom distinct from the iron. For there he said that the end of the iron kingdom is weaker, and here likewise he said that three horns were uprooted from among the ten, clearly because they were in a weaker state. These kingdoms, then, he says, will be dissolved, and the true and endless kingdom will be given to the saints of the Most High. So, he says, long for that kingdom, and count as nothing the kingdoms of this present age, which will shortly come to an end. Then:

19. “I inquired carefully about the fourth beast, which was different from every other beast, exceedingly fearsome. Its teeth were of iron and its claws of bronze; it devoured and crushed, and trampled what was left with its feet.” We should note that he calls the teeth iron and the claws bronze. The Roman kingdom receives tribute from all, and so he called its teeth iron. And since many from the Macedonian kingdom also serve in its heavy infantry, and soldiers are to a king what claws are to a beast, he rightly called the claws bronze, since he had also called the third kingdom bronze. For I asked, he says,

20. “also about the ten horns on its head, and about the other one that came up and shook out three of the earlier ones, that horn which had eyes and a mouth speaking great things, and whose appearance was greater than the rest.” We should not be surprised that above he called the horn small, while here he says its appearance was greater than the rest; we need to attend carefully to what is said. When he saw the horn sprouting, he called it small, because it appeared out of a small nation, that of the Jews, and its kingdom was as yet obscure. But after it had uprooted three of the horns before it, he rightly says that its appearance was greater than the rest. He then goes on asking: 21. “Why did that horn make war with the saints and prevail against them?” That is, why did it bring them low? 22. “Until the Ancient of Days came and gave judgment for the saints of the Most High, and the time arrived, and the saints took possession of the kingdom.” I begged, he says, to learn what that horn signifies, which behaves with arrogance, utters boastful words and brings low the company of the saints, until the Ancient of Days delivers his just verdict, gives the kingdom to the saints and destroys its power. 23. “And he said to me,” he says, “this: The fourth beast will be a fourth kingdom on the earth, which will surpass all the kingdoms; it will devour the whole earth, trample it down and cut it to pieces.” Those of old learned these things through riddles, but we have learned them by experience. For we see the prophecy fulfilled: the exaction of levies, the poverty that grips most people, and the other things we see happening every day. 24. “And as for its ten horns,” he says, “ten kings will arise.” We must note that he did not say they would arise one by one, each succeeding the other, but at the same time. And that this is so is confirmed by what follows: “For after them,” he says, “another king will arise, who will surpass in evils all those before him, and he will bring low three kings.” If they did not reign at the same time, but each succeeded the one before him, how will this one bring low three of his predecessors at the same time? So it is clear that he is foretelling that the ten will arise together at the end, and that the Antichrist will arise last and seize the kingdom. He will make war on them, he says, and three of them he will … [?]

“Only he who now restrains will do so until he is taken out of the way, and then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will consume with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming; his coming is according to the working of Satan, with all power and with lying signs and wonders, and with every deception of unrighteousness among those who are perishing.” What he means is this: what restrains must be taken out of the way. For the error that now holds sway will be extinguished, and the deceit of idols will cease, and then the lawless one will be revealed. The Lord too said this in the holy Gospels: “For the Gospel will be preached to all the ends of the earth as a testimony to them, and then the end will come.” Having learned this from there, the blessed Paul teaches the Thessalonians, and through them all lovers of piety: Do not think that

the enemy of the truth will appear now. First the error of idols that now holds sway must be extinguished and the preaching of the Gospels must be made strong, and only then will the lawless one be revealed. Next he points out his destruction too: “Whom the Lord Jesus,” he says, “will consume with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming.” Then he shows in what way he appears: “Whose coming,” he says, “is according to the working of Satan.” For the devil will imitate the incarnation of our God and Savior. Just as the Lord appeared through human nature and accomplished our salvation, so too the devil will take a fitting instrument of his own wickedness and through him will display his own working, deceiving the careless among men with lying signs and wonders and illusory miracles. And to teach why the God of the universe allows these things to happen, he added: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved. Therefore God will send them a working of error, so that they believe the lie, in order that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but delighted in unrighteousness.” The Lord said this very thing to the Jews: “I have come in my Father's name, and you did not receive me; another comes in his own name, and him you will receive.” Teaching these things, the angel said to Daniel: “He will speak words against the Most High, and will wear out the saints of the Most High, and will think to change times and law; and it will be given into his hand until a time, and times, and half a time. And the court sat, and they will take away his dominion, to destroy it and make it perish to the end.” See how the blessed Paul taught clearly what the angel had interpreted in riddles. And the Lord too, foretelling the uprisings against the saints, said: “There will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever will be. And if those days had not been cut short, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short.” Then he counseled his holy disciples, and through them all people, not to be deceived by those who say that the Christ is here or there, since he will no longer come secretly and in hiding, but will appear openly in glory. And he added: “Then they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory, and he will send out

his angels with a great trumpet, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other.” Foretelling these things to Daniel too, the angel added to what he had already said:

27. “And the kingdom, the authority and the greatness of the kings under the whole heaven were given to the saints of the Most High; and his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions will serve and obey him.” Here is the end of the account. That is, this is the end of all the affairs of this life: all the kingdoms of the earth will cease, and the eternal kingdom will be given to the saints of the Most High. And as they reign, they will obey him and serve him gladly, for his kingdom is eternal and admits no end. When I heard these things, he says, I, Daniel, was filled with great fear, so that my thoughts found no rest within me but were stirred up and continually troubled, and my appearance was greatly changed as a result. Yet I did not divulge the mysteries shown to me, but kept them in my heart. This, then, is what the blessed Daniel taught us. For the present I set aside my charge against the Jews. But I am truly amazed at some teachers of piety who have called the fourth beast the Macedonian kingdom. They should have noticed, first, that the third beast had four heads, which clearly indicated the division of the kingdom into four parts that took place after Alexander's death. Next, they should have observed that the fourth beast had ten horns at the same time, and that the little horn uprooted three of those before it, whereas four kings, not ten, succeeded to Alexander's kingdom. And, to pass over the rest and come to the end, they should also have noticed that he said the kingdom would be given to the saints of the Most High after the fourth beast was destroyed. That is why the court sat. But the saints of the Most High did not receive the kingdom after Antiochus Epiphanes. Even if the blessed Maccabees gained some power, it did not last very long. Judas was commander for three years, Jonathan for nineteen and Simon for eight. As for the others, so as not to lengthen my discourse by going through each one, they held power for a short time and were then either cut off by death or, while still alive, stripped of their leadership by one circumstance or another. Besides, not all of them were holy; some of them were even wicked. And even if we grant that they were all holy, Herod overthrew them and was proclaimed king of all Judea. How then can the angel's words be true, that after the overthrow of that horn the kingdom, the authority and the greatness of the kings under the whole heaven were given to the saints of the Most High, and that his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom? None of this fits the Maccabees. Nor …

[…] for they were [not] entrusted with kingship [?], but they won their victories as generals, and they quickly met their end. It remains, then, to understand the fourth beast as the Roman empire. At its end the ten kings will arise at the same time, and the last craftsman and teacher of all wickedness will appear, doing and suffering what we have been taught. After his overthrow the coming of our God and Savior will appear, and the judgment of all humanity will take place, and the books will be opened, that is, the records of what each person has lived. The body of the beast will be handed over to fire: that is, those who took sovereignty away from the soul, gave authority to the body, and followed the mind of the flesh all their lives. And the righteous Judge will give the kingdom to the saints, crying out: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you before the foundation of the world.” May we all attain it, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

CHAPTER 8. 1. “In the third year of the reign of Belshazzar a vision appeared to me, I Daniel, after the one that appeared to me at the beginning.” While the kingdom of the Chaldeans, or rather of the Assyrians, was still in power, he says, I saw another revelation after that earlier one. The date also shows that this one is later: he saw the earlier one in the first year of Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, and this one in the third. He does not give the date idly. He is teaching that he received foreknowledge of these things from the God of the universe long before the events took place. 2. “And I saw,” he says, “in the vision, and

“And I was,” he says, “at the Ubal.” “I seemed,” he says, “to be standing by the gate”; for this is how some of the translators have rendered it. 3. “And I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, a single ram standing before the Ubal, and it had high horns, and one was higher than the other, and the higher one came up last.” He sees the Persian kingdom as a ram, since it was rich and had a great abundance of resources. He sees two horns on the ram because Cyrus was the first of them to reign, yet he handed the kingdom on only as far as his sons. When his son Cambyses died, the magi held the kingdom for a few months. But shortly afterward Darius son of Hystaspes took it over, and he handed the kingdom on to his descendants and their descendants, down to the last Darius, whom Alexander the Macedonian killed and whose kingdom he took over. So the two lines of kings are signified by the two horns. He sees both as high, but the second higher than the first. For, as we have already said, the kingdom grew larger under Darius and Xerxes. Cyrus subdued the Euxine Pontus and Asia; Darius added the nomad Scythians to his subjects; and Xerxes tried to lay the yoke of his kingdom on Europe as well. This is why he sees two horns on the ram, one first and the other second, and the second higher than the first. 4. “And I saw,” he says, “the ram butting toward the sea, and the north, and the south.” It held all the northern and southern regions in subjection, and likewise the western ones as far as the sea itself; and it forced most of the islands into servitude. Thus Cyprians, Rhodians, Samians, Lesbians, Chians and all the Cyclades fought as allies of Xerxes when he made his campaign against Greece. For this reason “he saw the ram butting toward the sea, and north, and south. And none of the beasts,” he says, “will stand before it, and there was none to deliver from its hand, and it did as it pleased, and grew great.” Here again he calls the other, lesser kingdoms beasts: those of the Syrians, the Cilicians, the Arabs and the Egyptians. He names them beasts because they were fearsome to their subjects. No kingdom, then, he says, could withstand that kingdom as it butted toward the south and north and the sea. Nor could any human being set anyone free from that dominion; it carried out whatever it chose. 5. “And I,” he says, “was considering.” As I watched these things, he says, I was reasoning within myself, longing to find out what was signified by

them. And as I was inquiring, “Behold, a he-goat came from the southwest across the face of the whole earth.” In some copies this is also added: “and it did not touch the ground, and that goat had a single conspicuous horn between its eyes.” Here the riddle of the vision signified the Macedonian kingdom. He called it a he-goat because of its speed and agility, for a goat is swifter than a ram. He said it came from the southwest because it subdued Egypt first and only then came to the land of the Persians. He did defeat Darius in Cilicia; but from there he overran Syria, Phoenicia and Palestine, taking some of the cities by agreement and others by force, and set out for Egypt. Then, having taken over that kingdom too, he reached Persia and destroyed their very great kingdom. By the conspicuous horn, that is, the notable and admired horn, he means Alexander himself. He says the horn grew between the goat's eyes because Alexander's mind was shrewd, intelligent and quick. 6–7. “And the goat came,” he says, “as far as the ram that had the horns, which I saw standing before the Ubal, and ran at it in the rush of its strength. And I saw it reach the ram, and it was enraged against it, and it struck the ram and shattered both its horns, and the ram had no strength to stand before it. It threw it to the ground and trampled it, and there was none to deliver the ram from its hand.” First, engaging that king's generals in the regions of Asia, he took the whole of that territory from them. Then, when Darius met him in Cilicia with a large army, another battle took place: Darius was put to flight, and Alexander destroyed much of his army and took Darius's daughters captive. Then again, after his return from Egypt, he drew up his forces near Babylon, killed Darius himself, and destroyed the Persian kingdom. He says both its horns were shattered because the Medes and the Persians were named together. Cyrus, who reigned first, was a Mede on his mother's side and a Persian on his father's. Since their first king bore both these names, his subjects necessarily called his people both Medes and Persians, for the two kingdoms had come together into one empire. Secular writers too call them both Persians and Medes. When the ram's horns had been shattered in this way, he says, 8. “the he-goat grew exceedingly great.” For when the Persian, or rather Median, kingdom had been destroyed, Alex-

ander took power over all. But he too lived only a short time and then came to the end of his life. Blessed Daniel saw this as well. That is why he says: “And when it had grown strong, the great horn was shattered.” After that very great victory, he says, Alexander met the end common to all human beings. “And there came up,” he says, “four horns beneath it toward the four winds of heaven.” By the four horns he hints at the four kings who succeeded Alexander at the same time. Ptolemy son of Lagus took over the government of Egypt. Seleucus Nicanor held Babylon and the other regions reaching as far as Syria. Antigonus ruled Asia, and Antipater ruled Macedonia, or, as some historians think, Philip, also called Arrhidaeus, who was Alexander's brother. Note that he also saw the third beast with four heads, and the goat sprouting four horns after its one horn was broken. So it is clear that the same things are signified both by the goat and by the third beast. 9. “And from one of the horns,” he says, “came out a single strong horn.” He means Antiochus Epiphanes, the son of Antiochus called the Great. “And it grew exceedingly great toward the south, and toward the east, and toward the southwest, and toward the power.” Once he had become powerful, he says, he prevailed over the king of Egypt and brought the nations to the east under his rule. He also campaigned, he says, against the Jews and overthrew the holy mother-city. He called it “the power” because of the divine grace that then flourished in the temple. To make this clearer he added: 10. “And it grew great as far as the power of heaven, and some of the power and of the stars fell to the earth, and it trampled them.” The book of Maccabees, both the first and the second, teaches us these things more clearly, and the historian Josephus also recorded them precisely. We too will briefly recount his deeds. When members of the high-priestly family rebelled against the man who was then high priest of the Jews, those who coveted the office went to Antiochus and persuaded him to change the Jewish way of life into a Greek one and to build a gymnasium in the city. When this was done, the pious went into mourning at the sight of the open breach of the laws, while the rest of the crowd trampled on the divine law without fear and treated the commandment of circumcision with contempt. When the strife grew more violent, Antiochus arrived and killed very many of the

pious, and he even dared to enter the inner sanctuary of the temple. Once inside, he stripped the whole temple, seizing the treasures and all the votive offerings: cups, bowls and mixing bowls, the golden table, the golden altar of incense, the lampstands made of gold, and in short all the instruments of the divine service. Besides this he built an altar to Zeus in the temple of God, filled the whole city with idols, and forced everyone to sacrifice. He himself sacrificed a pig on the divine altar, and he renamed the temple the temple of Olympian Zeus. Blessed Daniel teaches all this in advance. Through the horn he sees Antiochus himself, and sees that “it grew great as far as the power of heaven”; that is, he turned his madness against the God of the universe himself, to whom both the people and the temple were dedicated. “And some of the power and of the stars fell to the earth, and it trampled them.” Very many of the people broke the law of God and fell from their heavenly rank, and they were trampled under his tyranny, having brought ruin on themselves. He called them stars because of the brilliance and splendor of their piety. He also alludes to the promise to Abraham: “I will make your offspring like the stars of heaven.” He was not content, he says, with trampling many of those called stars; 11. “he even exalted himself as far as the commander of the power.” He turned his fury and madness against the very God and King of this power, that is, of the holy people. And he kept on doing this, he says, “until the chief commander rescues the captivity”; that is, until we receive help from above and obtain salvation through the archangel appointed to protect us. Then what Antiochus would dare to do is foretold more clearly: “And because of him the sacrifice was disrupted by transgression.” He did not allow the sacrifices to be offered according to the law, but forced them to be performed in the Greek manner. Then he adds: “For it happened, and he prospered.” For the time being nothing arose to hinder his

12. “And the sanctuary,” he says, “will be made desolate, and sin was set upon the sacrifice, and righteousness was thrown to the ground, and he acted and prospered.” Acting with madness and tyranny, he dared to defile the altar with an unlawful sacrifice. He stripped the divine temple bare of its adornment, and he trampled the laws of righteousness, bringing unjust

slaughter on the pious; and for the time being, he says, “he prospered” in doing these things. Then, 13. “I heard a holy one speaking, and one holy one said to Phelmouni, who was speaking: How long will the vision stand, and the sacrifice that was taken away, and the sin of desolation that was imposed? And how long will the sanctuary and the power be trampled?” “Phelmouni” means “a certain one” in Greek. The Syriac language, which is close to Hebrew, confirms this. So blessed Daniel is saying: “I heard one holy one asking another holy one.” Clearly he sees angels conversing and wanting to learn how long the impiety and lawlessness being committed would last, along with the desolation of the temple, the unlawful and abominable sacrifice, and the oppression of the people. 14. “And he said to him,” he says, “Until evening and morning, two thousand three hundred days, and then the sanctuary will be cleansed.” He called the beginning of the calamities evening, and their end morning, since sorrows resemble night and darkness. From now, he says, that is, from the beginning of the evils, until the end, this is the length of time. When counted, these days come to six years and six months by Hebrew reckoning; for that is how long the calamity prevailed over the Jews. 15. “And when I, Daniel, saw the vision, I sought understanding.” Having seen these things, he says, I wanted to understand and learn exactly what these riddles signified. “And behold, there stood before me something like the appearance of a man.” I seemed, he says, to see a man. 16. “And I heard a man's voice between the Ubal, and he called out and said: Gabriel, make that man understand the vision.” I also heard another, speaking with a human voice, ordering the one standing beside me, whom he named Gabriel, to interpret for me the riddles of the revelation. From what has been said we can also infer that the one who gave the order is the Lord. 17. “And he came,” he says, “and stood near where I stood.” As soon as he was commanded, he says, he came and stood near me. “And when he came I was terrified, and I fell on my face.” This is enough to refute the arrogance of Eunomius, who boasts that he knows the very essence of God. If so great a prophet could not bear the sight of angels, a sight that was itself measured to the capacity of the one who saw it, what could be more impious or more loathsome than people who pride themselves on knowing the very essence of God? But let us return to our subject. “And he said

to me: Understand, son of man; for the vision is still for the end of the time.” Do not think, he says, that these things are being fulfilled now; they will happen after a great number of years. When the appointed time has been completed, then each of these things [will reach] its end.

18–19. “And while he was speaking with me I fell on my face to the ground, and he touched me and set me on my feet. And he said: Behold, I am making known to you what will happen to the sons of your people at the last of the wrath; for it still awaits the end of the time.” Seeing me fallen down in fear, he says, he first raised me up. Then he comforted me by explaining that he had come for this purpose: to foretell to me, since I longed to know, what was to come, and what would again overtake my people because of the wrath of God. Then, wishing to take away the fear that lay upon me, he made clear that these things would happen only after some time. And he interpreted for me each of the things I had seen, saying: 20. “This ram that you saw, which has the horns, is the king of the Medes and Persians.” Darius the Mede took over the kingdom of the Chaldeans, or of the Assyrians, first, and then Cyrus the Persian transferred the kingdom to the Persians; and Cyrus was both a Mede and a Persian because the two peoples had intermarried. So he necessarily placed the Medes before the Persians and says that “the ram is the king of the Medes and Persians.” For the last Darius too, called the son of Arsames, whom Alexander the Macedonian overthrew, ruled both kingdoms. 21. “And the he-goat,” he says, “is the king of the Greeks; and the great horn that was between its eyes is the first king.” He means Alexander. 22. “And as for its being shattered, and four horns rising up beneath it: four kings will arise from his nation, but not with his strength.” After his death, he says, his kingdom will be divided into four kingdoms. Though there will be four of them ruling, they will not be able to achieve what he achieved, being far inferior to his might.

23. “And at the end of their kingdom,” he says, “when their sins are reaching their full measure.” That is, when they reach the height of impiety and break the law beyond the limits of my patience. “There will arise a king with a shameless face, who understands riddles. 24. And his strength will be mighty, but not by his own strength.” By these words he alludes to the cunning of Antiochus and, besides his cunning, to the power he possessed. Then, teaching

that he will do these things only because God permits it, he necessarily added: “but not by his own strength.” God also says to the Assyrian through the prophet Isaiah: “Shall the axe be glorified without the one who cuts with it? Or shall the saw be exalted without the one who draws it?” So here too, he says, Antiochus will dare these things not because he is powerful, but because God permits it. “And he will cause astonishing destruction,” he says, “and will succeed, and will act, and will destroy the mighty and the holy people. 25. And the yoke of his collar will prosper.” That is, nothing will stand in his way; whatever he wishes, he will do. Blessed David gives advice about people like this: “Do not envy the one who prospers in his way, the man who does what is lawless.” For it often happens that even those who live in impiety and lawlessness prosper while committing grossly lawless deeds. “So the yoke of his collar will prosper”; that is, whatever he commands his subjects, he will force them to carry out. Then he foretells his cunning and treachery: “Deceit,” he says, “is in his hand, and in his heart he will grow great, and by deceit he will destroy many.” At first he ordered a gymnasium to be built in Jerusalem, then he ordered them to eat pork, and later he even forced them to sacrifice. He also used smooth words in an effort to deceive the pious, and he promised royal gifts, longing to see everyone break the law. That is why he says: “Deceit is in his hand, and in his heart he will grow great.” He considered himself the greatest of all human beings, “and by deceit he will destroy many,” namely all whom he could deceive. “And he will stand for the destruction of many”; that is, he will keep up his opposition until he sees many lose their own salvation. Not content with raging against human beings, “he will also stand,” he says, “against the ruler of rulers.” That is, he will turn his fury against the King of kings and Lord of lords himself, attempting to defile the temple dedicated to him. And to show the permission granted him against the Jews, he says: “And he will crush them like eggs in his hand.” He will accomplish all these things, he says, as easily as someone crushing eggs in his hand. Here he also hints at the negligence of the Jews themselves: because they neglected divine things, they were abandoned by God and stripped of providence from above. To this he adds: 26. “And the vision of the evening and the morning that was told is true.” That is, the time appointed for the calamities is certainly true. But since a long time lies in between,

“And you,” he says, “seal up the vision, for it is for many days.” That is: Leave it obscure to the many. To you, because you long for these things, I have made them clear before the events take place. 27. “And I, Daniel,” he says, “fell asleep and was sick for some days. Then I rose and went about the king’s business, and I was astonished at the vision, and there was no one who understood it.” Having learned of the evils that would again befall my people, I was so grieved that I even fell ill. Yet even in that state I went on managing the affairs the king had entrusted to me, and no one knew the cause of my illness. This man knew how to say with the blessed Paul: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” And: “to weep with those who weep, and to rejoice with those who rejoice.” And: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.” Such was his disposition, and such was his tender affection for his fellow servants. When he learned of the calamities that would overtake them many generations later, he kept on lamenting and wailing, even though he knew perfectly well that he himself would not experience any of them and would depart this present life before long. We too ought to have this love for those of our own race and for our fellow servants. We ought to be of one mind toward one another and to imitate the sympathy the members of a body have for one another, since we have been called members of one another and have been counted worthy to be named the body of Christ. To him be glory to the ages of ages. Amen.

1. “In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, who reigned over the kingdom of the Chaldeans, in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, understood from the books the number of the years about which the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah the prophet for the completion of the desolation of Jerusalem: seventy years.”

From this too it is clear that the kingdom of Darius the son of Ahasuerus was one thing and that of Cyrus the Persian another. What has now been read also agrees with what was said earlier. He did not simply call Darius a Mede but said “of the seed of the Medes.” This makes it clear that he was not a Mede on both sides, I mean on his father’s side and his mother’s. All the same, he reigned over the kingdom of the Chaldeans after Belshazzar had been killed by night, struck down by God for his impiety. It seems to me that this Darius reigned for a very short time. For the blessed Daniel saw that the term of the captivity had now been fulfilled. He reckoned up the number of the seventy years that the God of all had foretold through the prophet Jeremiah, and he began to offer supplication to the Master on behalf of the people. The time was fulfilled under Cyrus, king of the Persians, as the blessed Ezra says. Right at the beginning of his book, after the preface, he briefly recalls the capture of Jerusalem, the enslavement of the homeland and the deportation of the captives to Babylon, and then adds: “And they were servants to him and to his sons until the Persians reigned, to fulfil the word of the Lord by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed its sabbaths. All the time of its desolation it shall keep sabbath, to complete seventy years, in the first year of the reign of Cyrus over the Persians, for the accomplishment of the word of the Lord by the mouth of Jeremiah.” The most divine Jeremiah also speaks this way: “Behold, I will send and take the family of the north, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring him against this land, against those who live in it, and against all the nations around them. I will utterly destroy them and make them a desolation, a hissing and an everlasting reproach. I will take from them the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the scent of perfume and the light of the lamp. The whole land shall become a desolation, and they shall serve among the nations for seventy years. And when the seventy years are fulfilled, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation for their iniquities, says the Lord, and the land of the Chaldeans, and I will make them an everlasting desolation.” So the blessed Jeremiah hinted that the time of the captivity would be completed with the overthrow of the Chaldean kingdom, while Ezra made this even clearer by mentioning Cyrus. But we find that the most divine Zechariah reckons this period differently. For after the death of Cyrus and of his son Cambyses, when Darius the son of Hystaspes [Apparatus: B: “previously said”; “for at the beginning” [?]. had taken up the rule of the Persians, the prophet records the date: “On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month Shebat, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah the prophet, the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo.” Shortly afterwards he adds: “And the angel of the Lord answered and said: Lord Almighty, how long will you withhold mercy from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which you have disregarded? This is the seventieth year.” Some who are sick with unbelief think that the holy prophets disagree. But those who have been nurtured on the sacred words and are enlightened by divine grace discover the harmony of the holy prophets. Come, then, let us pray to receive that radiance and make this harmony plain to those who do not know it. All of them set down the time of the captivity in agreement: the divine Jeremiah, the inspired Zechariah and the blessed Ezra all give the number of seventy years. But they do not begin counting this period from the same point, and so some said the number ended with Cyrus and another with Darius. Jeremiah and Ezra count from the beginning of the first captivity, so they rightly end the seventy years with Cyrus, king of the Persians. The most divine Zechariah counts from the last siege, in which the people suffered utter destruction, and says that the number of seventy years was completed under Darius, king of the Persians. And in fact it was under Darius that the divine temple was rebuilt. The people were taken captive three times: first under Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah; second under Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim; and third under Zedekiah, the brother of Jehoiakim and uncle of Jeconiah. So they also had to return three times. First Cyrus the Persian released them, then Darius the son of Hystaspes, and then Artaxerxes the son of Xerxes, when he sent first Ezra and after him Nehemiah to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. For the first captives, then, the seventy-year period was fulfilled under Cyrus the Persian. For the desolation of the temple, the same period came to its end in the second year of Darius the son of Hystaspes. So both prophecies, Jeremiah’s and Zechariah’s, and likewise Ezra’s history, are free of falsehood and true. The blessed Daniel, he says, understood this period, reckoned it and found that it was drawing near. 3. “I set my face,” he says, “toward the Lord God, to seek him by prayer and supplication, with fasting, sackcloth and ashes.” I did not simply wait for release from captivity, he says, but offered supplication to the Master and asked for freedom for my kinsmen. For even if he promises

good things ten thousand times, if we make ourselves unworthy of the gift, we become an obstacle to the divine promise [?]. God says this through the prophet Ezekiel too: “At another time I will speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build it up and to plant it. But if that nation turns and does evil, I will not bring upon it all the good that I spoke of.” Having been taught this, the blessed Daniel gave his prayer wings “with fasting, sackcloth and ashes” and offered it to God. 4. “And I prayed,” he says, “to the Lord my God, and made confession, and said: O Lord God, great and wonderful, who keeps covenant and mercy with those who love you and keep your commandments.” He calls him great and wonderful because he is able to do great and wonderful things. Holy men like to give God his titles from his works. He said that God keeps covenant and mercy with those who love him, recalling the promises made to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Praying with complete precision, he teaches that God keeps them not unconditionally, but “with those who love him and keep his commandments.” For if anyone transgresses your commandments, he says, he makes himself unworthy of your promises. And this is what has happened to us. 5. “For we have sinned,” he says, “we have done wrong, we have acted impiously, and we have turned aside from your commandments and your judgments.” Having very fittingly applied those honourable and wonderful titles to God, he applied the diametrically opposite ones to his people. He was not content to say “we have sinned” but added “we have done wrong and acted impiously.” That is, we were ungrateful for your benefits. And we acted impiously by choosing other gods instead of you, lifeless and senseless gods that have no strength. Then, to show God’s continual care for them and the great callousness of the people, he added: 6. “And we did not listen to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, to our rulers, to our fathers and to all the people of the land.” Your grace never stopped watching over us and speaking to us through the prophets, sometimes to kings and rulers, sometimes to priests and teachers (for these are the ones he calls fathers), and often to the whole people. Yet even so we persisted in contradicting them. So he rightly added: 7. “To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness, and to us shame

of face, as at this day, to the men of Judah, to those who live in Jerusalem and to all Israel, those near and those far off, in every land where you have scattered them because of the faithlessness with which they broke faith with you, O Lord.” What you have done, Master, he says, proclaims your righteousness. But we, who have been brought to shame by our great lawlessness, accuse our own ingratitude. Our impiety did you no harm; it is we who have reaped the fruit of what we sowed. And it is moving that, in accusing his kinsmen, he joins himself to the transgressors. 8. “To us,” he says, “belongs shame of face, to our kings, to our rulers and to our fathers, because we have sinned against you.” Each of these words is enough to bend even the cruellest of men to pity, let alone the gentlest and most loving of all. His words show that it was not only the poor and obscure among the people who were covered with shame, but also the kings themselves, the rulers and the priests, for these are the ones he called fathers. And to show that the punishment was just, he added: “because we have sinned against you.” We have received the fruits our lawlessness deserved, 9. “but to the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness.” It befits you, who are gentle and loving, to treat us with mercy and compassion. He persists in accusing their lawlessness, for he had heard God saying through another prophet: “First tell your iniquities, so that you may be justified.” So he makes the people’s lawlessness his own and accuses it, while appealing to the divine mercy. 10. “For we turned away,” he says, “and did not obey the voice of the Lord our God, to walk in his laws, which he set before us through his servants the prophets.” Though the prophets enlightened us, he says, and guided us toward what was right, we went on contradicting them the whole time. 11. “And all Israel transgressed your law and turned aside so as not to hear your voice.” If some had transgressed while others had been strict guardians of your laws, they would not have suffered this calamity. But since all had dared to break the law together, he rightly says: “The curse and the oath written in the law of Moses, the servant of God, have come upon us, because we sinned against him.” By the oath he means the one God made in Deuteronomy: “For I will lift up my hand to heaven,” he says, “and swear by my right hand, and

say: As I live for ever, I will sharpen my sword like lightning, and my hand shall take hold of judgment. I will take vengeance and render justice to my enemies, and I will repay those who hate me. I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh, with the blood of the slain and the captives, from the heads of the rulers of the nations.” A little before this he says: “I said: I will scatter them, and I will make the memory of them cease from among men.” By the curse he means the one pronounced by the six tribes on Mount Ebal. That oath, he says, and the curse in the law of Moses, have been fulfilled upon us. 12. “And he has confirmed the words that he spoke against us and against our judges who judged us, by bringing great evils upon us.” And to show the extremity of the evils, he says: “such as have never happened under the whole heaven as have happened in Jerusalem.” For I can find nothing to compare with our evils, he says. Then, to teach that the divine prediction did not lie: 13. “As it is written,” he says, “in the law of Moses.” And to show that the punishment was just: “All these evils have come upon us, yet we did not entreat the face of the Lord our God, turning from our iniquities and gaining understanding in all your truth, O Lord.” Not even when so many and such great calamities had been brought upon us were we willing to repent, to give up our former lawlessness and to serve you by keeping the laws. So he says: 14. “The Lord our God kept watch over our wickedness and brought it upon us.” As though shaking off his long-suffering like a kind of sleep, he brought upon us the punishment our conduct deserved. “For holy,” he says, “is the Lord our God in all the works he has done, because we did not obey his voice.” He is guiltless, he says, and deserves no blame for what he has done. It is we who lived in impiety and wickedness and so brought the punishment on ourselves. Having made this accusation of lawlessness, he now turns to supplication and asks for loving-kindness. 15–16. “And now, O Lord our God, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand and made a name for yourself, as at this day: we have sinned, we have acted lawlessly. O Lord, in all your mercy, let your anger turn away from your city Jerusalem, your holy mountain.” He recalls God’s former benefits, by the gratitude

These things will be spoken in riddles, and you need careful understanding to grasp them. Divine things are spoken and written in riddles so that what is revealed to the saints may not be plain to everyone; for in that case they would easily have become despised, being known alike by all. He calls him a "man of desires" either because he had given himself over to fasting and hardship and was manfully struggling against the desires of the body, or because he desired to know and longed to learn what would befall the people, or because he is lovely and exceedingly lovable, sending forth the flashing rays of virtue. Having thus roused the prophet to understand what was about to be said, the divine archangel offers his teaching. 24. "Seventy weeks have been determined upon your people and upon your holy city, until the transgression grows old and sin is brought to completion, and to seal sin, and to wipe away iniquities, and to make atonement for wrongdoing, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal vision and prophet, and to anoint a Holy of Holies." Before anything else we must note that the prophet in his prayer had spoken to God about the people and Jerusalem, saying, "Your people, and your city, and your sanctuary"; God turns this around and says to Daniel, "Seventy weeks have been determined upon your people and upon your holy city," as though he no longer deigned to call his own the people long named his people, or indeed the city likewise long called his. He did the same in the case of the great Moses. For when they had fashioned the calf and offered it divine worship, God said to the prophet, "Hurry, go down from here quickly, for your people, whom you brought out of Egypt, have acted lawlessly." So God says to Daniel through the archangel: "I have accepted your petition: I will allow Jerusalem to be rebuilt, and I will command your people to obtain their return. After the rebuilding of Jerusalem they will continue for four hundred and ninety years, living under the law"; for the seventy weeks make that length of time, each day being taken as a year. [?] he limited their captivity to a period [of seventy years?], and by multiplying this period sevenfold by itself he sets the limit of their life under the law. "Seventy weeks have been determined" means "have been tested and judged," for that is how some of the translators have rendered it, "upon your people and upon your

holy city, until the transgression grows old and sin is brought to completion"; that is, until their impious outrage increases and sin reaches its end. By "sin brought to completion" and "transgression growing old" — that is, increasing and arriving at its extreme — he means the cross they dared to inflict on the Lord. Before this, though they had dared countless evils, they paid the penalty and suffered punishment for their offenses, but then obtained pardon again and were thought worthy of kindness. After their madness against the Master, however, and the cross they dared to inflict, they obtained no recall, as the facts themselves cry out: more than four hundred and forty years have passed, and they have remained scattered, sojourners throughout the world. This is why the holy archangel says to blessed Daniel: "Seventy weeks have been determined upon your people and upon your holy city, until the transgression grows old and sin is brought to completion." And since Christ the Master was going to grant forgiveness of sins to those who believe in him, as blessed John also cried out, saying, "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world," he fittingly added: "and to seal sins, and to wipe away iniquities, and to make atonement for wrongdoings." For he wiped away the iniquities of those who believed in him, having blotted out the bond that stood against us, as blessed Paul says. And he sealed up sins by putting an end to life under the law and granting the grace of the Spirit, with whose help those who live spiritually overcome the passions. To these he added: "and to bring in everlasting righteousness." Everlasting righteousness is, in the proper sense, Christ the Master himself. For blessed Paul says of him, "He was given to us as wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." And writing to the Romans about the Gospel he said, "The righteousness of God is revealed in it." Since, then, in his generosity he bestowed on those who believed in him the righteousness that brings eternal life — the righteousness he also told them to ask for when they pray, saying, "Ask for the kingdom of God and his righteousness" — holy Gabriel necessarily said, "and to bring in everlasting righteousness." He had also put forward: "and to seal vision and prophet"; that is, to bring all the prophecies to their end — "For Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes" — and from then on to stop the grace of prophecy among the Jewish nation. For if Christ the Master had not appeared and done and suffered what the prophets foretold, the truth of the prophets would not have been

shown. So he fulfills, and as it were seals and confirms, what the prophets foretold, doing and suffering everything they had prophesied. To these again he added: "and to anoint a Holy of Holies." Who is this Holy One of the holies? Let the Jews say. And if they do not know, let them learn from us that it is Christ the Master himself, who foretells through Isaiah, "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me," and to whom David bears witness: "He loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions." Blessed Peter, the chief of the apostles, also bears witness, saying: "Jesus of Nazareth — how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power; he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him." So blessed Daniel the prophet is taught that it had been decreed to grant Jerusalem a period of four hundred and ninety years to enjoy the divine gifts as it was accustomed, until it should dare that unholy and dreadful outrage — I mean the cross against the Savior. He is named Holy of Holies, since he is the source of holiness; he is anointed with the Holy Spirit in his humanity, he seals and confirms the ancient prophecies by fulfilling everything they foretold, and he grants forgiveness of sins to those who believe in him. Then the divine archangel teaches where the count of the seventy weeks must begin. 25. "And you will know," he says, "and understand: from the going forth of the word to answer and to rebuild Jerusalem until Christ the leader, there are seven weeks and sixty-two weeks." Now some suppose that the start of the rebuilding under Cyrus is the start of the count of the weeks, while others begin the count from the sixth year of the reign of Darius son of Hystaspes, since that was when the building of the temple reached its proper completion. In the intervening time the neighboring peoples, out of hostility toward the Jews, had obstructed the building, and Cambyses son of Cyrus, deceived by them, had stopped it. But neither view is true. First, anyone who chose to count from there would find a larger number of years. Second, one cannot find in anyone else the wiping away of sins, the forgiveness of wrongs, the gift of everlasting righteousness, the fulfillment of the prophetic oracles, and the anointing of a Holy of Holies; these are found in Christ the Master alone.

If this is so, and those who tell us to count the weeks in this way agree, let them count the four hundred and ninety years from the end backward. For if we begin counting from the manifestation that took place at the Jordan, when our Savior and Lord began to preach, teach and work miracles, and go back in time, we will find that this number reaches not only not as far as Cyrus, but not even as far as Darius. Instead it is completed in the twentieth year of the reign of Artaxerxes son of Xerxes. At that time Nehemiah, who was this king's cupbearer, was moved by zeal; he entreated God and, receiving help from above, begged the king to entrust him with building the walls of Jerusalem. Finding the king favorable, he reached his homeland and with all eagerness added what was still lacking to the divine temple. He also raised the walls of the city, fortified them with towers on every side, and set up the gates; and by urging on the priests he filled the city, which had been empty of inhabitants, with residents. It was this that the divine archangel was hinting at when he said: "And you will know and understand: from the going forth of the word to answer and to rebuild Jerusalem until Christ the leader, there are seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. And it will return, and street and wall will be built, and the times will be renewed." What he means is: if you begin counting from the rebuilding of the city — when it recovered its own walls and received a multitude of inhabitants, so that it became broad because of the multitude living in it — you will find seven weeks and sixty-two weeks until Christ the leader. He again gave the name "Christ the leader" to the one he had called Holy of Holies, just as blessed Peter said when addressing the Jews: "You killed the Leader of life, whom God raised from the dead, loosing the pangs of death." He is our leader in his humanity, as the firstborn of all creation — that is, of the new creation: "For if anyone is in Christ," he says, "he is a new creation." He is also the firstborn from the dead, "so that," Paul says, "he might come to have first place in everything." For this reason holy Gabriel too called him "Christ the leader." So until him, from the rebuilding of Jerusalem, there are "seven weeks and sixty-two weeks." But so that no one may suppose we are talking idle nonsense, come, let us set out the actual number of years. From the twentieth year of the reign of Artaxerxes son of Xerxes, under whom Nehemiah came to Jerusalem and began to raise the walls
