of the city, to Darius son of Arsames, whom Alexander the Macedonian killed and so brought the kingdom of the Persians to an end, there are one hundred and fourteen years. From the sixth year of Alexander, in which Darius was killed, to Gaius Julius Caesar, the first emperor of the Romans, the years of the Macedonian kingdom total two hundred and eighty-two. From the reign of Julius Caesar to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when John the Baptist came to the Jordan preaching a baptism of repentance and crying out, "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world," there are seventy-three years. Added together, these make a total of four hundred and sixty-nine years, and this equals four hundred and eighty-three Hebrew years, which is what the seven and sixty-two weeks amount to. For we must know that the Hebrews, who reckon the year by the course of the moon, produce eleven surplus days, which we also call intercalary; for the moon's course is completed in twenty-nine days and six hours, and reckoning in this way they make the year three hundred and fifty-four days long. Since, then, the holy archangel was speaking with blessed Daniel, a Hebrew, and teaching him the number of the years, he was surely using the customary reckoning. So we must add the years that the intercalary days amount to, for when these are added, four hundred and eighty-three years will be found, and that is the total of the seven and sixty-two weeks. He did not divide them without reason, but to signal in advance certain changes in affairs. From the rebuilding of Jerusalem under Nehemiah and Ezra up to Hyrcanus, the last high priest of the Hasmoneans, whom Herod killed, the number of the sixty-two weeks is completed; and from his murder to the manifestation of our Savior and his coming to the Jordan, the remaining seven weeks run their course. During this time — I mean from the killing of Hyrcanus to the manifestation of our Savior — the high priests were from then on appointed unlawfully. For although the law commanded the high priests to serve for life, and their successors to take over after their death, Herod, and the Romans after him, made the high priesthood something to be bought, and so made the succession frequent; and they appointed as high priests some men who were not even descended from the priestly family. Josephus, the Hebrew historian, teaches this, saying: "Herod, having been entrusted with the kingdom by the Romans, no longer appointed high priests from the Hasmonean family (these were the so-called Maccabees), but certain obscure men who were merely Hebrews." And

a little later he says again: "Archelaus his son acted like Herod in appointing the Jewish high priests, and after him so did the Romans, when they had taken over the government." And elsewhere he says: "Valerius Gratus, the Roman governor, removed Ananus from the priesthood and declared Ishmael son of Phabi high priest. Not long after, he removed him too and appointed as high priest Eleazar, the son of Ananus the high priest. When a year had passed he removed him as well and handed the high priesthood to Simon son of Kathimus. Nor did this man hold the honor for more than a year, and Joseph, also called Caiaphas, succeeded him." Blessed Luke also teaches this, saying: "In the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas." Yet we have never learned of two high priests holding office lawfully at the same time. Foretelling these things, the holy [?]

26. "And after the sixty-two weeks," he says, "the anointing will be destroyed, and there is no judgment in it." This makes it clear that he has put the sixty-two weeks first, and the seven after them, in which, he says, "the anointing will be destroyed" — that is, the grace that flourished upon the high priests. And since those who were unlawfully appointed were also called high priests, he fittingly added: "and there is no judgment in it." For even if they are anointed, he means, they are not anointed rightly; rather they dare to do this unlawfully. Earlier, too, he had made it clear that he put the seven weeks last: "until Christ the leader, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks." For he placed the seven [?] weeks right next to his mention of Christ the leader, so that we might know that if we wish to count backward from Christ, we will find the seven weeks first and then the sixty-two. And he makes this clearer still: "It will return," he says, "and street and wall will be built, and the times will be renewed" — that is, the time before the rebuilding. "And after the sixty-two weeks," he says, "the anointing will be destroyed." He did not say after the seven, but after the sixty-two, after which come the seven, "in which the anointing will be destroyed, and there is no judgment in it." For Herod, a foreigner, was reigning — he was an Ascalonite on his father's side and an Idumaean on his mother's — and the so-called high priests were not appointed according to the law, but by foreign rulers: Herod and Archelaus and the Roman

governors. Then he also speaks of the utter destruction that will overtake the city, and this very foreign kingship, and the unlawful high priesthood: "And he will destroy the city and the sanctuary together with the leader who is coming." For the city, he says, will be laid waste, and the holy temple will suffer total destruction. The city will suffer this together with "the leader who is coming," that is, with the lawless rulers who are coming; for by "the coming leader" he meant the foreign kingship and the unlawful high priesthood. Then, teaching that they will endure evils far worse than those before, he added: "And they will be cut off as in a flood"; that is, they will suffer utter destruction, such as the people of old suffered when the flood covered the whole earth. And teaching that they will obtain no recall or relief, he says: "And until the end of a war cut short by desolations." For they will suffer complete desolation, he means, handed over to war as to a kind of flood; they will be bowed down under these evils to the end, and will never obtain any recall. Having thus foretold the utter destruction of the Jews, he returns again to the count of the seventy weeks, adds the week still lacking to the sixty-nine, and says: 27. "And one week will confirm a covenant with many, and in half of the week sacrifice and libation will be taken away, and upon the temple there will be an abomination of desolation, and until the consummation of time a consummation will be given upon the desolation." "I have already told you," he says, "what will happen in the seven weeks after the sixty-two weeks; but you should also learn what will take place in the remaining week. In it the New Covenant will be given to believers, and it will fill them with every power. And in the middle of this week, sacrifice and libation will be taken away." The sacrifice under the law will cease when the true sacrifice is offered, that of the spotless Lamb who takes away the sin of the world. For once this has been offered, that other sacrifice will come to an end. For this reason, as soon as the sacrifice was accomplished and our Savior gave up his spirit, the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom, making what had long been unseen visible to all, and showing that what had been untouchable and inaccessible was now accessible. For since the veil separated the holy place from the Holy of Holies, which contained the mercy seat, the cherubim and the ark, the tearing of the veil right through showed by the event itself that the grace dwelling among the things within had departed, and that they had become

common property, since the sacrifice had been offered for the whole world. If anyone also wishes to learn the time, he will learn it from the Gospel according to John. The Lord preached for about three and a half years and, after strengthening his holy disciples by his teaching and his miracles, he then underwent his passion. After the cross and death, the resurrection, the ascension into heaven, and the coming of the Holy Spirit, the holy apostles spent the rest of the week in Jerusalem preaching and working miracles; they led many thousands of people to the teaching of the Gospel, made them worthy of the New Covenant, and prepared them to receive the grace of all-holy baptism. Then, after what the Jews dared to do to holy Stephen, the others were scattered through the cities of Judea, while the divine apostles, after staying a short time in Jerusalem, went about Samaria and Caesarea, Lydda and Joppa, hastening to offer the saving doctrines to all people. This is why the divine archangel says to blessed Daniel, "One week will confirm a covenant with many," joining together the time before the Lord's cross and the teaching of the holy apostles in Jerusalem after the Savior's resurrection. Then he divides the week in two and says: "And in half of the week sacrifice and libation will be taken away." For when the true sacrifice is offered, the shadow of the law will come to an end. And in addition he says: "Upon the temple an abomination of desolation." For because of this sacrifice, he means, not only will that sacrifice cease, but an abomination of desolation will be set upon the temple; that is, what was once revered and awe-inspiring will be shown to be desolate. A sign of the desolation will be certain images, forbidden by the law, being brought into it. Pilate did this when he brought the imperial images into the divine temple by night, in violation of the divine law. The Lord, too, foretold this to his holy disciples in the sacred Gospels: "When you see the abomination of desolation spoken of through Daniel the prophet, know that its desolation has drawn near. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let the one on the housetop not come down to take anything out of his house." He said this to indicate how swiftly the utter destruction would overtake them. And a little before this he says: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing

[?]… you were not willing. Therefore I tell you that your house is left to you desolate.” The holy Gabriel foretold these things. After prophesying the end of the worship prescribed by the law, he added: “And upon the temple, the abomination of desolation.” So that the Jews would not think they would one day recover the former beauty and glory of the divine temple, he had to add: “And until the consummation of the time, a consummation shall be given upon the desolation.” For until the consummation of the age, he says, the consummation of the desolation will remain and will admit no change. The blessed David said the same: “In the wrath of consummation, and they shall be no more; and they shall know that God rules over Jacob and over the ends of the earth.” They will know it when they see the sign of the Son of Man in heaven. For then “they will mourn, tribe by tribe”; then “they will look on him whom they pierced.” But if this is not so, let them show in whose time the archangel’s oracle was fulfilled. The four hundred and ninety years have run their course, and more than four hundred and forty more besides. Was it fulfilled in the time of the Maccabees? But there are not four hundred and ninety years from Darius to them, nor even from Cyrus, the first to reign over the Persians. From Cyrus to Antiochus Epiphanes, in whose time the Maccabees took matters in hand out of zeal, there are about three hundred and seventy-two years. Besides, which of these men has been called Holy of Holies? Judas, or Jonathan, or Simon, or the one who came after them? Indeed, neither Abraham the patriarch, nor Moses the lawgiver, nor Elijah the greatest of the prophets was ever given the title Holy of Holies. So both the time and the titles clearly foretold to us the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Since we have believed in him and await his second coming, let us pray to obtain his loving-kindness on the day of judgment. May we all obtain it, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

1. “In the third year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, a word was revealed to Daniel, whose name was called Belteshazzar.” Some think the date is mistaken. They suppose that the original writer of the book put “third” where it should have been “in the first year.” As evidence they point to what the blessed Daniel said right after the beginning of the prophecy: “And Daniel continued until one year of King Cyrus.” “If the prophet lived on only until the first year of Cyrus’s reign,” they say, “how does he see the revelation in the third year?” But I think the earlier statement did not indicate a fixed date, nor did it limit the life of the blessed Daniel to the first year of Cyrus’s reign. For he did not say, “until the first year of King Cyrus,” but “until one year.” As it seems to me, he wanted to teach readers of the prophetic writing that Daniel lived on even into the reign of Cyrus, king of the Persians. Cyrus set free those of the captive Jews who wished to go, and ordered them to return to their homeland and rebuild the divine temple. The holy angel teaches us this clearly as well, when he speaks with Daniel a little later: “And it came to pass in the first year of Cyrus, I stood for strength and power.” That is: as soon as Cyrus became king, I kept working at everything to free the people from captivity. And at the end of the book he says: “Cyrus the Persian received the kingdom, and Daniel was the king’s companion, honored above all his friends.” So the number of the third year is confirmed on every side. In the third year of Cyrus’s reign, then, the word was revealed to Daniel, whose name was called Belteshazzar. “And the word is true, and great power and understanding was given to him in the vision.” He rightly calls it both a word and a vision. He saw holy angels, heard them conversing, and learned exactly what was to come. He says that the word is true, so that everyone would accept what was about to be said without hesitation. 2, 3. “In those days I, Daniel, was mourning for three weeks of days. Desirable bread … ”

The whole people also enjoyed great peace because of the king’s mildness. Indeed, anyone who studies the prophecy of the blessed Jeremiah, the history in Chronicles and the book of Ezra will find that in the first year of his reign Cyrus urged every Jew who wished to return to his homeland and rebuild the divine temple. So the prophet had reasons for joy on every side. Yet if one examines each of these things closely, one will find that these very things caused Daniel’s grief. The king allowed freedom and return to all who wished it. But most of them had built houses in Babylon, and that bond held them fast. They despised the return and preferred the foreign land to their own. Only the lovers of piety and the guardians of the ancestral laws despised their possessions in Babylon and preferred their desolate homeland even to the kingdom itself. This caused the blessed Daniel the greatest grief. He saw the truthfulness of the divine promise and the gentleness and humanity of the king, and he also saw the disobedience and unruliness of the people. This wore his soul down terribly, and he kept on mourning and lamenting. One might reasonably ask why he mourned and wailed over the others for being slack and despising the return, yet did not go back to his homeland himself. The answer will be found by considering the cause of the captivity itself. God did not allow him to become a captive because of his own faults. He did so out of concern for the people’s benefit, sending him with them as a kind of guardian and teacher. In the same way, at the time of the return, since most of them were content to live in Babylon, the divine prophet was again compelled to live among them, so that, deprived of spiritual care, they would not run aground completely in impiety. For this reason, although the king who then ruled honored his piety, showed him every attention and preferred him to all others, the blessed Daniel found no consolation. The people’s disobedience and their forgetfulness of the holy city distressed him and grieved him deeply. This is why he went without food for three weeks. “For desirable bread,” he says, “I did not eat, and meat and wine did not enter my mouth, and I did not anoint myself with oil, until three

weeks of days.” That is, he says: in all these days I gave my body no care at all, neither oil on the outside nor food on the inside. He did well, and very aptly, to attach the word “desirable” not to meat but to bread. Bread is everyone’s necessary food. The wealthier enjoy meat, but the poorer enjoy bread as much as the wealthier do. That is why he called bread “desirable”: it is the common food and the most delightful of all foods. 4. “And on the twenty-fourth day of the first month, in the third year, I was beside the great river, which is the Tigris.” We must also note the month and the days of the fast, because they expose the lawlessness of the Jews. The divine law commands that the Passover be kept toward evening on the fourteenth of the first month, yet the blessed Daniel went without food until the twenty-fourth. The Jews may say that he ate no desirable bread because he was eating unleavened bread. But in the first place they show their own folly by saying this, since both leavened and unleavened bread are called bread. Then what follows plainly stops their shameless mouths: “For meat and wine,” he says, “did not enter my mouth.” If he did not eat meat, how did he keep the Passover? The Passover is nothing other than an unblemished male lamb a year old, sacrificed and roasted toward evening. So how could a man who ate no meat keep the Passover? He did not keep the Passover, then, because he obeyed the law, which expressly commands that the three feasts be kept in the place that the Lord God chooses. Clearly, then, the Jews break the law when they dare to keep these feasts in a foreign land. But let us return to our subject. “On the twenty-fourth,” he says, “of the first month, in the third year, I was beside the great river, which is the Tigris.” Here again we learn that the date is not mistaken, since here too he said he saw the vision in the third year and not the first. 5, 6. “And I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, a man clothed in baddim, and his loins were girded with gold of Uphaz. And his body was like Tarshish.” In Greek, baddim means linen. He says, then, that he saw the one who appeared wearing a garment of linen and a belt of gold of Uphaz, that is, of the most brilliant and purest gold. “And his body was like Tarshish” means that it looked like the finest gold, brought from Tarshish; for Solomon’s refined

gold was brought from there. “And his face was like the appearance of lightning.” [?] A light-filled radiance, he says, shone from his face. “And his eyes were like torches of fire, and his arms and legs like the appearance of gleaming bronze, and the sound of his words like the sound of a multitude.” His eyes, he says, gave off fire, and his arms looked like the finest bronze. Hearing him, you would have thought you were hearing a great crowd talking. 7. “And I, Daniel, alone saw the vision. The men who were with me did not see the vision, but a great trance fell upon them, and they fled in fear.” Someone may ask why they fled if they did not see the vision. By “trance” he means here not only their fear but also their inability to see. This resembles what happened to the blessed Paul on the road near Damascus. There he himself saw a light flash around him, while those with him saw nothing and heard only the voice. In the same way here, those with the divine prophet flee, having heard only the voice, and he alone remains. 8. “For I,” he says, “was left alone, and I saw this great vision, and no strength was left in me. My glory was turned to corruption, and I retained no strength.” That is: such fear fell on me from that sight that my joints came loose, the color of my skin changed, and I was left bereft of all strength [?]

You showed yourself stronger than the body’s desires and became a lover of divine things, and in your tender love for the people you longed to learn what would happen to them. He calls him Daniel and not Belteshazzar. The latter was a Chaldean name and the former a Hebrew one; the one was given by the pious, the other added by the impious. In Greek, “Daniel” means “judgment of God.” So his name fits him, and the events themselves proclaim that God, using right and just judgment, counted him worthy of the grace of prophecy and made plain to him what would happen many generations later. “And when he had spoken this word to me, I stood up trembling.” That is: the word was enough to raise me up, but I did not shake off my fear entirely. 12. “And he said to me: Do not be afraid, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and to afflict yourself before the Lord your God, your words were heard, and I have come in your words.” This teaches us how much good voluntary affliction does us. The blessed Daniel afflicted himself by voluntary fasting and sought the Lord, and at once he won him over and obtained what he longed for. The one who appeared to him makes this clear: “From the first day,” he says, “that you set your heart to understand and to afflict yourself before the Lord your God, your words were heard.” And you have the greatest proof of this in my coming. “For I have come,” he says, “in your words.” That is: because of your words and the [?] you offered.

13. “And the prince,” he says, “of the kingdom of the Persians stood against me for twenty-one days.” On the very first day of your [?], he says, as soon as your supplication was received, I was sent to you. But all these days the prince of the kingdom of the Persians kept me from coming to you. “And behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, and I left him there with the prince of the king of the Persians.” The blessed Moses teaches us this more clearly: “When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.” And in the holy Gospels the Lord says to the apostles: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones, for their angels daily see the face of my Father in heaven.” And there are many other such passages in divine Scripture. From these, then, we learn

that each of the angels has been entrusted with the care of one of us, to guard and protect us and to rescue us from the plots of the evil demon, while the archangels have been entrusted [?] with the oversight of the nations, as the blessed Moses taught. The blessed Daniel agrees with this. He too speaks of a prince of the kingdom of the Persians, and a little later of a prince of the Greeks, and he calls Michael the prince of Israel. Since all this is clear from both sources, we must ask why the prince of the Persian kingdom seemed to oppose the one who was pleading on the people’s behalf. That the nature of angels is above passions and full of holiness is plain to everyone. That they follow the divine will without hesitation can likewise be learned from every part of Scripture. How, then, did the prince of the kingdom of the Persians seem to oppose the care shown to the Israelites? Anyone willing to consider the matter carefully will find the meaning of these words. The prince of the Persians and the prince of the Greeks were those entrusted with guarding and caring for these nations. Naturally they loved those in their care. Seeing the lawlessness of Israel, they were vexed to see the Israelites enjoying greater providence. For they did not know the mystery hidden in God who created all things. As the blessed Paul said, it was only after our Savior’s incarnation [?] that the manifold wisdom of God was made known through the Church to the principalities and powers. Not knowing this mystery, then, and seeing God’s great providence toward Israel, those entrusted with the care of the other nations were vexed. What vexed them most was to see that, after the law, the prophets and so much teaching and care, the Israelites were in a worse state than the nations they themselves shepherded, and entangled in more evils. This is what the angel who appeared to the blessed Daniel meant: “And the prince of the kingdom of the Persians stood against me for twenty-one days.” That is: all these days I kept trying to persuade him that these people rightly receive this providence, and Michael, who is one of the chief princes, supported my case. “And I left him there,” he says, “with the prince of the kingdom of the Persians.” 14. “And I have come to make you understand what will happen to your people in the last days, for behold, the vision is for days to come.” That is, he says: when I came to you to teach you in advance what would happen to your people before long, Michael stayed behind, conversing with the prince of the kingdom of the Persians. And he did not simply say “the prince of the Per-
-sians,” but “the prince of the kingdom of the Persians,” meaning the one entrusted [?] with ruling even the king of the Persians himself.

15. “And while he was speaking these words with me, I turned my face to the ground and was stunned.” That is: when I heard that even the chief angels were vexed at the care shown to the people, I was filled with dejection again. I stood bowed down and could not look up [?]

16, 17. “And behold, one in the likeness of a son of man touched my lips, and I opened my mouth and spoke. I said to the one standing before me: My lord, at the sight of you my insides were turned within me, and behold, I have no strength. And how can your servant, my lord, speak with this my lord? I have grown weak; from now on no strength will remain in me, and no breath is left in me.” He saw me full of anguish again, he says, and touched my lips as if with a human hand, and so gave me the power of speech. And I said to him [?]: The mere sight of you has left me bereft of all strength. It has filled my soul with confusion and turmoil and stripped my mind of its former composure. Fear has made me so weak that I cannot even breathe the air as I used to. How, then, will I be able to understand what you say or give a fitting answer? No one should think that the one who appeared was the Master himself because Daniel calls him “lord.” At the end of the vision this same figure, he says, “raised his hands to heaven and swore by the living Lord,” and so gratefully acknowledged his own servitude. Daniel calls him “lord,” then, not as God but as a way of paying him due honor. We too usually use this form of address when speaking to people of higher rank. So the blessed Abraham, seeing the angels as men and speaking to them as to men, said: “I beg you, my lord, if I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant.” And the blessed Rebekah said to the blessed Abraham’s servant: “Drink, my lord, and I will draw water for your camels too.” So here as well “lord” does not mean the God of the universe. We shall see this more clearly from the end; for the present let us follow the sequence of the text. 18, 19. “And again,” he says, “one with the appearance of a man touched me and strengthened me, and said to me: Do not be afraid, man of desires. Peace be with you; be courageous and be strong.” That is: do not be anxious at all, for I have not come to harm you, but to make known to you

…what you desired to learn. So cast off your fear, be brave and be strong.” And the deed followed the word. 20, 21. “And when he spoke with me,” he says, “I was strengthened, and I said: Let my Lord speak, for you have strengthened me. And he said: Do you know why I have come to you? And now I shall return to fight with the prince of the Persians; and I was going out, and the prince of the Greeks was coming. But I will tell you what is written in the Scripture of truth, and there is no one who stands with me in these matters except Michael your prince.” “Why do I mention the two,” he says, “the prince of the Persians and that of the Greeks? Because none of the heavenly powers wants your people to receive any good, clearly on account of their great lawlessness, except Michael alone, who was entrusted with your care.” He has put “to fight” in place of “to argue and persuade,” wishing to show both the other's just indignation against the people and his own goodwill toward the people. It is likely that the one speaking is the holy Gabriel, for he had already interpreted the other revelations to him.

1. “And it came to pass,” he says, “in the first year of Cyrus, I stood up for might and strength.” “As soon as Cyrus became king,” he says, “and the appointed term of the captivity was completed, I rose up [?] and worked to secure release and freedom for the people.” 2. “And now I will declare the truth to you.” “I tell you truly what is to come.” “Behold, three more kings will arise in Persia.” After Cyrus, Cambyses reigned; the Magi succeeded him and reigned for ten months; after them came Darius son of Hystaspes. “And the fourth,” he says, “will grow rich with great riches beyond them all.” He means Xerxes, the son of Darius. “And after he has taken hold of his wealth, he will rise up against all the kingdoms of the Greeks.” Historians and writers outside our faith, sophists and orators too, remember this man and recount both his arrogant expedition and his ridiculous retreat. Then, having taught Persian affairs in summary up to him, and passing over those who reigned after him as having become weaker, he turned his discourse to the Macedonian, and says: 3, 4. “And a mighty king will arise, and he will rule with great dominion and do as he pleases. And when his kingdom has stood, it will be broken and divided to the four winds of heaven.” For when Alexander, as we have already said, had assumed the kingship of practically the whole world, and then

met the common end of mankind, the kingdom was divided four ways, as we have already said many times. And here again the divine archangel spoke thus: “And it will be divided to the four winds of heaven, and not to his posterity, nor according to the dominion with which he ruled.” What he means is this. Alexander reigned twelve years in all, and in the last six years he destroyed both the kingdom of the Persians and that of the Egyptians, and brought all the nations in between under his power. He says, then, that those who reign after him will appear in no way like Alexander, neither in might nor in the authority he acquired in his last years. For this is what he means by “to his posterity, nor according to the dominion with which he ruled.” “For his kingdom will be uprooted and given to others besides these.” “For it will not only be divided among these four,” he says, “but will also be given to others apart from them.” For in their time Arsaces the Persian, having prevailed in war, assumed the kingship and recovered part of the Persian empire; from him down to the present the kings of the Persians are called Arsacids, whereas the earlier ones were called not Arsacids but Achaemenids. And the Romans too, once the Macedonian kingdom had been divided, gained greater strength; indeed they even exacted tribute from these very kings. Having thus foretold the division, he leaves out any mention of two of the kings, for neither the king of Asia nor the king of Macedonia lasted long, and besides, nothing grievous befell the Jews through them. So he mentions only the two through whom the Jews suffered grievous calamities. These are the king of Egypt and the one entrusted with rule over the nations lying to the east; they had their royal seats at Antioch and Babylon. But it is fitting for us first to state the subject of what is to be said, and only then to take up the detailed interpretation. The he-goat that blessed Daniel saw had, after the breaking of its one horn, four horns [?], namely these very kings; and from one of them grew another horn, which waged fierce war on Egypt and surrounded the nation of the Jews with countless calamities. This horn signifies Antiochus Epiphanes. And blessed Daniel saw that the fourth beast had ten horns, and that among the horns a little horn came up, having eyes and a mouth speaking great things, and it made war with the saints. From these again we learn that at the end of the Roman kingdom ten kings will arise at the same time, doing one another much harm and fighting to overthrow one another's kingdoms, just as the Macedonians continually did; and

that while these things are happening, the man of sin will appear, the son of perdition, that is, the Antichrist. Since, then, the end of the Roman kingdom resembles the division of the Macedonian kingdom, blessed Daniel is taught at the same time what will be done by these and by those. For some of what is to be said fits the Macedonians, and some fits the ten horns that are to come and the one that sprouts among them. And that this is so we shall learn from the prophecy itself. It is fitting for us, then, to pay attention with all precision and to distinguish properly what fits the one and what fits the other. We have an example of this in the teaching of the Gospel. For when the Lord said to the apostles about the temple in Jerusalem, “Amen, amen, I say to you, not one stone will be left here upon another that will not be thrown down,” and they then asked, “When will these things be, and what is the sign of your coming?”, they were putting a double question, and the Lord gives his answer mingled together, speaking at once of what was to befall Jerusalem and of what will happen at the time of the consummation. But those initiated into divine things clearly distinguish what fits the one time and what fits the other. This, then, is what we too shall do here, with the appropriate demonstration. So the one conversing with blessed Daniel, having taught him that the kingdom would be divided four ways, leaves aside the two (I mean the king of Macedonia and the king of Asia, or of the Hellespont), since they lasted only a short time and caused the Jews very little grief, and continues: 5. “And the king of the South grew strong, and one of his princes will grow strong against him and will rule a great dominion beyond his own authority.” He means Ptolemy Philopator, who was not content with the kingdom of Egypt but also annexed Phoenicia, Samaria and Judea. By “one of his princes growing strong” he means [?], whom Josephus the Hebrew historian also mentions, who as a most excellent general subjected to Ptolemy many lands lying outside Ptolemy's kingdom. Hinting at this he says, “And he will rule a great dominion beyond his own authority,” that is, he will gain control of many nations lying outside the authority assigned to him. 6. “And after his years they will join together, and the daughter of the king of the South will come to the king of the North to make agreements with him.” After the death of Ptolemy Philopator, his son Ptolemy, called Epiphanes, reigned. This, then, is what he means by “After his years they will join together”; and teaching how they will join together, he says, “The daughter of the king of the South will come to the king

of the North to make agreements with him.” By the king of the North he means Antiochus, not Epiphanes but the one called the Great, the father of Antiochus Epiphanes; for he was the contemporary of those Ptolemies. “And the strength of his arm will not prevail, and his seed will not stand, and she will be handed over, and those who bring her, and the young woman, and the one who strengthens her in those times.” “The marriage will indeed take place,” he says, “but the union will not last long; she will be given back to the one who sent her, through those who had brought her, together with what had been brought with her.” For this is what he means by “and the one who strengthens her in those times”: the wealth that makes the marriage strong and desirable. 7. “And there will arise,” he says, “from the flower of her root [one] upon his preparation.” That is, she will be given back to her father, but she will bear a king who will oppose the kingdom of the one who gave her. “And he will come,” he says, “against the power.” He calls Jerusalem “the power,” since it enjoyed divine grace and displayed the divine power through the miracles that happened from time to time. [?] The third book of Maccabees taught us this too. For Ptolemy, having defeated Antiochus the Great against all hope, came to Jerusalem and offered costly sacrifices to God; but when he tried to enter the inner sanctuary of the temple and refused to yield to the priests who begged him to desist, he was scourged with invisible scourges. Then, having threatened the Jews, he reached Alexandria [?] and set about doing the things that the history relates. This is what the prophecy also foretells: “He will come,” it says, “against the power, and will enter into the supports of the king of the North, and will act among them and prevail.” By “supports” he means the cities that paid him tribute; for the taxes paid in support and prop up the kingdom, as it were, since by them the military force is maintained. 8. “And their gods too, with their molten images, every desirable vessel of theirs, of silver and gold, he will carry off with captives into Egypt, and he himself will stand above the king of the North.” For in the first and second engagements the Ptolemies were victorious, as the histories teach. And Josephus too says this: “For it happened that, while Antiochus the Great was reigning over Asia, the Jews themselves suffered much hardship, their land being ravaged, and so did those who inhabited Coele-Syria. For as he was at war with Ptolemy Philopator and with his son Ptolemy,

surnamed Epiphanes, it befell them to suffer hardship, and to suffer the same whether he was winning or losing.” And a little later: “However, Antiochus, having defeated Ptolemy, annexed Judea. When Philopator died, his son sent out a large force with Scopas as general against those in Coele-Syria; he took many of their cities, and our nation too, for when attacked it went over to him. Not long afterward Antiochus defeated Scopas, engaging him near the sources of the Jordan, and destroyed much of his army. Later, when Antiochus had subdued the cities of Coele-Syria that Scopas had held, and Samaria as well, the Jews went over to him of their own accord, and receiving him into the city, they provided abundant supplies for all his army and his elephants, and eagerly fought alongside him as he besieged the garrison that Scopas had left in the citadel of Jerusalem.” And so as not to lengthen this work beyond measure by recounting the rest as well, I refer whoever wishes to those writings. 9, 10. “And he will enter,” he says, “into the kingdom of the king of the South, and will return to his own land. And his sons will gather a multitude of many forces.” By “his sons” he means those entrusted with the army, just as men are called sons of men and prophets sons of the prophets; for this is an idiom of the Hebrew language. “And he will come on, coming and flooding.” That is, sweeping on with force and destroying everything like a flood. “And he will pass through, and settle down, and engage as far as his stronghold.” That is, using all his might he will rush against Egypt, quickly pitch camp, and carry the war into that country. In response to this:

11, 12. “And the king of the South will be enraged, and will go out and fight with the king of the North, and he will set up a great multitude, and the multitude will be given into his hand. And he will take the great multitude, and his heart will be lifted up, and he will cast down tens of thousands, and he will not prevail.” For when the king of the South is drawn up against him with a great host, Antiochus, he says, will overcome him and take the host into his power, and as victor he will behave arrogantly and shoot down many tens of thousands. Yet he will not prevail over Egypt, nor gain control of Ptolemy's kingdom; and chafing at this, he says: 13. “The king of the North will return and bring a great multitude, greater than the former, and at the end of the times he will come on with an entry in great power and with much substance.” For again, he says, having gathered

an army greater than the former, he will rush against Egypt, and he will do this toward the end of his reign. For this is what is meant by “at the end of the times, and he will come on with an entry in great power.” Here there is a Hebrew doubling, for he meant that he will make a great entry. It is an idiom of both Hebrews and Syrians, for both are accustomed to say “entering he entered,” “going out he went out,” “eating he eats,” and all other such expressions likewise. [?] So the translators, aiming at exactness, followed even the Hebrew idioms. 14. “And in those times,” he says, “many will rise up against the king of the South.” For once Antiochus has thus overcome Ptolemy, even his neighbors will thereafter despise him as weak. “And the sons of the pestilent ones of your people will be lifted up to establish a vision, and they will be lifted up and will be weak.” Here again he has called the lawless “pestilent.” “For those who live in wickedness and depravity of character,” he says, “and who prefer living impiously to piety, will try through these kings to abolish the worship of the Law, and they will not prevail.” For these kings, being less impious, continued to treat the Jewish nation with consideration. 15. “And the king of the North,” he says, “will come and pour out a siege mound and capture fortified cities.” That is, he will use siege, earthworks and engines. “And the arms of the king of the South will not stand”; that is, he will be bereft of all power. “And his chosen ones will rise up, and there will be no strength to stand.” Even gathering his champions, he will gain nothing. 16. “And the one who comes against him will do as he pleases, and there is no one standing before him.” “For from then on,” he says, “it will be easy for anyone to despise him, since he cannot fight back and overcome his opponents.” “And he will stand in the land of Sabeir.” Some copies have “in the land of Sabaeim”; and some of those who have rendered the Hebrew into Greek have called the land of Sabeir “the land of desire.” It signifies the land of promise, which is desirable, and Mount Zion, which God loved and in which he was pleased to dwell. And “Sabaeim” is interpreted “of power.” So whether Judea is called the land of good pleasure or the land of power (for above he called it “power,” and here “Sabaeim” or “Sabeir”), the king of the North, he says, will enter this land too. “And it will be

accomplished by his hand.” That is, he will succeed. For Josephus too has taught us this in his history: that the Jews received Antiochus of their own accord and were greatly honored by him. 17. “And he will set his face,” he says, “to come with the strength of his whole kingdom.” For he will attempt to appropriate the whole kingdom of the king of the South. “And he will do all things uprightly with him,” he says. For he will give back to him everything he had seized. “And he will give him a daughter of women to corrupt her, and she will not remain, and she will not be his.” What he said obscurely above, he says clearly here. “He will give him his own daughter as wife,” he says, “but before long she will be given back to the one who gave her, and the union will be dissolved.” Having thus dealt with Egypt, he says, 18. “he will turn his face to the islands and capture many, and will make rulers cease from their reproach; but his reproach will return to him.” For having brought many of the islands under his power and stopped their rulers from ruling, he made them laughingstocks. “But he himself,” he says, “will reap the fruit of this reproach.” For the Romans defeated him at Thermopylae, put an end to his great audacity, imposed on him a tribute of a thousand talents and compelled him to pay it every year; and they also took his son Antiochus, the one surnamed Epiphanes, as a hostage and kept him under guard in Rome. The first book of Maccabees teaches us this too; for the writer, having spoken of those who received Alexander's kingdom, added: “And there came forth from them a sinful root, Antiochus Epiphanes, son of King Antiochus, who had been a hostage in Rome.” Foretelling this to Daniel, the one conversing with him said, “But his reproach will return to him.” [?]

19. “And he will turn his face to strengthen his land.” “Having done these things in the islands,” he says, “he will return to his own kingdom.” “And he will grow weak, and will fall, and will not be found. (20.) And there will arise from his root a shoot of kingship, passing over onto his preparation.” He means Antiochus Epiphanes, who escaped from Rome and succeeded his brother Seleucus. For Antiochus the Great was succeeded by Seleucus, called Philopator, who was his son; and when Seleucus died, Antiochus Epiphanes took over the kingdom. Of him he says, “There will arise from his root a shoot of kingship, passing over onto his preparation”; that is, imitating his father's power

[?] …despised, and yet able to seize the kingdom prepared by the other. Pointing to this, he added, “And practising the glory of the kingdom,” that is, using his energy to excess. “And in those days they will be crushed, and not face to face, nor in battles.” For he will be able, he says, by his reputation alone, without a fight and without bloodshed, to strike everyone with terror and bring them under his control. [?] He was not held in esteem, although he was a king; he was thought a man of no account, held under guard in Rome. “And he will come in prosperity, and will gain power over a kingdom by slippery means.” Nevertheless, he says, though utterly despised, he will come with great wealth and very great forces, and will take hold of the kingdom with deceit as his accomplice, relying on trickery rather than force. The blessed Daniel saw this in the second vision as well, and heard the holy Gabriel saying, “Deceit is in his hand, and he will be magnified in his heart, and he will destroy many, and will stand for the ruin of many.” And here likewise: “For he will gain power,” he says, “over a kingdom by slippery means.” [22] “And the arms of the one who floods will be swept away before him, and will be crushed.” Here again he hinted at the kingdom of the Egyptians. They too were very powerful, and like a flood destroyed those who resisted them, making them vanish without a trace; yet they too will be swept away by him and crushed. And not they alone, but “yes, and the leader”

[23] “And from the alliances made with him he will practise deceit.” Here he foretells the revolt raised against Onias the high priest by Jesus, also called Jason, and by Onias, also called Menelaus. Of these, Jason came first: he ran to Antiochus and drove his own brother out of the high priesthood. Then Menelaus, who had been sent to bring gifts and gold to Antiochus, transferred the high priesthood to himself in turn and expelled Jason. From then on terrible and grievous disasters overtook the Jewish nation. The blessed Daniel, being taught these things in advance, hears that “the arms of the one who floods will be swept away by him.” He means Ptolemy Philometor, for he succeeded Ptolemy Epiphanes. To this he added, “Yes, and the leader of the covenant.” He means the pious high priest, the brother of Jason, and foretells that he too will be removed from the high priesthood. Then he teaches the manner: “And from the alliances made with him he will practise deceit.” [?] … A γάρ. Omitted in B. B ἡγησάμενος. A συναναμίξεων [?]

For he will use as his agents, he says, men who pride themselves on being of the same race, and with deceit as his accomplice he will inflict countless horrors on the nation. “And he will go up and overpower it with a small nation.” For he deceived the inhabitants of Jerusalem, as though he meant to enter in peace. First he dared to set foot in the inner sanctuary of the divine temple; then he stripped away all its adornment and the vessels consecrated to the divine service, and so departed. Later he marched against the city again and slaughtered eighty thousand people. Not content even with these, he sent his own generals and committed countless further murders. Foretelling this, he says, “And he will overpower it with a small nation.” [24] “And he will come in prosperity and into rich lands.” For he will not arrive with few men out of want, he says, but out of the arrogance of his mind; for he has prosperity and the enjoyment of countless rich nations that pay him heavy tribute. “And he will do what his fathers did not do, nor his fathers' fathers: he will scatter plunder and property and spoils among them.” For whereas all his fathers and all his ancestors honoured the Jewish nation, he will do the very opposite in everything, killing, plundering and enslaving, and giving their possessions as gifts to his fellow soldiers. “And against Egypt,” he says, “he will devise his schemes, and until a time.” That is, not [?]…

[25] “And his strength and his heart will be stirred up against the king of the South with a great army.” This attack of his on Egypt is also recorded in the First Book of Maccabees. “For Antiochus,” it says, “entered Egypt with a heavy force, with chariots and elephants and cavalry and a large fleet, and waged war against Ptolemy king of Egypt. Ptolemy turned back before him and fled, and many fell wounded; and they captured the fortified cities in the land of Egypt and took the spoils of the land of Egypt.” Being taught these things in advance, the blessed Daniel heard: “And the king of the South will join battle with him with a great and exceedingly strong army, and he will not stand, for they will devise schemes against him.” That is, they will use many ambushes of every kind against him. [26] “And they will eat,” he says, “his provisions.” That is, they will consume all his revenue, and will plunder the tribute paid to him and transfer it to themselves. “And they will crush

him, and he will destroy his forces, and many will fall wounded.” For he will destroy like a flood not only him but his army as well, and will make great slaughter. [27] “And both kings,” he says, “their hearts will be set on evil, and at one table they will speak lies, and it will not succeed.” For the Romans, as Josephus the historian tells us, learned of this campaign of his and urged him to withdraw from Egypt. So he made peace, it says, and shared a table with Ptolemy. Showing the treachery hidden in this friendship, the one speaking with Daniel says, “And both kings, their hearts will be set on evil, and at one table they will speak lies, and it will not succeed”; that is, the peace will not be secure. “For the end will yet be at the appointed time.” That is, once this time has run its course, they will clash and draw up for battle again. [28] “And he will return,” he says, “to his land with great wealth.” Nevertheless, he says, he will then return to his own kingdom with great riches and much abundance. “And his heart will be set against the holy covenant.” From then on he will have one single aim: to abolish the law given by God to the Jews. And having planned this, he will also carry his plans through. “For he will act,” he says, “and return to his land.” This too is told in the book of Maccabees and in the history of Josephus. [29] “And at his time he will return and come into the South, and it will not be as the first and the last.” That is, he will not conquer and prevail in the same way, but will return defeated. “At his time” signifies the time suitable for war. [30] “And the Kittim who come in will come against him, and they will be humbled.” For he will take many Cypriots and other islanders with him (Citium is a town of Cyprus to this day) and will launch an attack on Egypt, but he will return defeated and humbled. “And he will return,” he says, “and be enraged against the holy covenant.” For all the anger that his defeat stirs up in him, he says, he will vomit out against the holy covenant. And showing the deed, he says, “And he will act.” For at his second coming he will commit great slaughter and enslave those who escaped. “And he will return and show favour to those who have forsaken the holy covenant.” He will take every care, he says, of those who broke the law, who renounced Judaism and embraced Hellenism. [31] “And arms will rise up from him, and they will profane the sanctuary of power, and

they will remove the perpetual sacrifice, and will set [?] …the second expedition that Antiochus made into Egypt. Then, after saying something in between about the rivalry of the illegitimate high priests, the writer added: “When news of what had happened reached the king, he concluded that Judea was in revolt. So he returned from Egypt, savage in spirit, took the city by storm, and ordered his soldiers to cut down without mercy everyone they met.” Then, having described how the slaughter spared no age and eighty thousand dead were counted, he says again shortly afterwards: “Antiochus, being bitterly hostile to the Jews, sent Apollonius the Mysarch with an army of twenty-two thousand, ordering him to slaughter all those in the prime of life.” And again, shortly afterwards, he says: “Not long after, the king sent an elderly Athenian to compel the Jews to abandon the laws of their fathers and cease to live by the laws of God, and also to pollute the temple in Jerusalem and name it after Olympian Zeus.” Foretelling this, the one speaking with the blessed Daniel said: “And arms will rise up from him, and they will profane the sanctuary of power, and will remove the perpetual sacrifice,” that is, the worship offered to God every day. “And they will set up in it an abomination of desolation”: the altar that the impious king set up to Zeus, on which he offered a pig. [32] “And those who act lawlessly against the covenant,” he says, “they will lead astray by slippery means.” For by using deceitful words they will induce those who live in lawlessness to commit open impiety. “And a people who know their God will prevail and act.” Here he hints at the blessed Mattathias and his companions. Mattathias was the first to resist the decrees of Antiochus, and [?] together with his sons he took the field and defeated that man's generals. [33] “And the wise among the people,” he says, “will understand much.” For those who rightly use the knowledge supplied by God will utterly despise

his laws, and [?] for the sake of the divine law [?] they will enjoy [?] days. That is why he called the respites that occurred in the midst of the wars “a little help.” “And many will join them,” he says, “by slippery means.” For seeing this courage, he says, many of those who had slipped and denied their piety will repent and run to them. [35] “And of those who understand,” he says, “many will grow weak.” That is, some even of those who seemed pious will turn to the opposite course. “To refine them by fire, and to choose them, and to make them white, until the time of the end; for it is yet for a time.” Not even this, he says, will harm the people of times to come, for from it they will learn not to rely on their past good deeds, but always to fear and tremble, according to the exhortation of the blessed Paul: “Let whoever thinks he stands,” he says, “take heed lest he fall.” For changes of fortune act like fire: they test and separate the counterfeit from the genuine. Not only that, but they also whiten, as one whitens wool, and test whether its colour is natural or applied, and whether it is ingrained through and through or lies only on the surface. These things, he says, happen in part in the present life; but in the age to come there will be a universal examination of all people. Having said this about Antiochus Epiphanes, he now passes from the image to the archetype. The archetype of Antiochus is the Antichrist, and the image of the Antichrist is Antiochus. For just as the former compelled the Jews to be impious and to live

[?] …he will accomplish, at one moment trying to deceive and cheat by deceitful wonder-working, at another using force and inflicting every kind of punishment on those raised in piety. If anyone seeks the sequence of the prophecy and does not believe that this is how matters stand, let him consider the teaching of the Gospel. For there too the Lord foretells, in the same passage, things concerning the common end of all things and things concerning the end of Jerusalem. Having said, “Pray that your flight may not be in winter, nor on a Sabbath” (and this applies to the Jews alone), he immediately added, “For there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever will be. And if those days had not been cut short, no flesh would have been saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short.” And showing that none of this concerns the Jews, he added, “Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ,’ or ‘There he is,’ do not believe it.” And having said a few words beforehand about the false christs, he adds, “For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will the coming of the Son of Man be.” And all the rest is similar, so that I need not go through each point. Guided by this, then, we shall understand that the prophecy too passed from Antiochus to the Antichrist, as from image to archetype, and clearly teaches us in advance what concerns him. [36] “For the king,” he says, “will do as he pleases, and will exalt himself and magnify himself above every god, and against the God of gods, and will speak monstrous things, and will prosper.” That is, he will succeed, but not to the end. “Until the wrath is accomplished.” That is, he says, until he has fiercely kindled the divine wrath and drawn it down on himself. He calls punishment “wrath,” for the Divine is free from passion. “For it comes to an end, and in haste,” he says. For he, he says, foreknowing his own end, will act with great haste, calling everyone to impiety and wishing to take many as partners in his punishment. What follows refutes even more clearly the folly of those who think this was said about Antiochus. For he says: [37] “And he will pay no heed to all the gods of his fathers.” But we find that Antiochus filled both Jerusalem and all Judea with idol altars, sacrificed to Zeus in the temple of God, and named the temple in Jerusalem after Olympian Zeus and the one on Gerizim after Zeus Xenios. How then could a man so superstitious, so given to idolatry, “pay no heed to the gods of his fathers”? For Antiochus

did the very opposite throughout: he honoured his ancestral gods and rejected the God worshipped by the Jews. These things, then, in no way fit Antiochus, but the very archetype of Antiochus, of whom Antiochus was the image and type, and who strove to outdo in impiety all the kings who had come before him. So he says of the Antichrist: “He will pay no heed to all the gods of his fathers. And he will pay no heed to the desire of women, or to any god.” This too is directly contrary to the habits of Antiochus. For he was not content even with the women joined to him by the law of marriage, by whom he fathered Antiochus Eupator and Alexander, but also consorted with licentious concubines. The Second Book of Maccabees mentions one of them, and the writer says: “It happened that the people of Tarsus and Mallus revolted, because they had been given as a gift to Antiochis, the king's concubine.” How then could a man so enslaved to licentiousness that he gave cities of such size and importance to a courtesan “pay no heed to the desire of women”? So here too those who try to apply these words to Antiochus are clearly shown to be mistaken. But let us return to where we left off. “And he will pay no heed to the desire of women,” he says, “or to any god, for he will magnify himself above all.” That is, he will think himself the greatest of all. [38] “And in his place he will glorify a god Maozim, and a god whom his fathers did not know he will glorify with silver and gold and precious stone and with costly things.” For whereas all his fathers knew their own nature and did not dare to call themselves the God over all, this man calls himself a strong and mighty God (for that is what “Maozim” means). For “in his place” means that he has set himself there. [39] “And he will act for the strongholds of refuge with a foreign god whom he has acknowledged, and he will increase its glory, and will make many subject to them, and will divide the land as gifts.” For he will set up for himself [?] and adorn them with silver and gold and precious stones, and will make many subject to them, namely those deceived by his wonders or broken by his punishments. And “he will divide the land as gifts”: for to those who obey him and choose impiety he will give a great deal of land. [40] “And at the end of the time,” he says, “the king of the South will lock horns with him, and the king of the North will gather against him with chariots and

with horsemen and with many ships, and he will enter the land in floods and will crush.” We have often said that the ten horns that appeared on the fourth beast signify ten kings who will reign at the same time at the end of the Roman empire. From among these, then, the king of the South will in turn make war on this man, who is called the king of the North. “For out of the north,” he says, “evils will be kindled against all who dwell on the earth.” Antiochus too, who was a type of this man, was called king of the North. So when the king of the South engages him, this man will march against him with a multitude and with fortifications by land and sea, and will carry off the victory. The Lord too foretold these wars in the holy Gospels: “For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and plagues and earthquakes in various places; but all these are the beginning of birth pains.” Since, then, we have the Lord's prediction in agreement with this prophecy, we shall understand what lies before us. “And he will pass through,”

[41] “And he will enter the land of Sabeir.” Again, by Sabeir he indicated Jerusalem. “And many will grow weak.” Clearly he means those who are deceived, or who are broken by the severity of the punishments. “And these will be saved from his hand: Edom and Moab and the chief of the sons of Ammon.” This too does not fit Antiochus; for he subdued these peoples and set governors over them, one of whom was Timothy, leader of the Ammonites. But under this impious one it is likely that these will escape, since they are not zealous in piety; for the impious one surely makes war on the zealous. But if these names must also be understood figuratively, Edom is interpreted as “red.” That is why Esau too was called Edom, because he craved the stew of lentils, which was red; and blood too is red in appearance. So those who are counted worthy of the Lord's blood, and live worthily of this gift, have the grace of the Lord's blood blooming upon them. And “Moab” means “one born of the father.” For this is what Lot's elder daughter, having conceived by her father and then given birth, named the child. So those who are called sons of God, “who were born not of blood, nor of the will of a man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God,” are fittingly named Moab. And “Ammon” signifies “son of the race”; for this is what the divine Scripture teaches. For the blessed Paul, addressing the Athenians, says: “Being then God's offspring, we ought not to think

…that the divine is like gold, or silver, or stone, an image shaped by human art and imagination.” And God himself called the saints his kin: “For my chosen race,” he says, “which I acquired to declare my excellences.” So it is not unlikely that those whom divine grace has made worthy of kinship with God are called Achiman. And he will gain control of the hidden treasures of gold and silver, and of all the desirable things of Egypt, and of the Libyans and the Ethiopians, and of their strongholds.” These things too fit Antiochus least of all. He never ruled Libya or Ethiopia, or even Egypt itself, for the Romans forestalled him and he turned back. So these are what is meant by the three horns that the little horn overthrew. For here too this man will overthrow three very great nations, Egypt, Ethiopia and Libya, held, it seems, by three kings, and will bring them under his power. 44. “And reports and alarms from the east and from the north will trouble him, and he will come in great fury to devote many to destruction and to annihilate them.” This does not fit Antiochus either. It was not rumours that troubled him and made him withdraw from Egypt, but the decree of the Romans, sent from the West, not from the East. Of this man, however, he says that after taking Egypt, Libya and Ethiopia and bringing them under his power, he will be troubled by some report and turn back, and will come in great fury “to devote many to destruction and to annihilate them.” He says the same thing with both terms: to annihilate is to strip of piety, and to devote to destruction is to declare them alien [?]. 45. “There,” he says, “he will pitch his tent in Apadno, between the seas, on the holy mountain Sabeir.” Nor do we find that this happened in the case of Antiochus. If it did, let them say what this place is, lying between the two seas, where Antiochus pitched his tent. But they will not be able to point to it. So none of these things has yet been fulfilled; all of them will be done by the common scourge of mankind. Sabeir, again, is what he calls the land dedicated to God, and Apadno is a certain place called by that name, not far from…

…destruction. “For he will come to his end,” he says, “and there will be no one to rescue him.” For he who dared such deeds, so many of them, and displayed such arrogance, will suddenly receive his punishment, with no one able to free him from it. The blessed Paul also says this clearly: “Whom the Lord will consume with the word of his mouth.” And: “With the Spirit through his lips he will slay the ungodly.”

1. “And at that time,” he says, “Michael will arise, the great prince who stands over the sons of your people.” That is, the archangel entrusted with your care will arise to help those who are then under attack. This will also become clear to those who do not know it from another passage. For through the prophet Malachi God says to the Jews: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the Tishbite before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes, and he will turn the heart of the father to the son, and the heart of a man to his neighbour, lest I come and strike the land utterly.” He teaches us that when the Antichrist dares those deeds, the great Elijah will appear, proclaiming to the Jews the coming of the Lord, and will bring many back [?]. This is what “He will turn the heart of the father to the son” means: that is, he will turn the Jews to those from the gentiles who have believed, for he called the Jews “father.” But he will join the believing Jew to the Church [?]…

[?] “…his neighbour,” teaching that the nature of these and of those is one, but that the knowledge of God was given to the Jews first. Yet they have shown themselves to be last; but once they believe through the preaching of the great Elijah, and are joined to the gentiles who seized the salvation that was sent to them, they will make up one Church. He hints at this here too: that while these things are being done by the Antichrist, the holy archangel Michael will arrange everything so that Elijah comes and announces the Master's coming beforehand, in order that the Jews of that time may obtain salvation. Then, describing the enormity of the evils that impious man will commit, he says: “And there will be a time of tribulation such as has not been since there was a nation on the earth until that time.” The Lord also said this in the holy Gospels: “For there will be tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of the world, nor ever will be; and…

…if those days had not been cut short, no flesh would have been saved; but for the sake of my elect I will cut those days short.” So the prophetic sayings agree with the oracles of the Gospel. To this he adds: “And at that time your people will be saved, everyone who is found written in the book.” That is, those worthy of salvation, who will heed the preaching of Elijah, whom he foreknows from above and from the beginning; for he has called God's knowledge a book. 2. “And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth,” he says, “will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to reproach and everlasting shame.” Let those who try to fit these things to Antiochus tell us who rose in his time, and how some obtained everlasting life while others reaped reproach and everlasting shame. And if they say that this refers to the Maccabees coming out of the caves, they will make themselves even more ridiculous. For the same people will turn out to be both lovers of piety and workers of impiety, since the prophecy says: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, and some to reproach and everlasting shame.” So if they apply these words to the Maccabees, they will be saying that the Maccabees themselves were both wicked and good, or that some of them were good and some bad. But this is not to be found either, for their whole company was pious. Nor does everlasting life in the present life fit them, for all of them were killed and departed this life. So let us leave those old wives' tales and learn from this passage the common resurrection of the dead, and the judgment that follows the resurrection: some of them will inherit everlasting life, while others will be objects of ridicule and reproach forever. He said “many” instead of “all.” For the blessed Paul too put “the many” for “all,” saying: “For if by the trespass of the one the many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound to the many.” 3. “And those who understand,” he says, “will shine like the brightness of the firmament.” The Lord too says in the holy Gospels: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun.” “And some of the many righteous like the stars, forever and ever.” For the most approved and choicest will be likened to the brightness of the firmament and to the very light of the sun; those inferior to them (this is what he signified by “the many”) will imitate the radiance of the stars, giving off this splendour forever. So too the blessed Paul distinguished the ranks of the…

…pious. “For there is one glory of the sun,” he says, “and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.” Having said this, the one conversing with Daniel adds:

4. “And you, Daniel, shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end, until many are taught and knowledge increases.” That is, put the seals of obscurity on the book, and do not make its contents plain to everyone, until knowledge increases and the whole earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas, according to the prophecy. After the appearing of our Saviour, the grace of the divine Spirit removed these seals and made what was obscure clear to believers. 5–6. “And I, Daniel, looked,” he says, “and behold, two others were standing, one on this bank of the river and one on that. And they said to the man clothed in baddim, who was above the water of the river: How long until the end of the wonders you have spoken of, and their cleansing?” That is: I stood silent, not daring to ask, but two others, standing on the banks on either side of the river, asked the one who was clothed in the linen garment and borne upon the surface of the water: How long will these fearful and dreadful things prevail? And when will there be deliverance from them? 7. “And I heard the man clothed in baddim, who was above the water of the river, and he raised his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it would be for a time, and times, and half a time.” From this we have learned precisely that the one speaking then was not the Master himself. For the Master, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, as the divine Apostle says, swore by himself, saying: “As I live, says the Lord.” And the blessed Moses shows him saying: “I will lift up my hand to heaven and swear by my right hand, and say: As I live forever.” But this one, being one of those subject and devoted to the Master, stretched both hands toward heaven and swore by him who lives forever. Daniel says he had hands because this is what he saw. Yet we know that the nature of angels is incorporeal; they shape their appearance for the benefit of those who see them. Often they appear gentler, showing greater condescension, and often more fearsome, making those who see them more earnest. So he swore by him who lives forever that it would be for a time, and times, and half a time. 1 Cor. [?]

This means three and a half years. The holy Gabriel also said this about the horn that makes war with the saints, which will sprout after the ten horns at the end of the Roman empire. For after saying, “He will bring down three kings, and speak words against the Most High, and wear out the saints of the Most High,” he added: “And it will be given into his hand until a time, and times, and half a time.” These are three and a half years. For he called a year a “time,” and we shall learn this more clearly from what follows: “For a time,” he says, “and times, and half a time. When the scattering of the sanctified people is completed, they will know the holy one, and all these things will be completed.” That is, for three and a half years the scattering of the sanctified people will prevail, and all these things will be completed. Then they will know the holy one. Here he hints at the great Elijah, for the great Elijah will appear toward the end of that man's reign and proclaim in advance the second appearing of our Saviour. To this the blessed Daniel adds: 8. “And I heard and did not understand, and I said: Lord, what will be the last of these things?” That is: not understanding what was said about the time, I was compelled to ask, wanting to learn more clearly; and I longed also to be taught what would happen after these things. And he 9–10. “said to me: Go, Daniel, for the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end. Until many are chosen, and made white, and refined by fire; and the lawless will act lawlessly, and none of the ungodly will understand, but the wise will understand.” That is: it is not for nothing that I have spoken these things rather obscurely and placed obscurity on the words like seals. For divine things must not be laid before everyone indiscriminately. The wise will understand through the knowledge supplied to them from above, but those who live in lawlessness and impiety will be unable to understand anything of what is contained here; when the events come, however, they will clearly learn the prophecies about them. Then too the workers of wickedness will be separated from the righteous, for the fiery trial will test everything. The blessed Paul also said this: “For each one's work will become manifest; for the day will disclose it, because it is revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one's is.” And again, on not laying divine things before everyone indiscriminately, the Lord says in the holy Gospels: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine.” But the blessed Daniel, who was holy and a loyal servant of the Master, the divine angel teaches the length of the Antichrist's tyranny, saying:
